questions.question: Money has taken many forms — shells, coins, paper, bank-account entries, Bitcoin. What do all of them depend on to work as money?
options: The material they're made of (metal, paper, electrons) determines their worth
Governments declare them valuable through law
A network of people collectively agrees to accept them
Their value is fixed once a central authority decides on an exchange rate
questions.correct_option_text: A network of people collectively agrees to accept them
questions.explanation: What makes something money is less the object itself than the shared agreement of everyone in the network to accept it. When that agreement breaks (hyperinflation is the classic case), the same notes stop buying anything. The four foundations are: trust, scarcity, utility, and network effects. Bitcoin asks whether all four can be engineered without any single authority — that's the question this course explores.

questions.question: The Cypherpunks believed privacy is a precondition for a free society.
options: True
False
questions.correct_option_text: True
questions.explanation: This is the heart of the movement: without privacy, individuals cannot act freely. Eric Hughes' 1993 manifesto opens on exactly this idea.

questions.question: Their motto 'Cypherpunks write code' meant software, not legislation, would protect privacy.
options: True
False
questions.correct_option_text: True
questions.explanation: They believed working code shipped into the world was more effective than lobbying for laws that could be ignored or reversed.

questions.question: To the Cypherpunks, privacy meant the power to selectively reveal yourself to the world.
options: True
False
questions.correct_option_text: True
questions.explanation: Hughes defined privacy not as secrecy but as control: choosing what to reveal, to whom, and when.

questions.question: Which concept did Adam Back's Hashcash (1997) directly inspire in Bitcoin?
options: Smart contracts
Blind signatures for anonymous payments
Proof-of-work mining
Peer-to-peer networking
questions.correct_option_text: Proof-of-work mining
questions.explanation: Hashcash was a proof-of-work system originally designed to combat email spam. Satoshi Nakamoto adapted this concept as the foundation for Bitcoin's mining and consensus mechanism.

questions.question: Satoshi embedded the newspaper headline "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks" in Bitcoin's Genesis Block. What does that message do?
options: It encrypts the first block so that only Satoshi can spend its reward
It shows the block was not made before that date, and is widely read as a comment on bailouts
It records the UK government's official approval of the Bitcoin network on the day it was launched
It sets the rule that limits the supply to 21 million coins
questions.correct_option_text: It shows the block was not made before that date, and is widely read as a comment on bailouts
questions.explanation: The headline works as a timestamp (the block cannot have been made before 3 January 2009) and is commonly read as a statement of Bitcoin's motivation: money that does not depend on banks or bailouts. It is commentary, not a protocol rule, and it does not by itself prove a single motive.

questions.question: A digital photo can be copied endlessly. Why has digital money traditionally needed a middleman such as a bank?
options: Because only banks own computers powerful enough to process payments
Because digital money must be converted into cash before it can be spent
Because someone has to keep score so the same money isn't spent twice
Because sending money over the internet is illegal without a bank licence
questions.correct_option_text: Because someone has to keep score so the same money isn't spent twice
questions.explanation: This is the double-spending problem: without a referee keeping the record, the same digital dollar could be spent twice. Historically that referee was always an institution — blockchain asks whether it has to be.

questions.question: On a public blockchain such as Bitcoin or Ethereum you are 'pseudonymous, not anonymous'. What does that mean?
options: Your transactions are visible to everyone under your address, but the address doesn't show your legal name
Your transactions are hidden from everyone except the sender and the receiver
Your legal name is stored on the chain, but only miners are able to read it
Nobody can ever work out which address belongs to you, whatever you do
questions.correct_option_text: Your transactions are visible to everyone under your address, but the address doesn't show your legal name
questions.explanation: You act through an address, not your name — but everything that address does is public, forever. Privacy depends on the address not being linked to you, not on hiding the activity.

questions.question: What happens if you change a single character in the input of a SHA-256 hash?
options: Only the last few characters of the hash change
The hash changes slightly, proportional to the edit
The entire hash output changes unpredictably (avalanche effect)
The hash stays the same if the change is small enough
questions.correct_option_text: The entire hash output changes unpredictably (avalanche effect)
questions.explanation: Cryptographic hash functions exhibit the avalanche effect: even a 1-bit change in the input produces a completely different output. This is what makes a hash a reliable fingerprint of data.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'previous hash' field in a block?
options: It encrypts the block's transaction data
It links the block to the one before it, forming the chain
It stores the miner's identity
It determines the block reward amount
questions.correct_option_text: It links the block to the one before it, forming the chain
questions.explanation: Each block stores the hash of the previous block. If anyone tampers with an earlier block, its hash changes — and it no longer matches the fingerprint stored in the next block, so the break is evident.

questions.question: Someone edits the data in an old block. Why is a blockchain called 'tamper-evident' rather than 'tamper-proof'?
options: The edit is physically impossible, because old blocks are locked
The edit is silently undone by the genesis block
The edit goes through only if the block's original miner approves it
The edit is possible, but it visibly breaks the next block's link
questions.correct_option_text: The edit is possible, but it visibly breaks the next block's link
questions.explanation: The chain doesn't stop you changing data — it makes the change obvious: the edited block gets a new hash, and the blocks after it still point to the old one.

questions.question: Google runs on thousands of servers in data centres around the world. Why is it still an example of centralized control?
options: Because its servers are all located in a single country
Because one company can change the rules or switch the service off
Because it runs on fewer computers in total than the Bitcoin network does
Because distributed systems are always centrally controlled
questions.correct_option_text: Because one company can change the rules or switch the service off
questions.explanation: Shape is not control. 'Distributed' describes where the machines sit; 'decentralized' is about who holds the power. Google is distributed but centrally controlled; Bitcoin is distributed and decentralized.

questions.question: On a proof-of-work chain such as Bitcoin, what can an attacker who controls more than half of the mining (hash) power actually do?
options: Read or steal other users' private keys
Rewrite recent history to double-spend their own payments, and censor transactions
Shut down the protocol permanently
Mint unlimited new coins beyond the 21 million cap, or spend coins that belong to other users
questions.correct_option_text: Rewrite recent history to double-spend their own payments, and censor transactions
questions.explanation: A '51% attack' is about hash power, not the number of nodes: running many nodes gives no extra say. A mining majority can build a chain with more work than everyone else's, so it can reverse its own recent payments (a double-spend) and keep other people's transactions out of blocks. It cannot forge signatures, take coins from other addresses or break the supply rules, because every full node still rejects invalid blocks. That is why proof-of-work chains want hash power spread across many independent miners. (Proof-of-stake chains have a similar threshold, measured in stake.)

questions.question: What does a crypto wallet actually hold?
options: The coins themselves, saved as files on your device
A full copy of the blockchain
The private keys that prove you control an address — the coins stay on the chain
Your legal identity, verified by the wallet company
questions.correct_option_text: The private keys that prove you control an address — the coins stay on the chain
questions.explanation: A wallet holds keys, not coins. The coins live on the chain; the wallet uses your private key to sign transactions and prove they come from you.

questions.question: What keeps Bitcoin's supply capped at 21 million?
options: A government regulation limits the supply
The rule is enforced by code: every node rejects blocks that violate it
Satoshi Nakamoto manually controls the issuance
Mining hardware physically cannot produce more
questions.correct_option_text: The rule is enforced by code: every node rejects blocks that violate it
questions.explanation: The 21 million limit is part of Bitcoin's consensus rules. Every full node independently verifies that new blocks follow the supply schedule and rejects any that do not. Changing the cap would require the vast majority of the network to adopt new rules, which holders have every incentive to refuse.

questions.question: Why is a 51% attack on Bitcoin generally considered a bad deal for an attacker who is after profit?
options: Because Bitcoin is protected by government regulations
Because majority hash power is very costly, and success would probably crash the value of the attacker's own coins
Because only 49% of nodes can ever be compromised at once
Because Satoshi Nakamoto still holds a master key that can be used to reverse any malicious transactions afterwards
questions.correct_option_text: Because majority hash power is very costly, and success would probably crash the value of the attacker's own coins
questions.explanation: Majority hash power on Bitcoin would take billions in hardware and electricity, and a visible attack would probably crash the price, destroying the value of the attacker's bitcoin and single-purpose mining machines. For anyone seeking profit, honest mining normally pays better. This is an economic deterrent, not a guarantee: an attacker with outside motives (a large short position, a hostile state) could still try, and smaller proof-of-work chains with little hash power have been 51%-attacked.

questions.question: What was Bitcoin's key insight for solving the Byzantine Generals Problem?
options: Appointing a trusted coordinator node to validate all messages
Encrypting all communications between nodes so traitors can't intercept them
Tying influence to Proof of Work, not identities, so that cheating is costly
Requiring every node to know the identity of every other node
questions.correct_option_text: Tying influence to Proof of Work, not identities, so that cheating is costly
questions.explanation: Bitcoin doesn't try to eliminate dishonest participants — it makes cheating expensive. Influence is weighted by work done, not by identities (which are free to fake), and miners are rewarded only if their blocks end up on the chain the rest of the network accepts. As long as most hash power is honest, an attack costs real energy and hardware and normally pays less than playing by the rules.

questions.question: Which node type performs full validation of the entire blockchain history but then discards old block data to save disk space?
options: SPV / Light Node
Mining Node
Archival full node
Pruned full node
questions.correct_option_text: Pruned full node
questions.explanation: A pruned node is still a full node: it downloads and validates every block from genesis — enforcing all consensus rules — then deletes raw block data older than a configurable threshold. Unlike an SPV node, it doesn't rely on others for validation; unlike an archival full node, it doesn't keep the entire history on disk. Both kinds validate everything; only how much they store differs.

questions.question: Why is the 2013 Cyprus banking crisis often linked to a jump in interest in Bitcoin?
options: The Cypriot government declared Bitcoin legal tender
Savers saw accounts frozen and large deposits partly confiscated, and wanted money no bank could seize
Mining became much cheaper in Cyprus that year because of a sharp fall in the island's electricity prices
The European Union recommended Bitcoin as a safe-haven asset
questions.correct_option_text: Savers saw accounts frozen and large deposits partly confiscated, and wanted money no bank could seize
questions.explanation: Banks closed for nearly two weeks, withdrawals were capped, and uninsured deposits (above €100,000) at Bank of Cyprus took a 47.5% haircut. That made the control question concrete: a bank balance can be frozen or clipped from above. Bitcoin's appeal was censorship resistance and self-custody — no operator to seize funds. (How much of the 2013 rally was Cyprus versus existing momentum is still debated.)

questions.question: Alice holds a single 0.5 BTC coin (a UTXO) and wants to pay Bob 0.4 BTC. Ignoring the miner fee, what happens?
options: The whole 0.5 coin is consumed, creating two new ones: 0.4 for Bob and 0.1 back to Alice as change
The coin's value is lowered from 0.5 to 0.1, and Bob's balance goes up by 0.4
Alice first asks a miner to split her coin into smaller coins, then sends one of them
0.4 goes to Bob and the leftover 0.1 is destroyed
questions.correct_option_text: The whole 0.5 coin is consumed, creating two new ones: 0.4 for Bob and 0.1 back to Alice as change
questions.explanation: Bitcoin works like cash, not a bank balance: a coin is spent whole, and the transaction creates fresh outputs — the payment and the change. Because the old coin is gone, it can't be spent twice.

questions.question: Why is it safe to give your Bitcoin address to anyone who wants to pay you?
options: Because the address changes automatically after every payment
Because the network keeps all addresses hidden from everyone except the miners who process payments
Because an address only works once the receiver enters a password
Because working back from the address to your private key is practically impossible
questions.correct_option_text: Because working back from the address to your private key is practically impossible
questions.explanation: Private key → public key → address is easy to compute forwards and practically impossible to reverse. That asymmetry lets you share the address while the private key stays secret.

questions.question: You hold your own bitcoin (self-custody) and lose your seed phrase and every device with your wallet. What happens to the coins?
options: Bitcoin's support team restores access once you prove your identity
They stay on the chain, but nobody can ever spend them
They are deleted from the blockchain after a waiting period
They are automatically passed on to the miners
questions.correct_option_text: They stay on the chain, but nobody can ever spend them
questions.explanation: There is no password reset and no support line: the seed phrase is the wallet. The coins remain visible on the ledger but are permanently unspendable — as in the landfill hard-drive case.

questions.question: Thousands of powerful new mining machines join the Bitcoin network. How does the network respond?
options: It raises the block reward so that every miner still earns the same
It lets blocks keep arriving faster and faster, so all 21 million coins are issued much sooner
It raises the difficulty at the next adjustment, so blocks return to about every 10 minutes
It blocks the new machines until the existing miners vote to admit them
questions.correct_option_text: It raises the difficulty at the next adjustment, so blocks return to about every 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Every 2,016 blocks (about two weeks) the difficulty retargets to keep blocks roughly 10 minutes apart, however much hash power joins or leaves. Until the next retarget blocks arrive a little faster; after it, the extra miners no longer speed up issuance.

questions.question: Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited: it has no loops and cannot keep general-purpose state. What does that design choice buy?
options: Predictability: every script is guaranteed to finish, leaving far less room for bugs and attacks
Speed: without loops, Bitcoin confirms transactions faster than programmable chains do
Privacy: simple scripts hide the amounts and addresses involved in a payment
Lower fees: with limited scripts, miners do not need to be paid for including transactions
questions.correct_option_text: Predictability: every script is guaranteed to finish, leaving far less room for bugs and attacks
questions.explanation: Simplicity was a security choice: a script that cannot loop always finishes, and fewer features mean a smaller attack surface. Script can still express spending conditions such as multi-signature or time locks, but not arbitrary programs — which is why people who wanted programmable money built Ethereum instead. The limit does not make Bitcoin faster, private or free.

questions.question: What is the fundamental shift that Web3 aims for compared to Web2?
options: Faster internet speeds and better streaming quality
Users, not platforms, hold and control their own digital assets and identity
Free access to all premium content and services
Government control and regulation of all internet content
questions.correct_option_text: Users, not platforms, hold and control their own digital assets and identity
questions.explanation: Web3's promise is to shift ownership from platforms to users: you control your identity and assets with your own keys. How far a given application delivers on that depends on how it is built.

questions.question: Which layer of the Web3 ecosystem contains protocols like Ethereum, Solana, and Arbitrum?
options: The Interface layer (wallets and dApps)
The Application layer (DeFi, NFTs, DAOs)
The Blockchain Layer (L1 / L2)
The Infrastructure layer (nodes and validators)
questions.correct_option_text: The Blockchain Layer (L1 / L2)
questions.explanation: Ethereum and Solana are L1 chains, and Arbitrum is an L2 scaling solution built on Ethereum. They sit between the infrastructure (nodes, validators) and the applications built on them.

questions.question: A smart contract holding funds, with no pause or upgrade function, turns out to have a bug, and someone uses it to take money. What does the 'vending machine' idea tell you?
options: The contract's author can pause it and refund everyone
The code runs exactly as written — bug included — and nobody can simply undo the result
The network spots the bug and refuses to run that part of the code
The contract deletes itself as soon as a bug is used
questions.correct_option_text: The code runs exactly as written — bug included — and nobody can simply undo the result
questions.explanation: A smart contract runs exactly as written, for everyone, and there is no built-in undo. In the 2016 DAO hack about $60M was drained by code doing exactly what it said — which is why audits, and deliberately designed pause switches, matter.

questions.question: Which statement about Ethereum's two kinds of account is correct?
options: A smart contract is controlled by a private key that is held by its author
A wallet account (EOA) contains code that runs automatically
A smart contract runs only when a wallet or another contract calls it
A smart contract can wake itself up at a time it has scheduled
questions.correct_option_text: A smart contract runs only when a wallet or another contract calls it
questions.explanation: Every action starts with a wallet's key; contracts only react. A contract has no key and no clock — if nothing calls it, nothing happens.

questions.question: A flight-delay insurance smart contract must pay out when a flight is late. How does it find out about the delay?
options: An oracle, which you must trust, writes it on-chain
The contract looks up the airline's website by itself
Miners vote on whether the flight was late
The passenger's wallet detects the delay automatically
questions.correct_option_text: An oracle, which you must trust, writes it on-chain
questions.explanation: A contract sees only the chain. Outside facts must be brought in by an oracle — and then the contract is only as trustworthy as that oracle.

questions.question: Why does Ethereum charge a fee (gas) for every step of computation?
options: To pay dividends to the company that owns Ethereum
To convert ETH into dollars before a transaction is recorded
To reward the users who have held their tokens the longest
To pay for the work, and to stop endless loops or spam from jamming the shared network
questions.correct_option_text: To pay for the work, and to stop endless loops or spam from jamming the shared network
questions.explanation: A contract runs on thousands of computers at once. Charging per instruction pays for that work and stops an endless loop or spam from freezing the network for everyone.

questions.question: Which of these would be represented by a unique, non-fungible token (ERC-721) rather than a fungible one (ERC-20)?
options: Loyalty points in an airline programme
Shares in a company
The deed to one specific house
A stablecoin worth one dollar
questions.correct_option_text: The deed to one specific house
questions.explanation: If any unit can be swapped for any other, it is fungible — you count them. A deed refers to one specific house, so it is one of a kind — you name it.

questions.question: Bitcoin's miners spend a large electricity bill on every block. According to this section, what is a business that relies on Bitcoin really paying them for?
options: Speed — the more energy miners spend, the faster payments are processed.
Customer service — miners can be asked to reverse a payment that was sent by mistake.
Security — the cost of adding blocks makes rewriting the payment history prohibitively expensive.
Storage — miners keep users' private keys safe on their machines.
questions.correct_option_text: Security — the cost of adding blocks makes rewriting the payment history prohibitively expensive.
questions.explanation: Proof of Work is a cost, not a puzzle: you are not paying miners to process payments, you are paying them to make rewriting history unaffordable in practice. That buys finality without a referee — nobody can be asked to reverse a payment, and every block added on top makes a reversal harder — and it costs slow blocks, limited throughput and a large energy bill.

questions.question: You send a Bitcoin payment with a valid signature and a very low fee. Hours later it is still unconfirmed, while payments sent after yours have gone through. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It is waiting in the mempool, a queue that miners rank by fee (per byte).
The nodes rejected it at the relay check, so it has to be signed again.
It is already in a block; Bitcoin simply hides a payment until it has six confirmations.
Your wallet is still solving the Proof-of-Work puzzle for it.
questions.correct_option_text: It is waiting in the mempool, a queue that miners rank by fee (per byte).
questions.explanation: A valid transaction waits in the mempool, a queue ranked by the fee it offers for the space it takes: higher fee rate, sooner pick. The wait can be seconds or hours. Invalid transactions never get that far — nodes stop them at the relay check — and it is miners, not wallets, who do the Proof of Work. Confirmations only start counting once a miner has put the transaction in a block.

questions.question: A payments app needs 5,000 transactions per second. Which corner of the trilemma does Bitcoin give you least of — and what does that imply?
options: Security — Bitcoin's small blocks make it easy to attack, so the app should pick a chain with more validators.
Scalability — Bitcoin's base layer handles single-digit tx/s, so the app needs a Layer 2 or a different platform.
Decentralization — Bitcoin is run by a handful of mining pools, so the app should move to a consortium chain instead.
None — difficulty adjustment speeds blocks up when demand rises, so 5,000 tx/s is reachable on the base layer.
questions.correct_option_text: Scalability — Bitcoin's base layer handles single-digit tx/s, so the app needs a Layer 2 or a different platform.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin chose security and decentralization and paid with throughput: roughly 7 transactions per second on the base layer and 10-minute blocks. That is a design choice, not a bug. A high-volume app either moves payments off-chain into Lightning channels and settles on Bitcoin, or picks a platform that made a different trade — Ethereum rollups, or a permissioned chain when the participants are known. Difficulty adjustment only keeps blocks near 10 minutes; it never makes them faster.

questions.question: Alice and Bob open a Lightning channel, pay each other 500 times over a month, then close it. How many of those transactions does the Bitcoin blockchain record?
options: 502 — the opening, the closing and every payment in between.
2 — only the opening and the closing; the 500 payments happen off-chain.
500 — every payment is recorded, just with a lower fee.
None — Lightning is a separate blockchain with its own miners.
questions.correct_option_text: 2 — only the opening and the closing; the 500 payments happen off-chain.
questions.explanation: The channel is a 2-of-2 vault on Bitcoin. Each payment inside it is just a signed agreement on how to split the vault, so the blockchain only ever sees two transactions: open and close. That is how Lightning makes everyday payments instant and almost free while Bitcoin is used only to open and settle.

questions.question: A startup tells investors: "Our app runs on a Bitcoin sidechain, so it is exactly as secure as Bitcoin itself." Going by this section, what is wrong with that claim?
options: Nothing — every Bitcoin full node validates the sidechain's transactions too.
Sidechains are actually safer than Bitcoin itself, because far fewer parties have to agree on each block.
Bitcoin has no sidechains; Lightning is the only thing built around it.
A sidechain is a separate chain with its own trust model; it does not inherit Bitcoin's security.
questions.correct_option_text: A sidechain is a separate chain with its own trust model; it does not inherit Bitcoin's security.
questions.explanation: Liquid and Rootstock are separate programmable chains pegged to BTC. Each has its own trust model — a federation (Liquid), or merge-mining with a federated peg (Rootstock) — and neither inherits Bitcoin's security. Other 'Bitcoin layers' such as Stacks differ again. Bitcoin's base layer stays deliberately simple; everything built around it brings its own trust model.

questions.question: Which of these is Bitcoin actually the right tool for?
options: A retail loyalty-points programme run by one supermarket chain.
A fixed-supply reserve asset with no issuer, for a long-term holder who accepts price swings.
An in-game economy with thousands of micro-trades per minute.
Private, confidential invoices exchanged between four B2B partners who already know each other.
questions.correct_option_text: A fixed-supply reserve asset with no issuer, for a long-term holder who accepts price swings.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin fits where neutrality and scarcity matter more than features: a fixed supply, no issuer, and a security budget that makes rewriting history extremely expensive — the case for holding it as a long-term reserve, although the holder still carries price volatility and custody risk. Loyalty points have one trusted issuer who must be able to change the rules — a database. A game economy needs fast, cheap, programmable trades — a smart-contract platform. Private B2B invoices need confidentiality between known parties — a permissioned chain (Section 3).

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Three investors want a return on ETH. Ana locks 32 ETH on her own machine. Bruno deposits 5 ETH into Lido and receives stETH. A pension fund buys shares of a spot ETH ETF. Who is actually running a validator?
options: All three. Any product that follows the ETH price counts as staking on the network.
Ana and the pension fund. Both hold more than 32 ETH of exposure, which is the threshold for validating.
Only Ana. Bruno's ETH is staked for him by the pool's validators and he keeps a tradable receipt; the fund holds off-chain shares.
Only Bruno. Liquid staking pools replaced solo validators after the Merge.
questions.correct_option_text: Only Ana. Bruno's ETH is staked for him by the pool's validators and he keeps a tradable receipt; the fund holds off-chain shares.
questions.explanation: Ana does the whole job herself: 32 ETH, a machine online, the slashing risk. Bruno is inside the loop indirectly: Lido's operators validate with the pooled ETH, and stETH is his claim on it, still usable elsewhere in DeFi. The pension fund owns shares in a brokerage account while a custodian holds the ETH. Even when a fund stakes, the shareholder has no keys, no validator and nothing to use on-chain.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: An EIP-1559 transaction sets maxFeePerGas = 30 Gwei and maxPriorityFeePerGas = 2 Gwei. The current base fee is 25 Gwei. What does the sender actually pay per gas, and where does each part go?
options: 30 Gwei per gas, all of which is paid to the validator who includes the transaction.
25 Gwei base fee (burned) + 2 Gwei tip (paid to the validator) = 27 Gwei per gas.
25 Gwei base fee paid to the validator + 2 Gwei priority fee burned. Total 27 Gwei per gas.
30 Gwei (max fee) + 2 Gwei (priority fee) = 32 Gwei per gas, paid entirely to the validator.
questions.correct_option_text: 25 Gwei base fee (burned) + 2 Gwei tip (paid to the validator) = 27 Gwei per gas.
questions.explanation: The base fee (25 Gwei) is burned. The tip (2 Gwei) goes to the validator. Effective price is min(maxFeePerGas, baseFee + tip) = min(30, 27) = 27 Gwei per gas; the unused 3 Gwei is never charged. maxFeePerGas is a cap, not a target.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A scaling chain posts a valid proof for every batch to Ethereum, but keeps the transaction data on its own servers (a design known as a validium). One day the operator goes offline and nobody else has a copy of the data. What happens to users' funds?
options: They are frozen: without the data, nobody can show what their own balance is.
Nothing changes. A valid proof is all Ethereum needs to pay each user out.
Ethereum's validators rebuild the missing data from the proofs and reopen withdrawals.
The funds are burned, the same way a cheating validator is slashed.
questions.correct_option_text: They are frozen: without the data, nobody can show what their own balance is.
questions.explanation: A proof shows the batch followed the rules; it does not contain the transactions. To leave without the operator, a user must prove their balance to the contract on Ethereum, and that takes the data. This is why true rollups publish their data on Ethereum (in blobs since 2024), and why designs that keep data off-chain (validiums) are cheaper but add someone you have to trust to keep the data available.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A lending smart contract on Ethereum holds millions of dollars in ETH. Can the contract decide, by itself, to send a payment at midnight?
options: Yes — a contract has its own private key and signs its own transactions whenever its code tells it to.
No — a contract only reacts: a wallet (EOA) must sign and send a transaction that triggers it.
Yes, provided it holds enough ETH to pay its own gas.
No — contracts cannot hold a balance, so there would be nothing to send.
questions.correct_option_text: No — a contract only reacts: a wallet (EOA) must sign and send a transaction that triggers it.
questions.explanation: Only externally owned accounts — wallets controlled by a private key — can start a transaction. A contract account has code, storage and an ETH balance but no key: it runs only when it is called, and the wallet that triggered the call pays the gas. Every change on Ethereum starts as a signed message from a wallet.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: You call a smart contract, but the gas you allowed runs out halfway through the execution. What happens?
options: The half that was executed stays in place, and you are refunded for the rest.
The validator finishes the job at its own expense so that the block stays valid.
The transaction is cancelled and the whole fee is returned, as if nothing had happened.
The transaction reverts — its changes are undone — but you still pay for the gas already used.
questions.correct_option_text: The transaction reverts — its changes are undone — but you still pay for the gas already used.
questions.explanation: Gas prices every step of computation and guarantees that every program stops. When it runs out mid-execution the transaction reverts, yet you still pay for the gas already used. That is the price of letting a Turing-complete machine run on thousands of computers without ever getting stuck in an endless loop.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Withdrawing from an optimistic rollup back to Ethereum through its official bridge typically takes about 7 days; from a ZK rollup it typically takes hours. Why the difference?
options: Optimistic rollups leave a ~7-day fraud-proof window; ZK rollups prove each batch valid up front.
Optimistic rollups post their data to Ethereum only once a week; ZK rollups post every few hours.
ZK rollups keep transactions secret, so Ethereum has nothing to check and releases funds sooner.
Optimistic rollups run on Proof of Work and need more confirmations; ZK rollups run on Proof of Stake.
questions.correct_option_text: Optimistic rollups leave a ~7-day fraud-proof window; ZK rollups prove each batch valid up front.
questions.explanation: Both batch transactions off-chain and settle on Ethereum; they differ in how L1 checks the batch. Optimistic is "innocent until proven guilty": trusted by default, so withdrawals wait out the challenge window. ZK is "prove it up front": Ethereum verifies the maths and no challenge is needed. And "ZK" here buys cheap checking, not secrecy — a standard ZK rollup is as public as Ethereum itself.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: TerraUSD (UST) lost its dollar peg in May 2022 and erased roughly $40 billion in market value. Which kind of stablecoin was it, and what went wrong?
options: Fiat-backed: the bank holding its dollar reserves failed.
Crypto-backed: the ETH locked as collateral fell faster than positions could be liquidated.
Algorithmic: a mint-and-burn peg without full reserves spiralled once confidence broke.
Crypto-backed: a bug in its contract let attackers mint tokens for free.
questions.correct_option_text: Algorithmic: a mint-and-burn peg without full reserves spiralled once confidence broke.
questions.explanation: A stablecoin is only as stable as what backs it. Fiat-backed coins hold dollars and T-bills 1:1 and can lose their peg when reserves are stuck, for example at a failed bank (USDC hit $0.87 in March 2023). Crypto-backed coins lock more collateral than they mint and break when a crash outruns the liquidators. Algorithmic coins hold little or no collateral, so when confidence breaks the peg spirals — no large, purely algorithmic stablecoin has so far held its peg through a crisis.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: ETH has no hard cap, yet at times its total supply actually shrinks. What makes that happen?
options: A halving cuts the validators' reward every four years, as on Bitcoin.
Base fees are burned (EIP-1559); with enough activity, more ETH is burned than is issued.
Validators are slashed more often when the network is busy, and their stakes are destroyed.
The protocol stops issuing new ETH whenever supply rises above 120 million.
questions.correct_option_text: Base fees are burned (EIP-1559); with enough activity, more ETH is burned than is issued.
questions.explanation: Ethereum's supply is what the protocol issues to validators minus what it burns. The Merge cut issuance by about 88%, and EIP-1559 destroys the base fee of every transaction. Quiet network: issuance beats the burn and supply drifts up. Busy enough network: the burn beats issuance and supply shrinks. Bitcoin sells scarcity by rule (21M cap, halvings); Ethereum sells scarcity by usage.

questions.question: PharmaA, PharmaB and a Hospital are on the same Fabric network. PharmaA and PharmaB want to share pricing data that the Hospital must NOT see. Which Fabric feature makes this possible?
options: Pluggable consensus: the two pharma companies run a separate Raft ordering service that excludes the Hospital.
A separate MSP: the Hospital is issued a different type of certificate that limits what it can read.
A private channel: only PharmaA and PharmaB are members, so the Hospital sees none of its transactions or data.
Zero-knowledge proofs: the two pharma companies submit proofs instead of raw data, hiding prices from the Hospital.
questions.correct_option_text: A private channel: only PharmaA and PharmaB are members, so the Hospital sees none of its transactions or data.
questions.explanation: Channels are Fabric's main privacy mechanism (private data collections are a finer-grained option inside a channel). A channel is a private ledger with its own members, chaincode and transaction history; organisations outside it hold no copy and see nothing. The MSP answers "who are you?", not "what may you read?", and the ordering service only sequences transactions. Compare a transparent public chain, where every participant can see every transaction.

questions.question: The world's largest shipping line builds a Fabric network to track containers and invites its rivals to join. The software works well and ports sign up, but the network closes after four years. Going by this section's case studies, what is the most likely reason?
options: Too few rival carriers were willing to commit their data to a network owned and branded by a competitor, so it never reached critical mass.
Fabric could not process the volume: global shipping generates more events than a permissioned chain can order.
Without a native token there was no way to pay the organisations running the nodes.
Channels exposed each carrier's prices to the others, and the members left when they found out.
questions.correct_option_text: Too few rival carriers were willing to commit their data to a network owned and branded by a competitor, so it never reached critical mass.
questions.explanation: This is the TradeLens story (Maersk + IBM; launched 2018, closure announced November 2022, offline in early 2023). The technology worked and handled hundreds of millions of events a year; channels kept commercial data private; and a consortium pays for its nodes like any shared IT, so no token is needed. What failed was governance: competitors are reluctant to commit to a ledger that a rival controls, and although some large carriers signed up, it never reached industry-wide coverage. Networks that last have a convener everyone accepts — a dominant buyer such as Walmart, or a public body such as the EU for EBSI.

questions.question: A supply-chain channel has three organisations: Producer, Distributor and Retailer. The endorsement policy for a delivery record is "Producer AND Distributor". The Retailer submits a delivery update. What must happen for it to be accepted as a valid update to the ledger?
options: The Retailer's own peer endorses it; the organisation that submits a transaction can always approve it.
All three organisations must endorse it, because Fabric requires unanimity among channel members.
The ordering service endorses it on behalf of the others once a majority of orderer nodes agree.
A Producer peer and a Distributor peer must both sign it; the Retailer's own signature does not count towards the policy.
questions.correct_option_text: A Producer peer and a Distributor peer must both sign it; the Retailer's own signature does not count towards the policy.
questions.explanation: The endorsement policy is the business rule, and it applies no matter who submits. The Retailer's application sends the proposal to Producer and Distributor peers, collects their signed results, and only then passes the transaction to the ordering service. Orderers sequence transactions; they never endorse. Every peer then re-checks the signatures against the policy before committing: a transaction that falls short is still recorded in the block, but flagged invalid and has no effect.

questions.question: In a Fabric network, what is the ordering service's job?
options: It runs the chaincode and decides whether each transaction makes business sense.
It puts endorsed transactions into one agreed order and cuts them into blocks.
It issues the certificates that identify each organisation's people, apps and nodes.
It holds the single master copy of the ledger that every organisation reads from.
questions.correct_option_text: It puts endorsed transactions into one agreed order and cuts them into blocks.
questions.explanation: Fabric splits the validator's job in two. Endorsing peers simulate the chaincode and sign; the ordering service only sequences — like a registry clerk stamping each filing with a number: order, not content. Certificates come from each organisation's certificate authority (MSP), and there is no master copy: every organisation's peer keeps its own copy of the ledger and re-checks every block.

questions.question: A retailer traces lettuce from farm to store on Fabric so that food safety can be proven. Which of these most clearly belongs on the shared ledger?
options: The price per kilo the farmer negotiated with the processing plant.
The shelf price the supermarket sets in its own tills.
The draft delivery schedule the distributor keeps for its own planning in its internal ERP system.
The temperature readings logged in the refrigerated truck during transport.
questions.correct_option_text: The temperature readings logged in the refrigerated truck during transport.
questions.explanation: Put on chain the shared facts that others must be able to verify: cold-chain readings are food-safety evidence, and tampering with them could conceal contamination. Prices, margins and internal records stay off chain — they are competitive or purely internal information that needs no multi-party verification.

questions.question: A consortium's ordering nodes will be run by rival banks that do not fully trust one another. Which ordering choice does this section point to, and at what cost?
options: BFT ordering (SmartBFT): it also tolerates a dishonest orderer, at the cost of more orderers and lower speed.
Raft: it tolerates dishonest orderers as well as crashed ones, at no extra cost.
Proof of Work: when the operators are competitors, only mining keeps them honest.
No ordering service at all: each bank orders the transactions on its own channel.
questions.correct_option_text: BFT ordering (SmartBFT): it also tolerates a dishonest orderer, at the cost of more orderers and lower speed.
questions.explanation: Consensus follows governance. Raft, the default, survives crashed nodes and suits operators who trust each other. BFT also survives dishonest ones, so it fits competitors — but it needs more orderers and runs slower. Either way there is no mining and no staking.

questions.question: Public chains charge a fee on every transaction, partly to stop spam. Fabric has no gas and no token. Why can it do without them?
options: Fees still exist, but they are settled in ETH behind the scenes.
The ordering nodes are paid in newly created Fabric coins instead.
Every member is a vetted, identified organisation, so spam is deterred by accountability, not fees.
Fabric transactions only record data and involve no computation, so there is nothing for anyone to pay for.
questions.correct_option_text: Every member is a vetted, identified organisation, so spam is deterred by accountability, not fees.
questions.explanation: On a public chain anyone can submit transactions, so a fee is what keeps the chain from being flooded. In a permissioned network every participant holds a certificate and is legally accountable, so a member that floods the network can be identified and dealt with, and a fee is not needed as the deterrent. The cost does not disappear: the consortium runs and pays for the nodes — predictable, with no crypto exposure.

questions.question: Which of these projects is a poor fit for a permissioned chain like Fabric?
options: Five known suppliers and a retailer sharing delivery records while keeping prices between each pair.
A neutral digital currency that no group of companies should be able to freeze, reverse or shut down.
Hospitals and insurers sharing claims under health-data rules, with the regulator on the network.
Universities issuing diplomas that employers in other countries can verify, convened by a public body.
questions.correct_option_text: A neutral digital currency that no group of companies should be able to freeze, reverse or shut down.
questions.explanation: A consortium can remove members, agree to correct entries and change the rules — good for compliance, fatal for neutrality. Fabric fits known, regulated partners who share selectively; open participation, or a neutral asset that must outlive the consortium, points to a public chain.

questions.question: You send 1 ETH through a lock-and-mint bridge and receive 1 wETH on another chain. A month later hackers empty the bridge's vault. What are you holding now?
options: 1 ETH — the bridge moved your coin across, so it is safe on the new chain.
1 wETH that the new chain's validators must replace, because they approved the mint.
1 wETH that is a claim on an empty vault — a ticket with nothing behind it.
Nothing at all — wrapped tokens are deleted automatically when a vault is drained.
questions.correct_option_text: 1 wETH that is a claim on an empty vault — a ticket with nothing behind it.
questions.explanation: A bridge never moves a coin. Your 1 ETH stayed in the vault on the first chain, and the wETH was only a claim ticket on it. Once the vault is empty the ticket is still in your wallet, but nothing backs it, so its price collapses — unless someone refills the vault, as Wormhole's backer did with $320M in 2022. That is why one shared vault guarded by a few keys makes bridges the biggest target in crypto, and why IBC and Layer 0 designs try to remove the middleman.

questions.question: Every Bitcoin node and every Ethereum node is connected to the same internet. Why can an Ethereum app still not simply use a bitcoin?
options: Each chain's nodes accept only what they can re-check themselves, and a bitcoin exists only in Bitcoin's ledger.
Bitcoin encrypts its ledger, so nobody outside the network can read it.
Regulators in most countries require each blockchain to be kept legally and technically separate from all the others.
It could, but Ethereum's validators charge a fee that makes it uneconomic.
questions.correct_option_text: Each chain's nodes accept only what they can re-check themselves, and a bitcoin exists only in Bitcoin's ledger.
questions.explanation: Being on the internet is not being interoperable. Each chain has its own validators, its own rules and its own ledger, and a blockchain is trusted because every node re-checks everything itself. Ethereum's nodes do not track Bitcoin's ledger, so by default they simply cannot see what happens there — the same wall as the oracle problem. To use a bitcoin's value elsewhere you need an explicit bridging mechanism: typically someone holds the real coin and issues a stand-in.

questions.question: Two Cosmos chains exchange tokens over IBC. Who are you trusting?
options: A company that holds the tokens in a vault while they are in transit.
A committee of signers — say 5 of 9 — who approve each transfer before the tokens are released.
The maths and the two chains' own validators: each chain checks the other's proofs itself.
One shared validator set that secures both chains at once.
questions.correct_option_text: The maths and the two chains' own validators: each chain checks the other's proofs itself.
questions.explanation: Three routes, one question: who do you trust? A bridge: an operator, a company or a few signers. A Layer 0: one shared validator set. IBC: no middleman — each chain keeps a light client of the other and checks every proof itself. Its limits: it is only as strong as the weaker of the two chains, and both must speak IBC.

questions.question: The Ronin bridge was guarded by 9 signer keys. In 2022 attackers stole 5 of them and took $625 million. Why were 5 keys enough to take everything?
options: Each key unlocked one user's account, and those five accounts held most of the money.
With 5 keys the attackers could rewrite Ethereum's transaction history.
The keys let them create new ETH on Ethereum out of nothing.
The bridge released funds whenever 5 of the 9 signers approved, and every user's coins sat in the same vault.
questions.correct_option_text: The bridge released funds whenever 5 of the 9 signers approved, and every user's coins sat in the same vault.
questions.explanation: A bridge puts everyone's coins in one vault and lets a few keys open it. Five of nine signatures were enough to approve any withdrawal, so the whole vault opened at once — not just one account. That is why bridges are structurally risky, and why the usual advice is to check who holds the keys, prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge where there is one, and move only what you need.

questions.question: A team is launching a new chain. It wants to be secure from day one without recruiting its own validators. Which option fits, and what does it give up?
options: Launch as a fully sovereign chain: sovereign chains get their security for free.
Rent security from a Layer 0 (for example as a Polkadot parachain), but follow its rules and pay for that security.
Connect through LayerZero, the Layer 0 that lends its validators to new chains.
Open a lock-and-mint bridge to Ethereum: a bridge passes Ethereum's security on to the new chain, with nothing given up.
questions.correct_option_text: Rent security from a Layer 0 (for example as a Polkadot parachain), but follow its rules and pay for that security.
questions.explanation: Shared security or full sovereignty: you rent one or build the other. Renting from a Layer 0 means inheriting its validators on day one, with messaging built in, in exchange for following its rules and paying it. A sovereign chain keeps full control but must recruit and pay its own validators. And despite the name, LayerZero is not a Layer 0: it is a messaging protocol, closer to a bridge.

questions.question: How does the XRP Ledger agree on which transactions are final?
options: Known validators vote: when 80% of the validators a node trusts agree, the ledger closes.
Miners race to solve a puzzle, as on Bitcoin, only with much smaller blocks.
Validators lock up XRP as a stake and are drawn at random to propose blocks, as on Ethereum.
A single company server approves each payment and publishes the result.
questions.correct_option_text: Known validators vote: when 80% of the validators a node trusts agree, the ledger closes.
questions.explanation: XRPL agrees by a vote among known validators: they propose, vote in rounds, and at 80% agreement the ledger is final — no rewards, no mining. Below 80% the network pauses rather than splits. The trade-off: most nodes use the default published list of validators, so you trust that list not to collude — a different bet from proof of work or proof of stake.

questions.question: In the course's layer model, which line describes the division of labour between the layers correctly?
options: L0 adds cheap scale, L1 connects chains to each other, L2 secures and settles.
L2 secures and settles, L1 adds cheap scale on top of it, L0 stores the data.
L1 secures and settles, L2 adds cheap scale on top of it, L0 lets many chains share security and talk to each other.
L1 secures and settles, L0 adds cheap scale on top of it, L2 lets many chains share security.
questions.correct_option_text: L1 secures and settles, L2 adds cheap scale on top of it, L0 lets many chains share security and talk to each other.
questions.explanation: Layers are a division of labour. An L1 such as Bitcoin or Ethereum secures and settles. L2s — Lightning, rollups — stack on an L1 for speed and low fees and settle their results on it. A Layer 0 such as Polkadot sits underneath and gives the chains plugged into it shared security and messaging. Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana have no Layer 0 underneath: they secure themselves.

questions.question: Three rival freight companies and their insurer want one shared rule: pay compensation automatically when a shipment arrives late. What is the strongest reason to run that rule as a smart contract instead of in one company's database?
options: It is cheaper and faster to run than a database.
No single company has to be trusted to run the rule, and none of them can quietly change it.
The code automatically counts as a legally binding contract between them.
It can use judgement to treat unusual cases fairly.
questions.correct_option_text: No single company has to be trusted to run the rule, and none of them can quietly change it.
questions.explanation: Rivals will not accept a rule that sits in one competitor's database, because its owner could change it. A smart contract gives them one rule that no single party controls. The other answers are the hype: a database is cheaper and faster, code is not a legal contract by itself, and a smart contract has no judgement, so it runs exactly what was written.

questions.question: A supermarket chain wants to move its loyalty points "onto the blockchain". Points are earned and spent only in its own stores. What is the best advice?
options: Go ahead: a smart contract would make the points cheaper to run.
Do not: a smart contract cannot keep track of balances.
Do not: one company issues and controls the points, so its own database does the same job for less.
Go ahead: customers would then own points the chain could never cancel.
questions.correct_option_text: Do not: one company issues and controls the points, so its own database does the same job for less.
questions.explanation: A smart contract pays off when several parties need a rule that none of them controls. Here one trusted company issues, prices and redeems the points, so there is no one else to convince and a database is cheaper. The other answers fail on the facts: every on-chain step costs a network fee, contracts track balances perfectly well (that is what tokens are), and points spent only in the chain's own stores are worth whatever the chain decides to honour.

questions.question: The conditions written into a deployed smart contract are finally met. What actually makes its code run?
options: A timer inside the contract that checks its conditions at set intervals
A transaction that someone sends, calling one of its functions
The contract itself: it executes automatically the moment the conditions are met
A validator who notices that the conditions are met and triggers it
questions.correct_option_text: A transaction that someone sends, calling one of its functions
questions.explanation: A contract never acts on its own: it has no timer and cannot watch the world. It sits idle until a signed transaction calls one of its functions, directly or through another contract. Only then does it run its checks, update state and emit events, all within that one transaction.

questions.question: In the escrow walkthrough, the contract's rule is that only the buyer may pay in. A stranger (not the buyer) calls deposit() with 2 ETH. What happens?
options: The contract keeps the 2 ETH but leaves the deal marked Unpaid
The transaction reverts, nothing changes, and the stranger's gas is refunded
The transaction reverts, nothing changes, and the stranger still pays for the gas used
The transaction stays pending until the real buyer approves it
questions.correct_option_text: The transaction reverts, nothing changes, and the stranger still pays for the gas used
questions.explanation: The contract checks its rules (here: is the caller the buyer?) before anything moves. A failed check reverts the whole transaction: balances, status and events stay exactly as they were, and the 2 ETH never leaves the stranger's wallet. The nodes still did the work of running it, so the gas already used is not refunded.

questions.question: A crop-insurance smart contract must pay out when rainfall is below 10 mm. Why can't the contract simply call a weather API itself?
options: Every node re-runs the contract, and a live API could answer each node differently
Calling an API would cost more gas than most contracts can afford
Weather data is too large to fit inside a block
It can, but only through the short list of APIs that the validators have approved in advance
questions.correct_option_text: Every node re-runs the contract, and a live API could answer each node differently
questions.explanation: Contract code runs in a sealed virtual machine on thousands of nodes, and all of them must reach the same result. A live API could answer each node differently, so outside calls are simply not available. An oracle solves this by writing the data on-chain in a transaction; from then on every node reads the same stored value.

questions.question: A lending protocol values collateral using the live price from one small trading pool. An attacker pushes that price up 4× for a few seconds and borrows against the inflated collateral. What was the root weakness?
options: A bug in the lending contract's code miscalculated the loan
Flash loans make it possible to borrow without collateral
The validators failed to spot and reject the fake price
The contract trusted a single price source that was cheap to manipulate
questions.correct_option_text: The contract trusted a single price source that was cheap to manipulate
questions.explanation: The lending contract ran exactly as written, and validators only check that the rules were followed, not that a price is fair. The weakness was the oracle design: one small pool is cheap to move, even for a few seconds. Flash loans merely make the attack cheaper to fund. Safer feeds combine many markets and average over time.

questions.question: TerraUSD (UST) collapsed in May 2022, wiping out roughly $40 billion in market value. What was the root cause?
options: The bank holding its dollar reserves failed, so the tokens could no longer be redeemed for $1.
Its peg rested on a volatile sister token (LUNA), not on redeemable reserves, so lost confidence fed a death spiral.
A bug in its smart contract let an attacker mint unlimited tokens and sell them on the open market, crashing the price.
Regulators froze the issuer's accounts, which stopped all trading and broke the peg overnight.
questions.correct_option_text: Its peg rested on a volatile sister token (LUNA), not on redeemable reserves, so lost confidence fed a death spiral.
questions.explanation: UST was an algorithmic stablecoin: the peg was held by swapping UST for LUNA, a volatile token from the same project, rather than by dollars or surplus collateral that holders could redeem. When confidence dropped, holders sold UST, LUNA was minted and dumped, its price collapsed and the cushion vanished. No bank failed and no contract was hacked: the design itself was reflexive. A bank failure is the fiat-backed risk (USDC wobbled in March 2023 when SVB held $3.3B of its reserves).

questions.question: An artist sets a 5% resale royalty on an NFT collection using the ERC-2981 standard. What ensures the artist is actually paid on each resale?
options: The blockchain: validators reject any NFT transfer that does not include the royalty payment.
The token contract: every ERC-721 transfer automatically deducts the royalty from the sale price and forwards it to the artist.
Nothing in the standard: ERC-2981 only declares the royalty, and each marketplace decides whether to pay it.
The buyer's wallet: it adds the royalty to the price before it signs the purchase transaction.
questions.correct_option_text: Nothing in the standard: ERC-2981 only declares the royalty, and each marketplace decides whether to pay it.
questions.explanation: ERC-2981 is a signal, not a rule. It lets a contract tell marketplaces how much royalty is expected and who should receive it, but a transfer goes through with or without that payment. An ERC-721 transfer does not even know the sale price. Blur launched with optional royalties in 2022 and OpenSea stopped enforcing them in 2023, and creator royalty income fell sharply. A revenue model that depends on marketplaces volunteering to pay is not enforced by code.

questions.question: In April 2022 an attacker drained about $182M from the Beanstalk protocol in a single transaction. How?
options: They stole the private keys of the multisig wallet that held the protocol's funds.
They exploited a reentrancy bug to withdraw the same deposit over and over.
They split their tokens across thousands of wallets to defeat a one-person-one-vote rule.
They flash-loaned a supermajority of the voting power and pushed through their own proposal.
questions.correct_option_text: They flash-loaned a supermajority of the voting power and pushed through their own proposal.
questions.explanation: Beanstalk counted voting power at the moment of the vote, so it could be borrowed. With a flash loan (borrowed and repaid inside one transaction) the attacker held more than the two-thirds supermajority required, executed a proposal they had submitted a day earlier, which sent the protocol's funds to their own wallet, and repaid the loan. No key was stolen and the code did what governance told it to. The defences are structural: measure voting power from an earlier snapshot, and put a timelock between a vote and its execution. The reentrancy bug belongs to The DAO (2016).

questions.question: In a property tokenisation structured like Propy's NFT home sales, what does the token holder actually own?
options: Ownership of a company (an LLC) that holds the deed, not the property itself.
Legal title to the property itself, recorded on the blockchain instead of in the land registry.
A right to occupy part of the property, which the smart contract enforces automatically.
A token whose price the contract keeps pegged to the property's latest appraised value.
questions.correct_option_text: Ownership of a company (an LLC) that holds the deed, not the property itself.
questions.explanation: The contract moves the token in seconds, but the property's legal title still sits in a land registry and changes hands off-chain. So the property is placed in a company and the token represents ownership of that company; exactly what the holder gets depends on the legal documents behind the token. That legal wrapper is where the risk sits: if the entity, the custodian or the law fails to honour the link, the token cannot enforce itself. Tokenising does not create buyers either: the secondary market can stay thin and the price can drift from the asset's value.

questions.question: TradeLens (Maersk and IBM) shut down in 2023, while GSBN, a similar shipping platform, is still running. Which explanation does the course's case study point to?
options: Technology: the permissioned ledger behind TradeLens could not cope with the volume of shipping documents sent to it.
Regulation: customs authorities in key ports refused to accept electronic bills of lading issued through TradeLens.
Ownership: TradeLens belonged to Maersk and IBM, so rival carriers were wary; GSBN is co-owned by carriers and port operators.
Funding: Maersk and IBM ran out of budget before the platform could go into production with paying customers.
questions.correct_option_text: Ownership: TradeLens belonged to Maersk and IBM, so rival carriers were wary; GSBN is co-owned by carriers and port operators.
questions.explanation: TradeLens ran in production from 2018 to early 2023, well funded and technically sound, with 100+ organisations on board. What it never achieved was the full industry-wide collaboration that makes a shared record valuable: rivals were wary of a platform controlled by Maersk, and even after several large carriers signed up, the official reason for closing was that it "did not reach the level of commercial viability necessary". GSBN tackles the same problem as a consortium co-owned by carriers and port operators. Who owns the platform decides who joins it.

questions.question: The California DMV put 42 million vehicle titles on a permissioned blockchain. What does the chain actually add over paper titles?
options: Lower storage costs: keeping records on a blockchain is cheaper than paper files or a database.
A tamper-evident digital title designed to transfer in minutes rather than weeks, still issued by the DMV.
Full public transparency: anyone can now look up who owns any car, with no identity checks.
An end to car theft and title fraud, because nothing recorded on-chain can ever be wrong or forged.
questions.correct_option_text: A tamper-evident digital title designed to transfer in minutes rather than weeks, still issued by the DMV.
questions.explanation: The gain is a shared, tamper-evident record: a paper title can be lost or forged and takes days or weeks of paperwork to transfer, while a digital title is designed to be checked and moved in minutes. Much of that speed comes from digitising the title at all; what the chain adds is a record that outside parties can verify has not been altered. The DMV still issues every title and runs the permissioned network, so you are still trusting the DMV, not removing it. On-chain storage costs more than a database, the records are not open to the public, and the chain cannot stop a car being stolen or correct a false entry made at the source.

questions.question: Estonia's e-Residency is the success story among the three cases. According to this section, why does it work?
options: It publishes every citizen's records on a public blockchain, so anyone can verify them.
It pairs an institution people already trust (the state) with blockchain used narrowly, to prove records have not been altered.
It replaced government offices with smart contracts, so citizens no longer need to trust any institution.
It issued a national token whose sales fund the country's digital public services.
questions.correct_option_text: It pairs an institution people already trust (the state) with blockchain used narrowly, to prove records have not been altered.
questions.explanation: Estonia is a hybrid: the government remains the trust anchor and the law gives digital signatures their weight, while the KSI blockchain does one narrow job, proving that records have not been tampered with. The records themselves stay in state databases; they are not published on a public chain. No institution was replaced and no token was issued. Blockchain here is infrastructure for integrity, not the product.

questions.question: After the 2016 DAO hack drained about $60M through a reentrancy bug, Ethereum hard-forked to return the funds and the chain split into ETH and ETC. What does the episode show about "code is law"?
options: Immutability has a social limit: with enough at stake, a community can override the code.
Validators reverse exploits as a matter of routine, so contract bugs carry little lasting risk.
The Ethereum Foundation holds an admin key that lets it reverse any transaction.
Reentrancy cannot be prevented, so every contract that holds funds is equally exposed.
questions.correct_option_text: Immutability has a social limit: with enough at stake, a community can override the code.
questions.explanation: The fork needed most of the network to agree, and those who disagreed kept the original chain (Ethereum Classic). There was no admin key, and the rescue has not been repeated for later hacks. So immutability is a strong default with a social limit, not an absolute. For builders the practical lesson is not to count on a rescue: audit before deploying, and give value-holding contracts a pause switch or an upgrade path. Reentrancy itself is preventable with standard coding patterns.

questions.question: The Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) spent 2016–2022 trying to replace its CHESS clearing and settlement system with a blockchain-style distributed ledger. In November 2022 it halted the project and wrote off about A$250 million. According to the independent review, what went wrong?
options: Blockchain technology is fundamentally incapable of handling securities clearing.
A security breach in the live system forced ASX to switch it off.
The solution design was too complex to meet ASX's needs, and delivery fell short.
Australian regulators forced the project to be abandoned for political reasons.
questions.correct_option_text: The solution design was too complex to meet ASX's needs, and delivery fell short.
questions.explanation: The independent review (Accenture, 2022) found significant challenges with the solution design and its ability to meet ASX's requirements: the design was too complex and struggled to scale, and ASX itself acknowledged technology, governance and delivery problems. ASX halted the project in November 2022, before it ever went live, and wrote off about A$250 million. The finding concerns this project's design, delivery and complexity; it is not a verdict that the technology cannot handle clearing, and the project was neither hacked nor stopped by regulators.

questions.question: Five logistics companies must all write to one shared shipment record. They do not fully trust one another, but every one of them accepts the same industry clearing house as a neutral operator. Following the decision tree, where do they land?
options: A smart contract platform.
A traditional database with access controls, run by one of the five companies.
A simple, Bitcoin-like blockchain.
A database managed by the trusted third party (the clearing house).
questions.correct_option_text: A database managed by the trusted third party (the clearing house).
questions.explanation: Walk the tree: shared database? Yes. Several writers? Yes. Do they fully trust each other? No, so access controls alone are not enough. Is there a third party everyone accepts? Yes, and the tree stops there: let the clearing house run the database. Blockchains only enter the picture when no such party exists; smart contracts only when, on top of that, complex business logic is needed.

questions.question: A retailer wants to move its internal staff-rota and holiday-approval workflow "onto the blockchain". One company runs it, the approval rules change every few months, and the records contain employees' personal data. What does this section's framework say?
options: Use a public-chain smart contract: immutability will stop managers from changing the rules.
Use a traditional database: a single trusted operator, frequently changing rules and personal data are all red flags.
Use a smart contract, but only after an independent security audit.
Use a simple, Bitcoin-like blockchain, because the logic is not complex.
questions.correct_option_text: Use a traditional database: a single trusted operator, frequently changing rules and personal data are all red flags.
questions.explanation: Three red flags from "When to rethink" appear at once: one party is already trusted to run the process, the rules must stay flexible (so immutability is a liability, not a benefit), and personal data does not belong on a ledger that cannot erase. An audit makes a contract safer; it does not make the use case fit. The decision tree agrees: with a single writer it exits at a traditional database long before any blockchain option.

questions.question: A startup's idea passes the decision tree: several parties that distrust each other, real savings from automation, and partners willing to join. It has budgeted for an audit and has a pause plan. But the design stores customers' names and addresses directly on a public chain. Which of the three checks fails?
options: Legal & regulatory: personal data on a ledger that cannot erase conflicts with GDPR's right to erasure.
Strategic fit: once personal data is involved, the parties no longer need trust-minimisation.
Risk & cost: storing names and addresses makes the security audit too expensive to afford.
None: an idea that passes the decision tree has already passed all three checks.
questions.correct_option_text: Legal & regulatory: personal data on a ledger that cannot erase conflicts with GDPR's right to erasure.
questions.explanation: The legal & regulatory check asks whether the law will stand behind the code, and one of its points is: no personal data on-chain, because GDPR's right to erasure meets a ledger that cannot erase. Strategic fit still holds (distrusting parties, real automation value, willing partners), and so does risk & cost (audit and pause plan are budgeted). The decision tree only says a smart contract could work; the three checks are a separate test. The usual fix is to keep personal data off-chain.

questions.question: The DAO (2016) and the ASX CHESS replacement (halted in 2022) both failed. Which contrast between the two failures is best supported?
options: The DAO was stopped by regulators; ASX was drained by a reentrancy bug.
The DAO relied on one trusted operator; ASX had no one in charge at all.
The DAO failed on a code bug; ASX on solution design, delivery and complexity.
There is none: both show that blockchains cannot handle financial applications.
questions.correct_option_text: The DAO failed on a code bug; ASX on solution design, delivery and complexity.
questions.explanation: The DAO was live when a reentrancy bug in a contract that could not be paused let about $60M drain away: a code failure after launch. ASX never went live: the independent review (Accenture, 2022) found significant challenges with the solution design and its ability to meet ASX's requirements, and the project was halted in November 2022 with a write-off of about A$250 million: a failure of solution design, delivery and complexity. Different failures at different stages.

questions.question: A bank wants to issue digital bonds. Its internal audit team holds the master record. It has 5 trusted institutional buyers, all KYC'd, based in several different countries. Settlement is currently T+2. Which is the strongest reason to STILL consider a smart contract on a public blockchain?
options: Reduces internal audit costs because the blockchain replaces the audit team entirely.
Cross-border settlement — buyers in several countries could settle on one shared ledger with fewer correspondent banks.
Public blockchains are cheaper than databases for any volume of transactions.
Smart contracts cannot be hacked once they are deployed, so they're inherently more secure than the bank's own internal database.
questions.correct_option_text: Cross-border settlement — buyers in several countries could settle on one shared ledger with fewer correspondent banks.
questions.explanation: The other three are common misconceptions: (A) a blockchain does not replace auditors; they still verify the business logic, with better evidence. (C) Public chains charge a fee per transaction, so they are not cheaper at any volume. (D) Smart contracts are hacked regularly; security is a discipline, not a property. The real potential gain here is cross-border settlement: with a suitable on-chain settlement asset, taking correspondent banks out of the chain can cut friction, cost and time. Santander's $20M bond on public Ethereum (2019) was an early test of settling a bond on-chain with fewer intermediaries. Inside one jurisdiction, with one issuer and trusted buyers, a database would win.

questions.question: A DeFi lending protocol uses a single on-chain DEX spot price as its collateral oracle. An attacker takes a $50M flash loan, manipulates the DEX price, borrows against inflated collateral, and repays the loan — all in one transaction. Which property of flash loans makes this attack unique compared to a standard market manipulation?
options: Flash loans are anonymous — the attacker cannot be traced or prosecuted.
Flash loans need no collateral — repaid within one atomic transaction, so the attacker needs almost no capital.
Flash loans exploit a bug in the Ethereum protocol itself, making them impossible to prevent at the contract level.
Flash loans allow attackers to bypass gas fees, making the attack economically viable even for small protocols.
questions.correct_option_text: Flash loans need no collateral — repaid within one atomic transaction, so the attacker needs almost no capital.
questions.explanation: Traditional market manipulation requires large capital held at risk over time. Flash loans change the economics: the attacker borrows an enormous amount without collateral, executes the attack, and repays everything (plus a small fee) within a single atomic transaction. If any step fails, the entire transaction reverts and the attacker loses only the gas. The attack is fully visible on-chain afterwards, but by then the funds are gone. So any protocol using a single on-chain spot price is exposed to an adversary with almost no capital. The fix: time-weighted average prices (TWAP) are much harder to move within one transaction, and decentralized oracle networks aggregate from multiple independent sources.

questions.question: Your team is building a tokenized real-estate platform for EU investors. You need: (a) full ERC-20 and ERC-721 support, (b) low fees for frequent rent distributions, (c) the ability to deploy proven smart contracts (OpenZeppelin), (d) the ability to code compliance controls such as investor whitelists into the token. Which platform fits BEST on technical grounds?
options: Hyperledger Fabric — a permissioned, enterprise-grade framework from the Linux Foundation, with no gas fees and no native token.
Solana — high throughput, low cost, fast finality.
An EVM-compatible Layer 2 such as Arbitrum or Base — ERC standards, low fees, OpenZeppelin and codable compliance rules.
Cardano — formal verification focus, Plutus/Marlowe for finance.
questions.correct_option_text: An EVM-compatible Layer 2 such as Arbitrum or Base — ERC standards, low fees, OpenZeppelin and codable compliance rules.
