questions.explanation: Three of the constraints are technical: full ERC support (rules out non-EVM Solana, Cardano and Hyperledger Fabric, where every standard would have to be rebuilt), low fees (rules out Ethereum L1 for frequent distributions) and OpenZeppelin compatibility (favours the EVM). An EVM Layer 2 such as Arbitrum or Base meets all three, and whitelists or transfer restrictions can be written into the token contract. What the chain cannot do is make the product legal: tokenised property interests will often count as securities under EU financial-markets law rather than falling under MiCA, so compliance comes from the legal structure and licences, not from the choice of chain. (Polygon PoS, often named in this context, is a sidechain with its own validators rather than an Ethereum Layer 2.)

questions.question: A lender must confirm that an applicant earns at least €40,000 a year before approving a loan. What does a zero-knowledge approach change?
options: The payslip is encrypted and stored on-chain, so only the lender can open it.
The applicant proves that "income ≥ €40,000" is true; the lender never sees the payslip or the exact figure.
The lender no longer needs to check anything at all: the blockchain itself guarantees that the applicant is honest.
The salary is hidden from everyone, regulators included, forever.
questions.correct_option_text: The applicant proves that "income ≥ €40,000" is true; the lender never sees the payslip or the exact figure.
questions.explanation: Zero-knowledge separates the claim from the data behind it. A trusted issuer (an employer or a bank) signs the facts once; the applicant's wallet turns them into a proof of one statement; the lender checks the proof. In this design the payslip never goes on-chain, in readable or encrypted form; a check still happens, and the applicant can produce further proofs for a regulator on demand. That is selective disclosure, not blanket secrecy.

questions.question: The prologue traces money from barter to Bitcoin and says each new form fixed a problem with the one before. What did Bitcoin set out to fix?
options: The weight and bulk of carrying metal coins around
The need to trust a central issuer or operator
The fact that money had never existed in digital form
The difficulty of dividing money into small enough amounts
questions.correct_option_text: The need to trust a central issuer or operator
questions.explanation: Earlier forms fixed portability, scarcity, divisibility and settlement speed, and bank ledgers had already made money digital; Bitcoin targeted the trust assumption itself.

questions.question: A new digital coin has a strictly limited supply and works flawlessly, yet it struggles to catch on while long-established currencies keep gaining users. Which idea from the 'Why does money have value?' slide best explains this?
options: Scarcity — a currency with a limited supply struggles to attract enough users
Intrinsic worth — a coin not made of a valuable material cannot hold value
Network effect — a currency grows more useful as more people accept it
Legal status — only money that a government declares official gains users
questions.correct_option_text: Network effect — a currency grows more useful as more people accept it
questions.explanation: The network-effect pillar: the more people accept a money, the more useful it is — 'new money struggles, established money compounds'.

questions.question: Paper notes began as IOUs that could be redeemed for gold. According to the prologue, what did money become once the gold standard ended?
options: A claim on silver instead of a claim on gold
Worthless, until Bitcoin later restored its value
A commodity whose value comes from the paper it is printed on
Pure trust in the issuer, with nothing physical behind it
questions.correct_option_text: Pure trust in the issuer, with nothing physical behind it
questions.explanation: Notes went from being redeemable for gold to resting on trust in the issuer alone — 'money became pure trust'.

questions.question: Maria keeps her savings in a bank account. According to the 'Who controls your money?' comparison, what does she actually hold?
options: A claim on the bank, which holds the money and can freeze the account
Physical custody of the money, in the same way as with cash
The private keys that control her balance on the bank's ledger
A balance that nobody except her is able to move or freeze
questions.correct_option_text: A claim on the bank, which holds the money and can freeze the account
questions.explanation: With a bank account the bank holds the money and you have a claim; the account can be frozen and transactions refused.

questions.question: Tom buys bitcoin and leaves it with an exchange that holds it for him. One day the exchange freezes his account. How does this fit with the claim that Bitcoin 'cannot be frozen'?
options: It contradicts the claim: the protocol allows any exchange to freeze any address it likes
It cannot really happen, because Tom's own keys still control coins held at an exchange
It shows that the miners must have voted to approve the freeze before it took effect
The Bitcoin protocol cannot freeze coins, but a custodian can freeze what it holds for you
questions.correct_option_text: The Bitcoin protocol cannot freeze coins, but a custodian can freeze what it holds for you
questions.explanation: The table says 'not at the protocol layer — custodians can freeze theirs'; 'your keys, your coins' applies only if you self-custody.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the prologue's definition of decentralization?
options: The system runs on a very large number of computers spread across many countries
There are no rules at all, so every participant is free to act as they see fit
No single party can freeze funds, censor transactions or change the rules alone
Nobody is in charge of anything, so no decisions about the system are ever made
questions.correct_option_text: No single party can freeze funds, censor transactions or change the rules alone
questions.explanation: Decentralization means no single point of control — power is spread across many independent participants; it does not mean no rules, no one in charge, or simply many machines.

questions.question: A classmate says: 'Decentralized systems have no rules — that's the whole point.' Which reply is consistent with the prologue?
options: "Correct — once the authority is removed, following the rules becomes optional."
"The rules are strict, but code and consensus enforce them, not an authority."
"There are rules, but they are set and enforced by the company that founded the system."
"There are rules, but they apply only to the miners and not to ordinary users."
questions.correct_option_text: "The rules are strict, but code and consensus enforce them, not an authority."
questions.explanation: Decentralization does not mean 'no rules': the rules are strict, just enforced by code and consensus instead of an authority.

questions.question: A company wants a system to record its own internal stock movements. All the users are its employees and everyone is content for the company to run it. In light of the prologue's view of decentralization, which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: A central database is probably the right tool, since decentralization is a trade-off with real costs
A decentralized ledger is the better choice, because decentralization makes any system more secure
A decentralized ledger would be faster, because thousands of computers would share the work
A decentralized ledger would be cheaper to run, because nobody has to be paid to operate it
questions.correct_option_text: A central database is probably the right tool, since decentralization is a trade-off with real costs
questions.explanation: The prologue stresses decentralization is a trade-off (slower, costlier, harder to use), not an automatic win — for many problems a central database is the right answer.

questions.question: According to the prologue, what was Satoshi Nakamoto's real contribution?
options: Combining existing cryptographic tools with economic incentives into one working system
Inventing hashing, digital signatures and proof of work from scratch in a single paper
Persuading banks and governments to put their backing behind a new digital currency
Writing the very first proposal for digital cash, which nobody had attempted until then
questions.correct_option_text: Combining existing cryptographic tools with economic incentives into one working system
questions.explanation: Satoshi invented no single component; the genius was combining existing primitives with incentive design into one coherent system that actually worked.

questions.question: Why did the Cypherpunks insist that privacy tools be open source?
options: Because open-source software tends to run faster than closed software
Because the law at the time required encryption software to be published
Because nobody can verify the privacy claims of code that is kept secret
Because it allowed them to sell licences for the tools to companies
questions.correct_option_text: Because nobody can verify the privacy claims of code that is kept secret
questions.explanation: Their open-source principle: tools must be public and auditable — if the code is secret, the privacy it claims is unverifiable.

questions.question: The Cypherpunks built their tools to be censorship-resistant, a trait Bitcoin inherited. What makes a system censorship-resistant in this sense?
options: It is protected by strong passwords that are known only to its operators
It is widely dispersed, with no single point where it can be shut down
It is registered in a country whose laws happen to forbid censorship
Its source code is kept confidential so that attackers cannot study it
questions.correct_option_text: It is widely dispersed, with no single point where it can be shut down
questions.explanation: The slides tie censorship resistance to having no single point of shutdown — 'a widely dispersed system can't be shut down'.

questions.question: Sofia in Lisbon needs to pay a supplier on another continent. Which statement matches the prologue's 'Who controls your money?' comparison?
options: Cash is the easiest option, because it can cross borders without limits or declarations
A bank transfer settles instantly, whereas a Bitcoin transfer needs several days to arrive
A payment platform works everywhere in the world, with no regional restrictions or checks
A Bitcoin transfer works like a local one; a bank transfer typically goes via SWIFT and can take days
questions.correct_option_text: A Bitcoin transfer works like a local one; a bank transfer typically goes via SWIFT and can take days
questions.explanation: In the comparison, Bitcoin cross-border is 'same as a local transfer'; banks typically route through SWIFT correspondents over days with an FX spread; cash and platforms are restricted.

questions.question: Which statement about physical cash is consistent with the prologue's comparison of cash, bank accounts, payment platforms and Bitcoin?
options: You hold it yourself and it cannot be frozen, but the central bank can inflate its supply
It has a fixed total supply that no authority can change, which protects holders from inflation
It can be frozen by your bank in the same way as the balance in a bank account can be frozen
It is the simplest of the four ways to move value across a border, as it needs no intermediary
questions.correct_option_text: You hold it yourself and it cannot be frozen, but the central bank can inflate its supply
questions.explanation: Cash gives you physical custody and cannot be frozen (though it can be lost, stolen or seized in person); it is hard to move across borders and its supply is inflated by the central bank.

questions.question: Ten villagers, with no bank, each keep an identical copy of one shared notebook of transactions. Mallory secretly alters an entry in her own copy. What does this expose about a shared ledger on its own?
options: A shared ledger only works if a bank or a notary holds the master copy of the notebook
Sharing copies is not enough: tampering must be made visible and one true copy agreed on
The villagers have no way of reading the full history of transactions in their notebooks
Only one villager at a time can ever be allowed to write new entries in the notebook
questions.correct_option_text: Sharing copies is not enough: tampering must be made visible and one true copy agreed on
questions.explanation: The shared ledger removes the middleman but raises a new problem — someone can edit their own copy — which hashing, linked blocks and consensus then address.

questions.question: How are 'blockchain' and 'Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)' related?
options: They are two different names for exactly the same thing
DLT is one particular kind of blockchain, the kind used by banks
Blockchain is one kind of DLT, but it is not the only kind
A blockchain becomes a DLT only once a central authority operates it
questions.correct_option_text: Blockchain is one kind of DLT, but it is not the only kind
questions.explanation: The slides define a blockchain as a form of DLT (shared, append-only, cryptographically linked) and stress it is one kind of DLT, not the only one.

questions.question: Alice signs a payment to Bob and broadcasts it to the network, but it has not yet been included in a block. Where is the transaction?
options: In the mempool, waiting for a miner to pick it and bundle it into a block
In Bob's wallet, waiting for him to accept or decline the payment
In the genesis block, where all new transactions are stored at first
In Alice's wallet, where it stays until every node has voted on it
questions.correct_option_text: In the mempool, waiting for a miner to pick it and bundle it into a block
questions.explanation: A signed transaction is broadcast, queues up in the mempool, and waits to be picked by a miner and bundled into the next block.

questions.question: The network is busy and many transactions are waiting. Dan attaches a higher fee to his transaction than Eva attaches to hers (the two transactions are the same size). What usually follows?
options: Whichever was sent first is picked first, because miners must follow the order of arrival
Both wait equally long, because miners choose the transactions for a block at random
Dan's is rejected, because paying a fee above the standard rate is not allowed
Dan's is likely to be picked first, because miners usually take the highest fees first
questions.correct_option_text: Dan's is likely to be picked first, because miners usually take the highest fees first
questions.explanation: Miners pick the next batch from the mempool 'highest-fee first, usually'.

questions.question: A colleague emails you a contract file and, through a separate trusted channel, the SHA-256 hash of the original. How can you use the hash to check that the file was not altered on the way?
options: Reverse the hash to recover the original text, then compare it with the file you received
Hash the file you received and compare: the same input always gives the same hash
Count the characters in the hash, because a longer file produces a longer hash than a short one
You cannot, because a hash is random and comes out differently each time it is computed
questions.correct_option_text: Hash the file you received and compare: the same input always gives the same hash
questions.explanation: Hashes are deterministic and any change alters the whole fingerprint, so matching hashes mean matching inputs; hashes are also one-way and fixed-size, which rules out the other options.

questions.question: A chain has six blocks, numbered #0 to #5. Someone changes the data in Block #2 and nothing else, so Block #2 gets a new hash. Which other blocks are affected?
options: None — the change stays contained within Block #2 itself
Blocks #0 and #1 — every block that came before the edit
Blocks #3, #4 and #5 — every block that comes after the edit
All five of the other blocks, both before and after the edit
questions.correct_option_text: Blocks #3, #4 and #5 — every block that comes after the edit
questions.explanation: Block #3 still stores Block #2's old hash, so the link breaks there and everything downstream is invalid; earlier blocks are untouched.

questions.question: Why would quietly changing a block's timestamp after the fact break the chain, just as changing its data would?
options: The network automatically deletes any block whose timestamp has been edited
Timestamps are stored only in the genesis block, so no other block carries one
The timestamp is one of the nonce values the miner tried while searching for a hash
The timestamp is part of what is hashed, so the block's hash would change
questions.correct_option_text: The timestamp is part of what is hashed, so the block's hash would change
questions.explanation: The timestamp 'becomes part of the hash', so editing it changes the block's fingerprint and the next block's 'previous hash' no longer matches.

questions.question: You are handed four blocks in scrambled order, each showing its Data, its Prev Hash and its Hash. How do you rebuild the chain?
options: Start from the genesis block, then match each Prev Hash to the previous block's Hash
Sort the blocks by the size of the amounts in their data, from the largest to the smallest
Sort the blocks alphabetically by their own hash, starting with the lowest value
Use any order you like, as long as the genesis block is placed in the first position
questions.correct_option_text: Start from the genesis block, then match each Prev Hash to the previous block's Hash
questions.explanation: Each block's Prev Hash must equal the previous block's Hash, so starting from genesis the chain can only be assembled one way.

questions.question: In a federated network — several hubs, each serving its own cluster of nodes — one hub goes offline. What happens?
options: The whole network goes dark, because that one hub was holding everything together
Nothing noticeable, because every node is a peer and traffic routes around the gap
The nodes that depend on that hub are cut off, while the other clusters keep working
All of the other hubs fail one after another, until the entire network is down
questions.correct_option_text: The nodes that depend on that hub are cut off, while the other clusters keep working
questions.explanation: Federated: killing a hub orphans its own cluster but leaves the rest intact — unlike centralized (all dark) or distributed (routes around).

questions.question: The 'Who's in Control?' exercise asks one question of each system: who can freeze it, censor it or shut it down? By that test, which of these has decentralized control?
options: Visa
Email (SMTP)
Google
Bank of America
questions.correct_option_text: Email (SMTP)
questions.explanation: Email has thousands of independent providers and no party that can switch it off; Visa, Google and a bank are each controlled by one organisation, however distributed their machines.

questions.question: After millions of attempts, one miner announces a hash that meets the target. What do the other nodes do before accepting the block?
options: Repeat the full search themselves, which takes as long as it took the winner
Accept it without checking, because the winner clearly spent a lot of electricity
Check it almost instantly, because verifying a solution takes very little work
Wait for a central server to confirm which of the miners was the winner
questions.correct_option_text: Check it almost instantly, because verifying a solution takes very little work
questions.explanation: 'Checking is cheap, finding is expensive': the other nodes verify the winning hash, and the transactions in the block, at once.

questions.question: How does Proof of Stake differ from Proof of Work, as introduced in Section 1?
options: Validators lock up tokens as collateral instead of competing in energy-hungry mining
A central authority chooses who is allowed to add each new block to the chain
Blocks are added without any rule for agreeing on which chain is the true one
Miners solve the same puzzle as before, only on much faster and cheaper hardware
questions.correct_option_text: Validators lock up tokens as collateral instead of competing in energy-hungry mining
questions.explanation: Proof of Stake 'replaces electricity with locked tokens — validators put up collateral instead of burning power' on mining.

questions.question: Proof of Work, Proof of Stake, PBFT and the other protocols in the 'protocol zoo' all answer the same question. Which one?
options: How can transactions be hidden from the public?
How can a block be made to hold more transactions?
Who should be allowed to own a wallet?
Which copy of the chain is the truth?
questions.correct_option_text: Which copy of the chain is the truth?
questions.explanation: Every consensus protocol answers 'which copy of the chain is the truth?' — they differ in their trade-offs in speed, energy and decentralization.

questions.question: The miner who wins the race for a block is paid in newly issued bitcoin. According to Section 1, what does this reward achieve?
options: It compensates ordinary users for the transaction fees they have paid to the network
It funds the brute-force work that keeps cheating prohibitively expensive
It pays the company that maintains and regularly updates the Bitcoin software
It refunds the electricity bills of the miners who lost the race
questions.correct_option_text: It funds the brute-force work that keeps cheating prohibitively expensive
questions.explanation: The block reward 'is what funds the brute-force work that keeps cheating prohibitive'.

questions.question: Ana posts her blockchain address on her public social-media profile, next to her real name, to collect donations. What does this do to her privacy?
options: Nothing changes, because the address itself still does not contain her name
Her past transactions become hidden, because the address is now registered to her
Only her future donations become visible, while her earlier activity stays private
Everything that address has done, or will do in future, can now be tied to her
questions.correct_option_text: Everything that address has done, or will do in future, can now be tied to her
questions.explanation: Every transaction from an address is public forever; privacy comes only from not linking the address to you.

questions.question: Rui sends a payment on a public blockchain to the wrong address. Apart from the recipient choosing to send the money back, who has the power to reverse the payment for him?
options: No one — the network has no administrator with the power to reverse transactions
The miner who included the transaction in a block, who is able to remove it again
The wallet company, whose support team can undo a payment when a customer asks
The founders of the blockchain, who keep an override key for cases like this one
questions.correct_option_text: No one — the network has no administrator with the power to reverse transactions
questions.explanation: 'No control organs': no admin can freeze accounts, reverse transactions or override the rules.

questions.question: The 1982 Byzantine Generals paper, Paxos and PBFT all showed how computers can agree even when some of them fail or misbehave. Why could none of them power a currency on the open internet?
options: They needed far more electricity than computer networks had available at the time
They broke down as soon as more than one participant in the network was dishonest
They required a fixed 'guest list' of known participants who had been approved in advance
They were kept secret by their designers and were never published for others to use
questions.correct_option_text: They required a fixed 'guest list' of known participants who had been approved in advance
questions.explanation: The classic pre-Bitcoin solutions needed known, pre-authenticated participants; 'the open internet has no guest list' — Bitcoin dropped the guest list.

questions.question: Five banks that know each other want a shared ledger run by their own five approved validators. A consultant claims that only Bitcoin-style mining can make them agree. Based on the Section 2 timeline, what is the best response?
options: He is right: before Bitcoin, computers on a network had no known method for reaching agreement
He is right: mining is the only method ever devised that can tolerate dishonest participants
He is wrong: with a small, known set of validators, earlier algorithms such as PBFT already work
He is wrong: a network of known participants needs no consensus method, as its members trust each other
questions.correct_option_text: He is wrong: with a small, known set of validators, earlier algorithms such as PBFT already work
questions.explanation: Paxos and PBFT work for fixed, known validator sets; Bitcoin's breakthrough (Nakamoto consensus) was agreement among open, unknown participants.

questions.question: How does Nakamoto consensus settle which version of the ledger is the truth?
options: Registered validators cast votes, and the version backed by most identities wins
The valid chain with the most accumulated proof of work counts as the truth, and mining replaces voting
The node that has been online for the longest time decides for everyone else
Satoshi's original node signs off each block before the others accept it
questions.correct_option_text: The valid chain with the most accumulated proof of work counts as the truth, and mining replaces voting
questions.explanation: Nakamoto consensus 'replaces voting with mining' with no fixed validator set: nodes follow the valid chain with the most accumulated work (usually also the longest, hence 'the longest valid chain' in the white paper's shorthand).

questions.question: Alice owns one coin and broadcasts two transactions at the same moment: one paying Bob and one paying herself. How does Bitcoin deal with this without a referee?
options: Both are accepted, and Alice's balance simply becomes negative until she tops it up
A central server looks at the two transactions and decides which one arrived first
Both are cancelled and the coin is destroyed, as a penalty for attempting to cheat
Only one is accepted: once the coin is spent, every node rejects a second use of it
questions.correct_option_text: Only one is accepted: once the coin is spent, every node rejects a second use of it
questions.explanation: Spending a UTXO destroys it: once one of the two transactions is confirmed, any other transaction referencing the same output is rejected by every node — 'no referee needed'.

questions.question: How does Bitcoin's UTXO model differ from the account model used by banks?
options: Each user has a single balance number on the ledger, which is adjusted with every payment
The ledger records separate unspent outputs, like coins, each of which can be spent only once
The coins are stored inside the user's own wallet app rather than on the ledger that the nodes share
A central operator places all of the payments in order, so that no two of them can conflict
questions.correct_option_text: The ledger records separate unspent outputs, like coins, each of which can be spent only once
questions.explanation: Bitcoin 'doesn't store balances' but discrete unspent outputs, like physical coins; the account model keeps one running balance per account and adjusts it with every payment.

questions.question: Earlier digital-money systems such as DigiCash and e-gold did prevent double-spending. What weakness did their approach share?
options: They relied on a central operator, who had to be trusted and could be seized or shut down
They consumed far more electricity than their operators could ever afford to pay for
They allowed anyone at all to create new coins, without any limit on the total supply
They published the legal name of every user next to each of the payments that user made
questions.correct_option_text: They relied on a central operator, who had to be trusted and could be seized or shut down
questions.explanation: The pre-Bitcoin fix was 'trust a referee': a central ledger stops double-spends, but the operator can be seized, hacked or turn evil.

questions.question: A dealer sells a car for bitcoin and waits about an hour before handing over the keys. What is the reasoning?
options: The payment needs roughly that long to travel across the network to the dealer's wallet
The dealer's bank needs about an hour to convert the incoming bitcoin into euros
After about six confirmations, the payment is considered practically irreversible
Bitcoin payments are approved by hand, and miners only do so during business hours
questions.correct_option_text: After about six confirmations, the payment is considered practically irreversible
questions.explanation: Six confirmations (about 60 minutes) is the conventional threshold for large payments: each extra block makes a reversal more expensive, so by then the payment is treated as practically irreversible.

questions.question: A café chain wants to take bitcoin for coffee, but Bitcoin's base layer handles only a few transactions per second and takes a long time to be final. What does Section 2 point to for this kind of use?
options: Running a pruned node in every café, so that each payment is validated locally
Asking the miners to produce a new block every few seconds instead of every ten minutes
Waiting for the next halving, which will make the base layer considerably faster
The Lightning Network — a layer on top of Bitcoin built for fast, small payments
questions.correct_option_text: The Lightning Network — a layer on top of Bitcoin built for fast, small payments
questions.explanation: Bitcoin's base layer is built for settlement, not point-of-sale; the Lightning Network adds a layer on top for fast small payments.

questions.question: Roughly every four years the newly issued coins a miner earns per block are cut in half. What does this mean for miners in the long run?
options: They will eventually be paid only by transaction fees, as new issuance falls towards zero
The 21 million cap will be raised when the time comes, so that miners can still be paid
Blocks will take longer and longer, stretching from ten minutes to several hours
Mining will come to an end, and transactions will then stop being processed
questions.correct_option_text: They will eventually be paid only by transaction fees, as new issuance falls towards zero
questions.explanation: The new-coin reward shrinks at every halving until issuance trends to zero (around 2140); after that, miners are paid only by transaction fees.

questions.question: An attacker wants to rewrite a block that already has ten blocks on top of it (for example, to erase a payment they made). What would this take?
options: Editing the block on the attacker's own computer, after which the other nodes copy the change
Redoing the proof of work for that block and every later one, faster than the rest of the network
Redoing the proof of work for that one block only, since the later blocks are unaffected
Finding the private key of the miner who originally created that particular block
questions.correct_option_text: Redoing the proof of work for that block and every later one, faster than the rest of the network
questions.explanation: To overwrite an old block you must redo the work for it and every block after it, faster than the rest of the world combined.

questions.question: Some mobile wallets run as SPV (light) nodes instead of full nodes. What trade-off does that involve?
options: They store the whole chain on the phone but skip checking the signatures on transactions
They validate every block from genesis and then delete the old blocks to save space
They need specialised mining hardware in order to send and receive payments
They keep only block headers and rely on Merkle proofs supplied by full nodes
questions.correct_option_text: They keep only block headers and rely on Merkle proofs supplied by full nodes
questions.explanation: An SPV/light node stores block headers only and trusts Merkle proofs from full nodes — it does not verify everything itself.

questions.question: In which order are a wallet's secrets and identifiers derived, each step being one-way?
options: Address → public key → private key → seed
Seed → private key → public key → address
Public key → private key → address → seed
Seed → address → public key → private key
questions.correct_option_text: Seed → private key → public key → address
questions.explanation: One-way derivation runs seed → private key → public key → address; going backwards is practically impossible.

questions.question: Leo photographs his seed phrase and saves the picture in a cloud notes app 'as a backup'. How does this square with the guidance in Section 2?
options: It is the recommended approach, because a copy kept in the cloud is safer than paper
It is harmless, because a seed phrase is useless to anyone without the original phone
It goes against it: the phrase should be kept offline, for example on paper, never in the cloud
It is unnecessary, because the wallet company can reset a seed phrase on request
questions.correct_option_text: It goes against it: the phrase should be kept offline, for example on paper, never in the cloud
questions.explanation: The seed phrase is the single point of failure: it regenerates the entire wallet on any device, so back it up offline (on paper or metal) and never put it in a cloud or photo app.

questions.question: Inês drops her phone into the sea. Her wallet app is gone, but her seed phrase is written on paper at home. What is her situation?
options: She can enter the phrase on a new device and regenerate her keys and addresses
Her coins are lost for good, because they were stored in the wallet app on the phone
She must ask the wallet company to transfer her coins into a newly created account
She has to wait until the miners reissue her coins to a brand-new address
questions.correct_option_text: She can enter the phrase on a new device and regenerate her keys and addresses
questions.explanation: The seed phrase regenerates the entire wallet on any device; the wallet holds keys, while the coins only ever live on the ledger.

questions.question: What is the Merkle root that is stored in a block's header?
options: The private key of the miner who created the block, kept as proof of authorship
A complete list of all the addresses that send or receive coins in the block
The hash of the very first transaction in the block, which stands in for the rest
One single hash that summarises all of the transactions contained in the block
questions.correct_option_text: One single hash that summarises all of the transactions contained in the block
questions.explanation: A block header stores the Merkle root: one hash summarising every transaction — change any transaction and the root changes.

questions.question: A block contains four transactions — A, B, C and D — arranged in a Merkle tree in which A is paired with B and C is paired with D. Someone alters transaction C. Which hashes change?
options: Only the hash of transaction C itself, and nothing above it in the tree
C's hash, the combined hash of the C–D pair, and the Merkle root
The hashes of all four transactions, but not the Merkle root above them
Only the Merkle root, while every hash below it stays exactly the same
questions.correct_option_text: C's hash, the combined hash of the C–D pair, and the Merkle root
questions.explanation: Tampering with one transaction changes its leaf hash and every node on the path up to the root; the A–B branch is untouched.

questions.question: Section 2 describes people in high-inflation countries turning to peer-to-peer crypto to protect their savings. What 'honest footnote' does it add?
options: That dollar stablecoins are often used more than Bitcoin day to day in these countries
That the price of Bitcoin stayed perfectly stable throughout the years in question
That the governments of these countries adopted Bitcoin as their official currency
That most of this activity was short-term speculation rather than an attempt to save
questions.correct_option_text: That dollar stablecoins are often used more than Bitcoin day to day in these countries
questions.explanation: The slide's caveat: in these countries dollar stablecoins are often used more than Bitcoin — 'the lesson is the exit, not the asset'.

questions.question: El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021. What does the outcome described in Section 2 suggest?
options: Legal status was enough to turn Bitcoin into the everyday money of most of the population
The Bitcoin network had to change its rules in order to serve the population of a whole country
Making something legal tender does not by itself make people use it in their daily lives
The experiment ended because the state had lost all of the bitcoin held in its treasury
questions.correct_option_text: Making something legal tender does not by itself make people use it in their daily lives
questions.explanation: A 2024 survey by a Salvadoran university (UCA) found that about 92% of Salvadorans had not used Bitcoin that year, and a 2025 legal reform made acceptance voluntary; the treasury kept its coins.

questions.question: A mining firm pipes the waste heat from its machines into a greenhouse and advertises 'climate-neutral Bitcoin'. Which assessment matches Section 2?
options: The claim holds, because the heat that is reused cancels out the electricity that was consumed
The claim holds, because mining machines produce very little heat compared with the work they do
The claim does not matter, because proof-of-work mining needs almost no electricity anyway
Reusing the heat helps, but the climate impact still depends on the source of the electricity
questions.correct_option_text: Reusing the heat helps, but the climate impact still depends on the source of the electricity
questions.explanation: Heat reuse makes the electricity do double duty but does not make mining energy-free: 'a rig heating a greenhouse on coal power is still a rig on coal power'.

questions.question: Which of these can be done with Bitcoin's built-in scripting language, as described in Section 2?
options: Running a lending application that keeps its own state
Requiring two signatures before coins can be spent
Issuing NFTs under a native on-chain token standard
Operating an organisation through autonomous on-chain rules
questions.correct_option_text: Requiring two signatures before coins can be spent
questions.explanation: Bitcoin Script handles simple conditions such as 'spend only with two signatures' or 'unlock after a delay' — no loops, no persistent state, no native token standard.

questions.question: Bitcoin's community declined to add more programmability, and Ethereum was built instead. How does Section 2 judge the two choices?
options: Bitcoin's choice was a mistake, and Ethereum was created in order to correct it for good
Ethereum's choice was reckless, and Bitcoin's refusal to change was the only safe option
Neither is 'right': Bitcoin keeps a smaller attack surface, Ethereum can do far more
The two choices come to the same thing, since Bitcoin went on to add the same features
questions.correct_option_text: Neither is 'right': Bitcoin keeps a smaller attack surface, Ethereum can do far more
questions.explanation: The slides frame it as a trade-off: Bitcoin does one thing extremely well; Ethereum does many things with a larger attack surface.

questions.question: What changed when Ethereum went through 'the Merge' in 2022?
options: It replaced mining with staking (Proof of Stake), cutting its energy use by about 99.95%
It merged with Bitcoin, so that the two networks now share a single chain and a single coin
It stopped running smart contracts and went back to handling simple payments only
It introduced a hard cap on its supply of 21 million coins, the same as Bitcoin's cap
questions.correct_option_text: It replaced mining with staking (Proof of Stake), cutting its energy use by about 99.95%
questions.explanation: The Merge moved Ethereum from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake and cut its energy use by roughly 99.95%.

questions.question: A buyer and a seller put a sale into a smart contract: when the price is paid in, the token representing the asset is released to the buyer automatically. From a business point of view, what is the main appeal?
options: The agreement can be reversed far more easily than one that is written on paper
The agreement enforces itself, so no middleman has to be paid to enforce it
The contract can work out by itself what a fair price for the asset would be
The terms of the sale stay hidden from both parties until the price has been paid
questions.correct_option_text: The agreement enforces itself, so no middleman has to be paid to enforce it
questions.explanation: 'An agreement that enforces itself removes the middleman you used to pay to enforce it' — escrow without an escrow agent. (For assets such as houses, legal title still has to follow off-chain: see the tokenisation questions.)

questions.question: A payroll smart contract is written to 'pay salaries on the 1st of each month'. The 1st arrives and nobody sends the contract a transaction. What happens?
options: The contract pays the salaries out automatically at midnight, as its code instructs
The network's validators trigger the contract as part of their normal block work
The contract pays the salaries out as soon as the next block has been created
Nothing — a contract has no clock, so someone must send a transaction to trigger it
questions.correct_option_text: Nothing — a contract has no clock, so someone must send a transaction to trigger it
questions.explanation: A contract cannot start itself: 'pay on the 1st' still needs someone — a person, or a bot paid to do it — to send a transaction on the 1st.

questions.question: Uniswap is an example of a contract account on Ethereum. Who or what controls such an account?
options: Whoever holds its private key, in the same way as an ordinary wallet
Its own code — it has no private key, and pays out only as its rules say
The validators, who are able to edit its code by a majority vote
The company that wrote it, by means of an administrator password
questions.correct_option_text: Its own code — it has no private key, and pays out only as its rules say
questions.explanation: A contract account has no key: the code sets the rules, holds its own balance and pays out as those rules say.

questions.question: Marta makes the same simple ETH transfer on a quiet Sunday and on a very busy Friday, and pays a higher fee on Friday. Why?
options: The transfer used many more gas units on Friday, because busy days make transfers complex
Her wallet provider charges its users a higher commission on weekdays than at weekends
The price per unit of gas was higher, because demand was higher; the units were the same
The validators add a penalty to any transaction that is sent during the busiest hours
questions.correct_option_text: The price per unit of gas was higher, because demand was higher; the units were the same
questions.explanation: Fee = gas units × gas price: the same job uses the same units, but a busier network means a higher price per unit.

questions.question: At the same moment, and at the same gas price, Pedro sends a simple ETH transfer and Clara deploys a new smart contract. Who pays the higher fee, and why?
options: Pedro, because moving money on the network costs more than publishing code to it
Clara, because deploying a contract is a bigger job and uses far more gas units
Both pay the same amount, because the gas price is the same for the two of them
Neither pays anything, because fees are charged only when a transaction fails
questions.correct_option_text: Clara, because deploying a contract is a bigger job and uses far more gas units
questions.explanation: Bigger job, more gas units: a simple transfer costs the base 21,000 gas, while deploying a contract typically costs hundreds of thousands of gas or more.

questions.question: How does trading on an AMM (automated market maker) differ from trading on a traditional order-book exchange?
options: A matchmaker pairs each buyer with a seller and keeps the spread between them as its margin
A trade can take place only at the moment when a buyer's bid and a seller's ask meet
The price is fixed once a day by the issuer of the token and applies to all trades that day
You trade against a pool of tokens held by a contract, and a formula sets the price
questions.correct_option_text: You trade against a pool of tokens held by a contract, and a formula sets the price
questions.explanation: 'Order book: a matchmaker. AMM: a formula.' On an AMM you trade against a liquidity pool, so no matching buyer or seller is needed at that moment.

questions.question: Starting from the same constant-product AMM pool, compare buying 1 ETH with buying 5 ETH in a single trade. What does the pool's pricing formula imply for the larger trade?
options: It earns a volume discount, so each ETH costs less than in the small trade
It pays exactly the same price per ETH as the small trade does
It moves further along the curve, so each additional ETH costs more
It is rejected, because a pool only accepts trades below a fixed size
questions.correct_option_text: It moves further along the curve, so each additional ETH costs more
questions.explanation: 'Bigger trades move further along the curve, so each extra ETH costs more.'

questions.question: Which is the most accurate summary of where DeFi stands today, according to Section 3?
options: It works and is open 24/7, but most of its volume is crypto being traded for other crypto
It has replaced banks for most everyday payments, loans and savings where it is available
It is still only a theoretical idea, and no working applications have been built so far
It carries little risk for users, because smart-contract code is checked by the network
questions.correct_option_text: It works and is open 24/7, but most of its volume is crypto being traded for other crypto
questions.explanation: The slide's 'hype vs real': DeFi works and is open 24/7, but most volume is crypto trading crypto, not everyday finance — and it carries risks such as contract bugs.

questions.question: Joana buys an NFT of a digital artwork. According to Section 3, what does she own?
options: The image file itself, which is stored inside the token on the blockchain for good
The exclusive legal right to decide who is allowed to view or copy the artwork
The on-chain record of ownership, but not necessarily the image file itself
A share in the future profits of the company that created the collection
questions.correct_option_text: The on-chain record of ownership, but not necessarily the image file itself
questions.explanation: An NFT is a unique token with an on-chain ownership history; 'the image usually lives off-chain: you own the record, not the file'.

questions.question: A DAO decides how to spend its treasury through on-chain votes that are weighted by the number of tokens each voter holds. What practical weakness does Section 3 point out?
options: The votes cannot be counted properly unless a trusted board supervises the count
Approved proposals take effect only after a board of directors has signed them off
The results of each vote are kept hidden from the people who hold the tokens
A few large token holders often decide the outcome, and many holders do not vote
questions.correct_option_text: A few large token holders often decide the outcome, and many holders do not vote
questions.explanation: DAO risks include voter apathy and whale capture: 'in practice a few large token holders often decide'.

questions.question: Why can wallets, exchanges and apps technically handle a newly created ERC-20 token without new software being written for it?
options: Because each new token is individually reviewed and approved by Ethereum's founders
Because tokens follow a shared standard, so the same software works with all of them
Because every token of this type is backed by exactly one US dollar held in a bank
Because the makers of each wallet update their software by hand for every new token
questions.correct_option_text: Because tokens follow a shared standard, so the same software works with all of them
questions.explanation: 'Because the standard is shared, every wallet, exchange and app can hold it.'

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company wants every pack of medicine to be traceable from the factory to the pharmacy, so that counterfeits can be spotted. Which of the recurring patterns from Section 3 does this illustrate?
options: Trust without intermediaries — money and claims settling directly between parties
Self-sovereign coordination — coordinating without a platform or registrar in the middle
Token-based governance — holders voting on how a shared treasury is spent
Verifiable provenance — an unbroken chain of custody built into the record
questions.correct_option_text: Verifiable provenance — an unbroken chain of custody built into the record
questions.explanation: Track-and-trace and drug-pack authentication are the slide's examples of verifiable provenance: an unbroken chain of custody.

questions.question: A music-streaming service changes its terms overnight and lowers what it pays artists. According to the 'App vs dApp' comparison, what makes this possible, and what is different in a dApp?
options: One company owns the servers and sets the payout; in a dApp, fees and incentives are set by governance
Traditional apps are obliged by law to revise their terms regularly, whereas dApps are exempt from this
In a dApp the artists are never paid for their work, so there is no payout that could be lowered
A dApp also runs on one company's servers, but that company has promised never to change its terms
questions.correct_option_text: One company owns the servers and sets the payout; in a dApp, fees and incentives are set by governance
questions.explanation: Traditional app: one company owns the servers, can change the terms and sets the payout. dApp: smart contracts on a public chain, with fees and incentives set by governance.

questions.question: Section 3 presents immutability as double-edged. Why?
options: It protects records against tampering, but mistakes and harms cannot simply be undone either
It makes the chain slower and slower with each new block that is added to the end of it
It applies only to the Bitcoin blockchain and does not apply to Ethereum or other chains
It keeps every transaction hidden from regulators, which makes the system impossible to audit
questions.correct_option_text: It protects records against tampering, but mistakes and harms cannot simply be undone either
questions.explanation: 'The same immutability that protects the chain from tampering also stops bad outcomes being undone' — transactions can't be reversed even when people are harmed.

questions.question: A report claims that blockchain will 'bank the unbanked', because anyone with a smartphone and a wallet can access financial services. Which practical barrier, raised in Section 3, does this claim overlook?
options: Creating a wallet requires a credit history, which most unbanked adults do not have
A wallet can only be opened by linking it to an existing bank account or card
Someone still has to provide the phone, the network signal and a safe way to keep a seed phrase
Public blockchains only admit users from countries that have formally approved them
questions.correct_option_text: Someone still has to provide the phone, the network signal and a safe way to keep a seed phrase
questions.explanation: The slide's 'ask yourself': a wallet needs a phone, a signal and a safe seed phrase — who provides those? The other three are not real barriers: a self-custody wallet needs no credit history, no bank account and nobody's approval, which is exactly why the claim sounds attractive.

questions.question: The same kind of ledger technology can send aid straight to people in need, with transfers that nobody can stop — or power state money in which any wallet can be frozen in seconds. According to Section 3, what decides which way it goes?
options: The consensus method: whether it runs on Proof of Work or Proof of Stake
The speed at which the network is able to confirm and settle transactions
The number of computers and countries that the network is spread across
The design and governance: who holds the keys, and who can change the rules
questions.correct_option_text: The design and governance: who holds the keys, and who can change the rules
questions.explanation: 'Design decides which.' The deciding question is who holds the keys and who can change the rules.

questions.question: What does a zero-knowledge proof make possible?
options: Proving that a fact is true without revealing the data behind it
Reversing a transaction without the consent of its recipient
Running a smart contract without paying for any of the gas
Reading another user's private key once they have given their agreement
questions.correct_option_text: Proving that a fact is true without revealing the data behind it
questions.explanation: Zero-knowledge proofs let you 'prove a fact without revealing the data behind it'.

questions.question: Earlier in the course, self-custody came with a hard user experience: no password reset and no support line. Which future trend from Section 3 targets this problem most directly?
options: Real-world assets — bonds, property and funds that are tokenised on-chain
Interoperability — a network of networks, with chains that talk to each other
Account abstraction — wallets that feel like normal apps, with recovery built in
AI + blockchain — proving what is real, with provenance for data and AI outputs
questions.correct_option_text: Account abstraction — wallets that feel like normal apps, with recovery built in
questions.explanation: Account abstraction is described as 'wallets that feel like normal apps: recovery, sponsored gas'.

questions.question: Several competing shipping firms, banks and customs agencies need one shared record of shipments. None of them is willing to let any single member — or an outside company — run the database. Following the course's 'could a blockchain fix this?' reasoning, why is a blockchain worth considering here?
options: Because a blockchain is faster and cheaper to run than a database shared between several firms
Because the core problem is trust between parties who have no single operator they would all accept
Because a blockchain would keep the shipment data secret from every one of the participants
Because a blockchain removes the need for the participants to agree on any common rules
questions.correct_option_text: Because the core problem is trust between parties who have no single operator they would all accept
questions.explanation: A shared ledger that no single party controls fits when trust or coordination between parties is the heart of the problem; where one trusted operator is acceptable, a database is enough.

questions.question: Public permissionless, consortium and private permissioned blockchains are presented as three types. According to the course, what actually separates them?
options: How many transactions per second each one can process
Whether the ledger is built from hashed, chained blocks
Who is allowed to read, write and validate
The strength of the cryptography each one uses
questions.correct_option_text: Who is allowed to read, write and validate
questions.explanation: The three types differ in who may read, write and validate, not in the cryptography underneath; speed is a consequence, not the definition.

questions.question: Six insurers who know one another, and can be held legally accountable, want a shared register of fraudulent claims. Each insists that its own claim volumes stay hidden from the other five. Using the course's "three questions to place your project", where does this project sit?
options: Off the spectrum: one insurer should simply host the register in its own internal database
Towards permissioned: all participants are known and accountable, and some data must stay hidden
Towards permissionless: competitors can only cooperate on a chain where nobody can be excluded
Towards permissionless: the more open the participation, the safer and more complete a shared register becomes
questions.correct_option_text: Towards permissioned: all participants are known and accountable, and some data must stay hidden
questions.explanation: Known, accountable participants and data that must stay hidden from some of them both point towards permissioned; and since no insurer is trusted to keep the register alone, a single-owner database does not fit.

questions.question: A retail group wants to track stock across its 200 stores and three warehouses, all of which it owns and operates. A consultant proposes a blockchain. What does the course's checklist say?
options: Use a public blockchain, so that every stock movement is tamper-evident to outsiders
Use a database: one organisation controls every participant, so it is cheaper and faster
Use a consortium chain, with each store acting as a separate validating member
Use a private blockchain, because a blockchain handles high volumes faster than a database
questions.correct_option_text: Use a database: one organisation controls every participant, so it is cheaper and faster
questions.explanation: If one organisation controls every writer you do not need a blockchain, you need a database: it is cheaper and faster. A blockchain earns its place when several parties share a record none is trusted to keep alone.

questions.question: A company keeps its ledger on 500 servers spread across 30 countries, but a single administrator can edit or delete any entry. By the definition used in this course, is the ledger decentralized?
options: Yes: once entries are spread over many machines, no single person can change them
Yes: a record copied across that many servers and countries is decentralized by definition
No: a ledger only counts as decentralized if it has a fixed supply and uses Proof of Work
No: what counts is who can change or censor the record, not the shape of the network
questions.correct_option_text: No: what counts is who can change or censor the record, not the shape of the network
questions.explanation: The course defines decentralization by control (who can change or censor the record), and treats the shape of the network as a separate question.

questions.question: A consortium chooses a permissioned chain instead of a public one. On the course's spectrum, which of these is it giving up by "moving right"?
options: Neutrality: a member can now be frozen out or removed
Compliance: participants can no longer be identified
Privacy: competitors can now see its volumes and prices
Control: members lose the ability to correct mistakes
questions.correct_option_text: Neutrality: a member can now be frozen out or removed
questions.explanation: Moving towards permissioned gains privacy, speed, compliance and control, and gives up what the permissionless end offers: open access, neutrality, censorship resistance and network effects.

questions.question: A large payment is recorded by mistake on a shared ledger. According to the "governance intuition" in this section, what can be done about it?
options: On a permissioned chain the members can agree on a correction; on a permissionless chain no one has the authority
On a permissionless chain the validators can simply vote to reverse it; on a permissioned chain nobody is able to do so
On either type nothing can be done, because every blockchain is immutable in exactly the same way
On either type, the sender can cancel the entry by signing a second transaction with the same key
questions.correct_option_text: On a permissioned chain the members can agree on a correction; on a permissionless chain no one has the authority
questions.explanation: Permissioned means known members agree the rules and can authorise a fix (normally a correcting entry, not an erasure of history); permissionless means nobody can be excluded and nobody is in a position to undo. Only an exceptional, community-wide fork, as after The DAO, has ever overridden that.

questions.question: A start-up plans to record "certified organic" labels for vegetables on a blockchain and tells buyers that this guarantees the produce really is organic. Which item on the course's "don't use a blockchain when…" list does the pitch run into?
options: One organisation controls every participant, so a database would do
All parties already trust a central party, such as a regulator
The truth lives off-chain: a blockchain cannot verify what it is told
The data must stay private and move in high volume
questions.correct_option_text: The truth lives off-chain: a blockchain cannot verify what it is told
questions.explanation: The ledger can make the label tamper-evident, but whether the vegetables are organic is an off-chain fact the chain cannot check: the oracle problem.

questions.question: A central bank pilots a digital currency in which it decides which institutions may run nodes and who may issue money. How does this section's sorting exercise classify the ledger?
options: Permissioned, because a known authority decides who may run nodes and issue
Permissionless, because every digital currency works the way Bitcoin does
Neither, because the two labels apply only to ledgers that use Proof of Work
Permissionless, because a currency meant for the general public has to be open to all
questions.correct_option_text: Permissioned, because a known authority decides who may run nodes and issue
questions.explanation: The question is who may write and validate: the central bank decides who runs nodes and who may issue, so the ledger is permissioned.

questions.question: Why would competing firms choose a consortium chain rather than letting one of them host a shared database?
options: It guarantees that every member can read all of every other member's data
It is open to anyone in the world, which gives the network the largest possible user base
It lets competitors share infrastructure without handing control to any one of them
It removes the need for the members to identify themselves to one another
questions.correct_option_text: It lets competitors share infrastructure without handing control to any one of them
questions.explanation: Consortium chains let competitors share infrastructure without handing control to any one of them; only vetted members transact and visibility is partial, among members.

questions.question: A team designs a digital savings token. Its whole appeal is that anyone, anywhere, can hold and send it without asking for approval, and that no participant can ever be frozen out. Which end of the spectrum does that requirement point to, and why?
options: Permissionless: open chains are faster and keep balances private
Permissioned: only vetted, known members can be relied on to keep a token safe
Permissioned: identities must be checked before anyone is allowed to hold value
Permissionless: the value depends on anyone in the world being able to join
questions.correct_option_text: Permissionless: the value depends on anyone in the world being able to join
questions.explanation: If the value depends on anyone in the world being able to join, lean permissionless; that end offers open access and neutrality, not speed or privacy.

questions.question: Which of these situations best "earns" a blockchain under the course's checklist?
options: A video service that stores millions of its customers' private viewing logs every hour
Carriers, ports and customs need one record of container hand-offs, and none trusts another to keep it
A hospital's internal staff rota, which only its own HR department ever needs to read or edit
A national land registry that buyers, sellers and banks all already trust to keep the record
questions.correct_option_text: Carriers, ports and customs need one record of container hand-offs, and none trusts another to keep it
questions.explanation: Several parties sharing one record that none is trusted to keep alone is the core case for a blockchain; the others are a trusted central party, a single owner, and private high-volume data.

questions.question: Bitcoin is described as four layers: application, network, consensus and data. Which layer does a typical business deal with directly, and what are the other three for?
options: The consensus layer (Proof of Work); the other three exist to make payments faster and cheaper
The application layer (wallets, exchanges); the other three make the record trustworthy without a bank
The data layer (blocks and Merkle trees); the other three exist to store users' private keys
The network layer (peer-to-peer gossip); the other three connect Bitcoin to other blockchains
questions.correct_option_text: The application layer (wallets, exchanges); the other three make the record trustworthy without a bank
questions.explanation: A business touches the app layer; the network, consensus and data layers are what make the record trustworthy without a bank.

questions.question: A finance director asks why Bitcoin blocks arrive only about every ten minutes instead of every second. According to this section, which layer sets that pace, and what is it buying?
options: The consensus layer: blocks are tuned to take about ten minutes of costly work, the security budget
The application layer: wallets deliberately hold payments back and batch them to save their users fees
The data layer: each block must be copied in full to every node before the next one can start
The network layer: a transaction needs about ten minutes to travel across the world to every node
questions.correct_option_text: The consensus layer: blocks are tuned to take about ten minutes of costly work, the security budget
questions.explanation: The consensus layer is the security budget and the reason blocks arrive every ~10 minutes: the difficulty is adjusted to hold that pace, which also gives each block time to reach the whole network. The network itself spreads a transaction to the nodes within seconds.

questions.question: Each Bitcoin block header contains the hash of the block before it. What follows if someone alters a transaction in an old block?
options: The link to every later block breaks, so the change is evident
The network accepts the altered block as the newest version
The altered block returns to the mempool to be mined again
Only that one block changes; the later blocks are unaffected
questions.correct_option_text: The link to every later block breaks, so the change is evident
questions.explanation: Each block header references the previous hash, so altering any block breaks all subsequent blocks.

questions.question: Someone broadcasts a Bitcoin transaction that tries to spend coins they have already spent. At which stage of the journey does it stop?
options: In the mempool: it waits in the queue until a miner finally rejects it for its low fee
At signing: the sender's wallet has to obtain the miners' approval before it is able to sign
At block acceptance: it is mined into a block first and removed once it reaches six confirmations
At relay and check: nodes verify that the coins are unspent and do not pass an invalid transaction on
questions.correct_option_text: At relay and check: nodes verify that the coins are unspent and do not pass an invalid transaction on
questions.explanation: Every node checks the signature and that the coins are unspent before passing a transaction on; invalid ones stop there and never reach the mempool.

questions.question: A dealer selling a car for bitcoin waits for about six confirmations before handing over the keys. What are those confirmations doing?
options: The payment is being copied onto six separate blockchains for safekeeping
Six different miners are each re-signing the same transaction in turn, to rule out a forgery
The transaction fee is being paid in six instalments, one per block
Each new block on top makes rewriting the block holding the payment more expensive
questions.correct_option_text: Each new block on top makes rewriting the block holding the payment more expensive
questions.explanation: Each new block on top makes rewriting yours more expensive; after about six blocks the payment is irreversible for all practical purposes.

questions.question: On Bitcoin and on Ethereum, a payment goes through the same basic steps (sign, broadcast, queue, block, confirm). According to the section, what is actually different between the two?
options: Whether nodes re-check each new block: they do on Bitcoin, but not on Ethereum
Whether the wallet signs the payment: it does on Bitcoin, but not on Ethereum
Who proposes the block (miner or validator) and how fast it becomes final
Whether payments wait in a fee-ranked queue: they do on Bitcoin only
questions.correct_option_text: Who proposes the block (miner or validator) and how fast it becomes final
questions.explanation: The steps are the same on both: sign, broadcast, queue, block, confirm. What differs is who proposes the block (a miner on Bitcoin, a chosen validator on Ethereum) and how fast the payment becomes final (about 1 hour on Bitcoin, about 13 minutes on Ethereum).

questions.question: Your wallet has built and signed a Bitcoin payment, but your phone loses its connection before the payment is broadcast. What is the state of the payment?
options: Nothing is on-chain yet: the transaction has not left your device
It has one confirmation, because signing a payment is what confirms it
It is final, because a valid signature cannot be withdrawn
It is waiting in the mempool, in a queue ranked by the fee it offers
questions.correct_option_text: Nothing is on-chain yet: the transaction has not left your device
questions.explanation: Signing happens in the wallet and puts nothing on-chain; the transaction only leaves the device when it is broadcast to the nodes.

questions.question: A new chain reaches very high throughput by requiring every validator to run powerful, expensive hardware. Going by the trilemma slide's example of Solana, which corner is most likely to pay for this?
options: None, because the trilemma applies only to chains that use Proof of Work
Scalability, because costly hardware slows each individual transaction down
Decentralization, because costly hardware concentrates the validator set
Scalability, because the fees must rise to pay for all of the validators' hardware
questions.correct_option_text: Decentralization, because costly hardware concentrates the validator set
questions.explanation: Platforms tend to optimise for two corners and pay on the third: Solana puts throughput first, and its high hardware requirements concentrate the validator set.

questions.question: Ordinals, BRC-20 and Runes let people put non-payment data and tokens on Bitcoin. Why does the section call them "contested"?
options: They move bitcoin onto sidechains run by a federation of exchanges
They raise Bitcoin's total supply above the 21 million cap that makes it scarce
They bloat the chain and spike fees, at odds with a minimal base layer
They replace Proof of Work with staking for the blocks that carry them
questions.correct_option_text: They bloat the chain and spike fees, at odds with a minimal base layer
questions.explanation: Inscriptions bloat the chain and spike fees; purists want the base chain kept minimal ("digital gold") while builders want a settlement layer for richer apps.

questions.question: What does "Bitcoin staking" through Babylon allow a BTC holder to do?
options: Earn a fixed rate of interest that Bitcoin miners pay out of transaction fees
Validate Bitcoin's own blocks by staking coins, as a low-energy alternative to mining them
Swap BTC for a wrapped token that a custodian then lends out on Ethereum
Lock BTC on Bitcoin to help secure other proof-of-stake networks, and earn yield
questions.correct_option_text: Lock BTC on Bitcoin to help secure other proof-of-stake networks, and earn yield
questions.explanation: Babylon lets BTC holders lock coins to secure other proof-of-stake networks and earn yield without wrapping or moving the BTC off Bitcoin; Bitcoin itself still runs on Proof of Work.

questions.question: An importer in a high-inflation country must pay an overseas supplier over a weekend, and no bank is willing to intermediate. According to "Where Bitcoin wins", which properties make Bitcoin a fit here?
options: High-volume payments that are free and instant for everyone on the base layer
Censorship resistance, no intermediary, 24/7 availability and settlement in minutes
Private channels that hide the payment from everyone except the two firms
Built-in smart contracts that hold the payment in programmable escrow until delivery
questions.correct_option_text: Censorship resistance, no intermediary, 24/7 availability and settlement in minutes
questions.explanation: For cross-border settlement the slide lists censorship resistance, no intermediary and 24/7 availability, settling in minutes versus days; programmability, privacy and base-layer volume are where Bitcoin loses.

questions.question: Three projects are pitched "on Bitcoin": (A) a lending app with programmable rules, (B) confidential records shared by four known suppliers, (C) thousands of small coffee payments a day. Following the section's "Not a fit for" guidance, where should each go?
options: A: Lightning; B: a programmable chain such as Ethereum; C: Bitcoin's base layer
A: a programmable chain such as Ethereum; B: Fabric; C: Lightning
A: Bitcoin's base layer; B: Lightning; C: a permissioned chain such as Fabric
A: a permissioned chain such as Fabric; B: Bitcoin's base layer; C: Ethereum
questions.correct_option_text: A: a programmable chain such as Ethereum; B: Fabric; C: Lightning
questions.explanation: Bitcoin is not a general-purpose computer: smart contracts and DeFi go to a programmable chain, private B2B consortia to Fabric, and high-volume retail payments to Lightning.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Before Ethereum, a team with an idea for a new blockchain application (say, a decentralised auction) ran into one of the Bitcoin limits listed in this section. Which one?
options: There was no shared environment for general-purpose logic, so projects typically had to launch a chain of their own
Bitcoin's blocks arrived too quickly, so an application could not keep its own records in step with the chain
Bitcoin's transactions were kept private, so an application had no way to read what was happening on the chain
Bitcoin's supply was capped at 21 million coins, so there was no way to fund the development of new applications
questions.correct_option_text: There was no shared environment for general-purpose logic, so projects typically had to launch a chain of their own
questions.explanation: Bitcoin's Script was deliberately limited and offered no shared environment for general-purpose programs, so a new application usually meant a new chain with its own security (or awkward workarounds on top of Bitcoin); Ethereum's answer was one chain that can run any program.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: The section compares Bitcoin Script to a vending machine and the Ethereum Virtual Machine to a kitchen. What is the point of the comparison?
options: Script is faster because it runs on a single machine, while the EVM is slower because it runs on many machines
Bitcoin is meant for individuals making small purchases, while Ethereum is meant for businesses with large orders
Bitcoin is cheaper to use than Ethereum, in the way that a snack from a machine is cheaper than a cooked meal
Script offers a fixed menu of operations, while the EVM can repeat, remember and decide, so it can run any program
questions.correct_option_text: Script offers a fixed menu of operations, while the EVM can repeat, remember and decide, so it can run any program
questions.explanation: Bitcoin Script is a fixed menu: one button, one fixed result. The EVM has loops, memory and conditions, so it can run any recipe you can write down, given enough gas.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Suppose Ethereum abolished gas altogether: no metering, no limits, no fees. Going by "Why gas exists", what would break?
options: ETH's supply would become capped, because gas fees are the mechanism by which new ETH is issued
Nothing important, because gas exists only to reward the developers who write smart contracts
Wallets could no longer sign transactions, because the gas payment is what makes a signature valid
The chain could be flooded with spam, and a program told to "repeat forever" would never stop
questions.correct_option_text: The chain could be flooded with spam, and a program told to "repeat forever" would never stop
questions.explanation: Gas guarantees that every program stops (the EVM is Turing-complete), deters spam, and prices scarce block space.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Your phone, with your MetaMask wallet on it, is destroyed. You still have the 12-word seed phrase written on paper. What has happened to your ETH?
options: It is safe only if you also kept a separate written copy of your public address
It is frozen until MetaMask's support team has verified your identity and reissued the keys
Nothing: the balance lives on-chain, and the seed phrase restores your keys in a new wallet
It is lost: the coins were stored inside the wallet app on the phone that was destroyed
questions.correct_option_text: Nothing: the balance lives on-chain, and the seed phrase restores your keys in a new wallet
questions.explanation: A wallet manages keys, not coins: balances live on-chain and the seed phrase regenerates every key. Lose the app and keep the seed phrase, and nothing is lost.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: The EVM is described as "deterministic". What does that mean, and why does it matter?
options: Contracts run only at scheduled times, so every node in the network stays in step with the others
The same input gives the same output on every node, so thousands of machines can agree on one result
Only one designated node runs each contract, so two machines can never produce conflicting results
Fees are fixed in advance by the protocol, so users always know exactly what a transaction will cost
questions.correct_option_text: The same input gives the same output on every node, so thousands of machines can agree on one result
questions.explanation: Deterministic means the same input gives the same output on every node; thousands of machines run the same program and must agree on one result.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Two transactions land in the same Ethereum block with the same tip: a plain ETH transfer and a call to a complex smart contract that stores a lot of data. Why does the contract call cost more?
options: It uses more gas: every operation is priced in gas, and heavier work uses more
Validators set a higher base fee for contract calls than they do for plain transfers
The contract's owner sets a surcharge, which the network adds on top of the gas fee
Contract calls pay the base fee twice: once to the validator and once to the contract
