questions.correct_option_text: It uses more gas: every operation is priced in gas, and heavier work uses more
questions.explanation: Cost = gas used × (base fee + tip). The base fee per unit of gas is the same for everyone in the block; what differs is the work done, and the harder the work the more gas it uses.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Demand surges and Ethereum blocks stay more than half full for many blocks in a row. Under EIP-1559, what happens to the base fee?
options: It stays where it is until the validators hold a vote and agree to change it
The protocol raises it automatically, block after block, while blocks stay over half full
It is suspended and replaced by an auction in which the highest bids win the block space
It falls, so that the transactions waiting in the queue can be cleared more quickly
questions.correct_option_text: The protocol raises it automatically, block after block, while blocks stay over half full
questions.explanation: The protocol sets the base fee and adjusts it every block to steer blocks towards 50% fullness, so blocks that stay fuller than that push it up; the blind first-price auction is what EIP-1559 replaced.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A firm deploys a smart contract on Ethereum, with no upgrade mechanism built in, and a week later wants to quietly change one of its rules. According to the "key properties" slide, what stands in the way?
options: A vote: validators must approve each code change by a two-thirds majority
Nothing: the wallet that deployed the contract can edit its code at any time
Only the cost: editing deployed code simply uses more gas than deploying it did
The deployed code cannot be changed, and it is public, so anyone can check what it does
questions.correct_option_text: The deployed code cannot be changed, and it is public, so anyone can check what it does
questions.explanation: Smart contracts are immutable (deployed code cannot be edited), deterministic and transparent, so nobody can quietly change one. Two caveats: a contract can be designed to be upgradeable (a proxy pointing to replaceable logic), which is why you check whether an admin or upgrade key exists; and while the on-chain bytecode is always public, readable source code is published and verified as a separate step.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Once an Ethereum block is finalised, what would undoing it cost, according to the "How Proof of Stake works" steps?
options: At least a third of all staked ETH would be destroyed (slashed)
Enough electricity to out-compute every miner for about an hour
Nothing beyond the gas fees of the replacement transactions
The 32 ETH deposit of the one validator who proposed the block
questions.correct_option_text: At least a third of all staked ETH would be destroyed (slashed)
questions.explanation: After enough validator votes a block is final, and undoing it would mean at least a third of all staked ETH being slashed: security moved from burning electricity to risking capital.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: In the staking simulation, a validator is picked to propose a block and signs two conflicting versions of it. What happens?
options: Nothing happens beyond a lost turn: the validator simply proposes again in a later slot
Both versions are added to the chain, and the network later keeps the longer branch
The other validators accept one version and share the cheater's reward among themselves
The validator is slashed: part of its stake is burned and it is ejected from the validator set
questions.correct_option_text: The validator is slashed: part of its stake is burned and it is ejected from the validator set
questions.explanation: A validator that cheats, for example by proposing two conflicting blocks, is slashed: part of its deposit is burned and it is forced out.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A treasurer wants staking rewards on the company's ETH but must be able to get out within minutes if needed. Which path allows that, and what is the catch?
options: Liquid staking: the token can be sold at once on the market, but it may trade below 1:1 when many holders want out
Solo staking: the 32 ETH deposit can be withdrawn instantly at any time, but the rewards are lower than on other paths
Any path: the protocol guarantees every staker an instant exit, but charges a penalty that is burned
A staked-ETH fund: shares are redeemed for ETH on-chain within minutes, but the fund charges a fee for doing so
questions.correct_option_text: Liquid staking: the token can be sold at once on the market, but it may trade below 1:1 when many holders want out
questions.explanation: A liquid-staking token can be sold at once on the market, though it can trade below 1:1 when many want out at once. Solo stakers wait in the exit queue (hours to weeks); fund shares are sold through a broker and settle in cash on the market's own timetable.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A pension analyst wants an asset whose future supply can be read off a fixed schedule decades ahead. Comparing the two "scarcity" models on the issuance slide, which asset fits and why?
options: ETH: the fee burn guarantees that the supply shrinks every year, whatever the level of network activity
ETH: its total supply is capped by the protocol at about 120 million, a level it reached at the Merge
BTC: a fixed 21 million with scheduled halvings, whereas ETH's supply depends on network usage
Neither: both supplies are reset each year by a vote of the miners or validators who secure the chain
questions.correct_option_text: BTC: a fixed 21 million with scheduled halvings, whereas ETH's supply depends on network usage
questions.explanation: Bitcoin sells scarcity by rule (fixed 21M, halvings, nothing burned); Ethereum sells scarcity by usage (issuance minus burn, no hard cap, policy changed by upgrade).

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Why does Ethereum not simply make its L1 blocks much bigger and faster to handle more transactions?
options: Bigger blocks would cause new ETH to be issued more quickly, making the supply inflationary
Bigger blocks need stronger computers to check them, so fewer people could run a node
Bigger blocks are impossible, because the EVM can process only a fixed number of transactions
Bigger blocks would make every transaction publicly visible, which today's small blocks prevent
questions.correct_option_text: Bigger blocks need stronger computers to check them, so fewer people could run a node
questions.explanation: Bigger blocks are not free: they need stronger computers to check them, so fewer people would be checking the chain. Ethereum keeps decentralisation and security on L1 and pushes scale to L2.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: The section's key point is that rollups "move execution off Ethereum while security stays on it". What does that look like in practice?
options: The rollup keeps its data and proofs on its own servers and reports to Ethereum only if there is a dispute
Users move their ETH to a separate chain whose own validators then take over the whole job of securing it
A sequencer executes transactions off-chain and posts one compressed update to Ethereum for verification
Ethereum's validators execute every rollup transaction themselves, but charge a lower fee for doing so
questions.correct_option_text: A sequencer executes transactions off-chain and posts one compressed update to Ethereum for verification
questions.explanation: A rollup batches thousands of transactions off-chain and posts one compressed update to L1: execution moves off-chain, the data stays on-chain, and security is inherited from Ethereum.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A company picks a general-purpose ZK rollup because it assumes "zero-knowledge" will hide its transactions from competitors. Is that right, according to this section?
options: No: a ZK rollup is less private than Ethereum, because it also publishes users' identities
Yes, but only during the challenge window; after about 7 days the data becomes public
No: "ZK" here buys cheap checking, not secrecy; such a rollup is as public as Ethereum
Yes: a ZK rollup encrypts every transaction, and only Ethereum's validators hold the key
questions.correct_option_text: No: "ZK" here buys cheap checking, not secrecy; such a rollup is as public as Ethereum
questions.explanation: In a standard ZK rollup the proof lets Ethereum check a batch cheaply; it does not hide anything, so the rollup is as public as Ethereum itself. (Privacy-focused designs such as Aztec are a separate category, built for that purpose.)

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: In an automated market maker such as Uniswap, what replaces the order book that matches buyers with sellers?
options: A bank that quotes buy and sell prices and keeps the spread
A committee of validators that votes on the price each block
A queue in which the oldest orders are served first
A pool holding two tokens, with a formula that sets the price
questions.correct_option_text: A pool holding two tokens, with a formula that sets the price
questions.explanation: In an AMM two tokens sit in a pool and a formula sets the price; there are no buyers and sellers to match.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A borrower locks $150 of ETH in a DeFi lending protocol and borrows $100. ETH's price then falls sharply and the collateral drops below the required threshold. What happens next?
options: Liquidator bots sell the collateral to repay the loan
The lender must go to court to recover the funds
The protocol reviews the borrower's credit score
The loan is paused until the price of ETH recovers
questions.correct_option_text: Liquidator bots sell the collateral to repay the loan
questions.explanation: DeFi loans of this kind are over-collateralised with no credit score; if the collateral falls below the threshold, anyone (in practice bots, which earn a reward) can liquidate the position.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A liquidity provider deposits two tokens into an AMM pool and earns trading fees, yet ends up worse off than if she had simply held the two tokens. Which risk named in this section explains it?
options: De-pegging: the pool's stablecoin lost its reserves
Impermanent loss: the two tokens' prices moved apart
Liquidation: her collateral fell below the threshold
Slashing: the pool was penalised for going offline
questions.correct_option_text: Impermanent loss: the two tokens' prices moved apart
questions.explanation: Impermanent loss: when the two tokens' prices diverge, a liquidity provider can end up worse off than by simply holding them.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A regulated issuer backs its stablecoin 1:1 with dollars and Treasury bills. According to the "breaks when" column, which event most directly threatens that coin's peg?
options: Ethereum's base fee rises sharply during a busy period
The bank holding the reserves fails, leaving part of the backing stuck
Holders lose confidence in the coin's mint-and-burn incentives
A crash in the price of ETH outruns the bots that liquidate the collateral
questions.correct_option_text: The bank holding the reserves fails, leaving part of the backing stuck
questions.explanation: A stablecoin is only as stable as what backs it: a fiat-backed coin can lose its peg when its reserves are stuck or impaired, as when the issuer's bank fails. A crash outrunning liquidators is the crypto-backed failure; a confidence spiral is the algorithmic one.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A collector buys an NFT of a digital artwork. A year later the server hosting the image file shuts down. What does she own now?
options: Nothing: the token is deleted from the chain as soon as its file disappears
The artwork itself, since the image file is stored inside the token on-chain
The token, still hers on-chain, but now pointing to a file that is gone
A refund claim, which the smart contract pays out automatically in ETH
questions.correct_option_text: The token, still hers on-chain, but now pointing to a file that is gone
questions.explanation: The token is on-chain but the file it points to usually is not; if the off-chain file disappears, you own a broken pointer.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A protocol advertises that it is "governed by its 50,000 token-holders". Based on the limits this section lists for DAOs, what should a sceptical analyst expect to find?
options: Votes and payments that are kept off-chain, so that nobody outside can audit them
A rule that every holder must vote on every proposal, or else the treasury stays locked
A chief executive who can move the treasury's funds without any vote taking place
Low turnout, a few large holders deciding, and a small core team doing most of the work
questions.correct_option_text: Low turnout, a few large holders deciding, and a small core team doing most of the work
questions.explanation: The listed limits: turnout is often in the low single digits, a few whales can decide, and many DAOs delegate to a small core team. Where execution is on-chain, the treasury is moved by code after a vote and leaves an audit trail.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Which of these projects does the section flag as the wrong job for Ethereum mainnet?
options: A consortium that has to store supplier contracts and health records
A ticketing scheme that issues each ticket as a unique token (NFT)
A community fund whose treasury is released by token-holder vote
A lending protocol that plugs into existing exchanges and stablecoins
questions.correct_option_text: A consortium that has to store supplier contracts and health records
questions.explanation: Mainnet is fully public, so it is unsuitable for KYC data, supplier contracts or health records; the other three (DeFi, NFTs, DAOs) are listed as best fits.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A studio wants every move in a fast action game, about 60 updates a second, recorded directly on Ethereum L1. What is the basic mismatch?
options: Ethereum's supply has no hard cap, which makes any in-game currency lose value
Ethereum L1 produces a block only about every 12 seconds, too slow for real-time play
Ethereum's rules do not allow a game's smart contract to hold a balance of ETH
Ethereum has no token standard that can represent a game item a player owns
questions.correct_option_text: Ethereum L1 produces a block only about every 12 seconds, too slow for real-time play
questions.explanation: With ~12-second blocks on L1, Ethereum is too slow for latency-critical, real-time applications; even fast rollups are not built to record 60 updates a second per player.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: The section says to choose Ethereum "when composability and shared liquidity are the product". What does composability mean here?
options: Applications can be freely rewritten by their developers at any time after they have been deployed
Each application runs on its own separate chain, with its own rules and its own set of validators
Protocols on the same platform snap together like "money legos", even within one transaction
Users can choose to pay their transaction fees in whichever token they happen to be holding
questions.correct_option_text: Protocols on the same platform snap together like "money legos", even within one transaction
questions.explanation: Composability means protocols snap together like money legos (three protocols, one transaction), because they share one platform and its standards.

questions.question: A permissioned network gives up "trustlessness". Where does this section say the trust goes instead?
options: To miners: they are paid in the consortium's own token to keep the record honest
To the general public: anyone can inspect every transaction and raise the alarm
To the software vendor: it guarantees the ledger against errors and fraud
To governance: the consortium agreement and whoever runs the ordering nodes
questions.correct_option_text: To governance: the consortium agreement and whoever runs the ordering nodes
questions.explanation: On a permissioned chain trust moves from maths to governance: you rely on the consortium agreement and on whoever runs the ordering nodes.

questions.question: Among the trade-finance networks in this section, the bank consortia (we.trade, Contour, Marco Polo) closed, while JPMorgan's Kinexys is still live. What explanation does the section give?
options: Kinexys rewards its members with a token; the consortia had no means of paying the banks that took part
Kinexys has a single owner whose own clients use it; the consortia worked technically but lost their funding
Kinexys runs on a public chain, so it inherited an existing base of users, while the consortia had to start from zero
Kinexys runs on better technology; the software that the consortia were using could not cope with the volume of deals
questions.correct_option_text: Kinexys has a single owner whose own clients use it; the consortia worked technically but lost their funding
questions.explanation: In trade finance the technology worked; the consortia closed when the banks stopped funding them, and the survivor has a single owner whose own clients use it.

questions.question: IBM Food Trust won real adoption among Walmart's suppliers, while TradeLens shut down after about four years, although both ran on Fabric. According to the case-study lessons, what made the difference for Food Trust?
options: It was open to anonymous participants, which let its network grow faster than TradeLens
It could process far more transactions per second than TradeLens, which struggled
Walmart could require its suppliers to join, and the old paper process had failed during recalls
It paid each supplier a token reward for every record uploaded, which TradeLens did not
questions.correct_option_text: Walmart could require its suppliers to join, and the old paper process had failed during recalls
questions.explanation: Permissioned networks succeed when someone can require participation and the old process is visibly broken, not when the technology is best. (This is a lesson about how adoption was won; check Food Trust's current commercial status before describing it as live.)

questions.question: The section argues that government-led networks such as the EU's EBSI are better placed than market consortia to get past the network-effect problem. What is the sound version of that argument?
options: EBSI runs on Bitcoin, which already has millions of users around the world
Public bodies issue a token whose rising price attracts users to the network
Governments can afford faster hardware and bigger data centres than private consortia
A public body can convene, fund and standardise it and, where the law allows, require its use
questions.correct_option_text: A public body can convene, fund and standardise it and, where the law allows, require its use
questions.explanation: A market consortium must persuade each competitor that joining pays; a public authority can act as the neutral convener, fund the infrastructure, set common standards and, where legislation provides for it, make participation mandatory. That eases the network-effect problem but does not abolish it: EBSI itself has grown through voluntary participation and pilots, and useful adoption still has to be earned.

questions.question: A sceptic asks why the partners in a Fabric network don't just use one shared database. What is the section's answer?
options: A database needs a native token to pay its operators; in Fabric the nodes are paid for by transaction fees
A database can be used by only one company at a time; in Fabric several organisations can be online at once
A database has one administrator who can change it; in Fabric every organisation checks every change itself
A database cannot hold as many records as a blockchain; in Fabric the ledger's storage grows without any limit
questions.correct_option_text: A database has one administrator who can change it; in Fabric every organisation checks every change itself
questions.explanation: A database has one administrator who can change it; in Fabric each organisation keeps its own copy and validates every change, so no single member can rewrite the record.

questions.question: Every Fabric peer stores two things: the blockchain and the world state. An auditor needs the full history of changes to a shipment record; a warehouse app only needs the record's current status. Which part serves each?
options: The auditor uses the blockchain (the full history); the app reads the world state (current values)
Both use the world state, since the blockchain is kept only as a backup in case of a crash
The auditor uses the world state (the full history); the app reads the blockchain (current values)
Both must ask the ordering service, since it holds the only complete and up-to-date copy of the ledger
questions.correct_option_text: The auditor uses the blockchain (the full history); the app reads the world state (current values)
questions.explanation: The blockchain is the full, append-only history of transactions; the world state is the current value of every record, kept for fast look-ups.

questions.question: Suppose a faulty ordering node places in a block a transaction that lacks the endorsements the policy requires. What stops it from taking effect?
options: The client application that proposed the transaction has to spot the problem and cancel it
Every peer re-checks the signatures against the policy itself and flags the transaction invalid
Nothing can stop it: once the ordering service has put a transaction in a block, it is final
The certificate authority notices the missing signatures and deletes the block from every ledger
questions.correct_option_text: Every peer re-checks the signatures against the policy itself and flags the transaction invalid
questions.explanation: Every organisation's peer re-checks the signatures itself before committing, so a faulty orderer cannot forge content; a transaction that falls short is flagged invalid.

questions.question: Fabric can reach thousands of transactions per second in benchmarks. According to the transaction-flow slide, where does that throughput come from?
options: Chaincode runs before ordering, so different peers can simulate many transactions in parallel
Blocks are far larger than on public chains, and the members run more powerful mining hardware
Transactions are not signed by anyone, which removes the slowest step in processing each one
Only one organisation validates each transaction, which avoids every peer repeating the same check
questions.correct_option_text: Chaincode runs before ordering, so different peers can simulate many transactions in parallel
questions.explanation: Execute-order-validate: Fabric runs chaincode before ordering, so peers can simulate many transactions in parallel, and separating ordering from execution is why it handles thousands per second.

questions.question: A retailer's ERP system is set to release payment the moment a delivery is recorded. On Fabric, how long must it wait before treating the record as final?
options: About an hour: as on Bitcoin, six further blocks must be added on top of it first
About 13 minutes: the validators need that long to vote on and finalise the block
Seconds: once peers commit the block and report the transaction as valid, it is final
Until the end of the day: the consortium reconciles all members' copies overnight
questions.correct_option_text: Seconds: once peers commit the block and report the transaction as valid, it is final
questions.explanation: Fabric gives finality in seconds, not after six confirmations: the peers commit the block and an event tells the ERP that the transaction was valid, so it can act on it immediately.

questions.question: On a public chain you create your own key pair and that is your account. How is identity handled in Fabric?
options: It is assigned afresh by the ordering service each time a new block is cut
It is an anonymous address that each user generates privately from a seed phrase
It is optional: members may choose to transact without identifying themselves
It is a certificate issued by your organisation's own certificate authority
questions.correct_option_text: It is a certificate issued by your organisation's own certificate authority
questions.explanation: In Fabric your identity is a key pair plus a certificate issued by your organisation, not just a key you create yourself; the certificate authority issues the certificate and can revoke it.

questions.question: On public chains, rule changes can be decided by on-chain governance such as token votes. How are the rules of a Fabric channel changed?
options: By a configuration update signed by the member organisations
By a vote among everyone who holds the network's native token
By whichever member organisation runs the most peers
By the software vendor, which pushes updates out to all peers
questions.correct_option_text: By a configuration update signed by the member organisations
questions.explanation: In Fabric, rule changes are configuration transactions signed by member organisations (a consortium vote), not token votes.

questions.question: Two projects need a platform. Project 1 is an app open to anyone in the world that depends on a shared pool of users and liquidity. Project 2 links seven identified banks that must keep deal data confidential. Following "choose by who your participants are", which platform fits each?
options: Fabric for Project 1 and Ethereum for Project 2
Ethereum for Project 1 and Fabric for Project 2
Fabric for both, because it processes more transactions
Ethereum for both, because it has the larger user base
questions.correct_option_text: Ethereum for Project 1 and Fabric for Project 2
questions.explanation: Ethereum sells openness to strangers; Fabric sells privacy and control to known partners. Choose by who your participants are.

questions.question: A consortium on a permissioned network wants to bring in a new logistics partner. What does this section say that involves, and which "give-up" does it illustrate?
options: The partner must be invited, sign agreements and be issued certificates: the loss of open access
The partner downloads a wallet and can start transacting the same day: the loss of censorship resistance
The partner buys the network's token on an exchange in order to pay its fees: the loss of network effects
The partner simply waits for the next block to be cut by the orderers: the loss of trustlessness
questions.correct_option_text: The partner must be invited, sign agreements and be issued certificates: the loss of open access
questions.explanation: On a permissioned chain nobody joins without an invitation; every new partner means onboarding, legal agreements and certificates. That is the open access you give up.

questions.question: Before a shared ledger, tracing a batch of mangoes back to the farm took Walmart about seven days. According to the "pain today" this section describes for supply chains, why so long?
options: Privacy regulations barred the suppliers from sharing any origin data
Each partner used a different channel, and channels cannot be searched
Each partner kept its own records, so a trace meant many separate systems
The records sat on a public blockchain whose blocks were slow to confirm
questions.correct_option_text: Each partner kept its own records, so a trace meant many separate systems
questions.explanation: Every partner keeps its own records, so a recall means going through each system in turn; one shared timeline cut the mango trace from 7 days to 2.2 seconds.

questions.question: The same token can trade at one price on Ethereum and a different price on Arbitrum. Which consequence of closed chains does this illustrate?
options: Costly connectors: the price gap shows that the token was stolen from a bridge between the two
Stranded assets: the token exists on only one chain's ledger and cannot be used on the other one
The oracle problem: neither of the two chains has any way to learn what the token is really worth
Split-up markets: each chain has its own exchanges and pools, and moving between them costs time
questions.correct_option_text: Split-up markets: each chain has its own exchanges and pools, and moving between them costs time
questions.explanation: Split-up markets: every chain has its own exchanges and pools, so the same token can trade at two prices, and moving between them costs time and fees.

questions.question: You used a lock-and-mint bridge to turn 1 ETH on Ethereum into 1 wETH on Solana. How do you get your original ETH back?
options: Burn (hand back) the wETH on Solana; the bridge then unlocks your original ETH on Ethereum.
Do nothing: the wETH expires after a set time and the ETH returns to your wallet by itself.
Send the wETH straight to your Ethereum address; it turns back into ETH when it arrives.
Ask Solana's validators to release it, because they are holding your original ETH.
questions.correct_option_text: Burn (hand back) the wETH on Solana; the bridge then unlocks your original ETH on Ethereum.
questions.explanation: A bridge never moves a coin: your original ETH stays locked in the bridge's vault on Ethereum, and the wETH on Solana is a claim ticket. To go back, you return the wETH to the bridge, which burns it and unlocks the original ETH on Ethereum. Wrapped tokens do not expire, cannot be sent directly to another chain, and Solana's validators do not hold the ETH.

questions.question: You hold 1 WBTC on Ethereum. How would you get real bitcoin on the Bitcoin network?
options: Wait for Ethereum's validators to convert it, since they keep a reserve of real BTC behind every WBTC
Send the WBTC back through the bridge (custodian) that minted it, which unlocks the real BTC on the Bitcoin chain
Ask Bitcoin's miners to release the BTC, since the miners are the ones who guard the vault where the BTC is locked
Send the WBTC to a Bitcoin address, where the network converts it back into BTC automatically
questions.correct_option_text: Send the WBTC back through the bridge (custodian) that minted it, which unlocks the real BTC on the Bitcoin chain
questions.explanation: A bridge never moves a coin: the real BTC stays locked with the custodian, and the WBTC is the claim ticket. To get the BTC back you hand the ticket back: the WBTC returns to the bridge (custodian) that minted it and is burned, and the locked BTC is released on the Bitcoin chain (the "burn → withdraw" arrow on the slide). Miners and validators do not hold the vault, and the Bitcoin network cannot read an Ethereum token. In practice this redemption step runs through the custodian's approved merchants.

questions.question: Which power does the issuer of a custodial wrapped token such as WBTC hold over your balance?
options: It can pause the token contract or refuse to redeem
It can spend the coins held in your own Bitcoin wallet
It can reverse payments already made on the Bitcoin chain
None: a wrapped token is as independent as the original coin
questions.correct_option_text: It can pause the token contract or refuse to redeem
questions.explanation: A wrapped token is an IOU: the issuer can pause the contract and can refuse to redeem, and the token is worth the original only while someone holds that coin and agrees to give it back.

questions.question: "The question to ask of any wrapped token is who holds the original." By that test, which of these involves no custodian or bridge operator?
options: wETH on Solana, which was issued to its holder through a lock-and-mint bridge
WBTC on Ethereum, which stands for bitcoin that is kept on the Bitcoin chain
A game item from another chain, bridged to an Ethereum marketplace
WETH on Ethereum itself, where a plain contract swaps ETH and WETH 1:1
questions.correct_option_text: WETH on Ethereum itself, where a plain contract swaps ETH and WETH 1:1
questions.explanation: Not every wrapper needs a custodian: WETH on Ethereum itself is a plain contract that swaps ETH and WETH 1:1 with nobody in the middle.

questions.question: A treasurer needs to move funds from Ethereum to Arbitrum. Following the section's practical advice on bridges, what should she do?
options: Use a bridge run by a small group of signers, since fewer keys are easier to guard
Use the rollup's own official (canonical) bridge, and move only the amount needed
Buy a custodial wrapped token first, since a custodian is safer than any bridge
Use whichever third-party bridge is fastest and move the whole treasury at once
questions.correct_option_text: Use the rollup's own official (canonical) bridge, and move only the amount needed
questions.explanation: Prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge, which is secured by the rollup's proof system rather than a separate group of signers, and move only what you need.

questions.question: The Nomad bridge was emptied within hours once a flaw was found. Which safeguard from "what safer looks like" would most directly have limited the loss?
options: A higher bridge fee, so that fewer users choose to withdraw their funds
A bigger vault, so that any loss is spread across a larger number of users
A smaller group of signers, so that withdrawals are approved more quickly
Rate limits or circuit breakers that cap how much can leave per hour
questions.correct_option_text: Rate limits or circuit breakers that cap how much can leave per hour
questions.explanation: Rate limits and circuit breakers cap how much can leave per hour; Nomad was drained within hours, and a limit would have capped the outflow and bought time to respond.

questions.question: A user on an optimistic rollup does not want to wait about 7 days to withdraw through the official bridge, so she uses a "fast" third-party bridge instead. What has she traded?
options: Nothing: a fast bridge is secured by the same proof system
Ethereum's security, in exchange for that of Bitcoin's miners
A shorter wait, in exchange for a third party she must now trust
A lower fee, in exchange for a longer challenge window
questions.correct_option_text: A shorter wait, in exchange for a third party she must now trust
questions.explanation: The canonical route back to L1 is slow (about 7 days on an optimistic rollup); fast third-party bridges fix that by adding a party, and its liquidity, that you must trust.

questions.question: A large, well-secured chain connects over IBC to a small chain with a weak validator set. According to the section's "where it breaks", how secure is the connection?
options: As strong as the larger chain, which protects both
As strong as the relayer that carries the messages
Only as strong as the weaker of the two chains
As strong as the Cosmos Hub, which approves each transfer
questions.correct_option_text: Only as strong as the weaker of the two chains
questions.explanation: IBC has no middleman, so it is only as strong as the weaker of the two chains; the relayer merely carries messages and cannot forge them.

questions.question: A group of banks runs a private Fabric settlement chain and wants tokens and final settlement on a public network. In the "Which connection?" exercise, why is IBC rated a poor fit?
options: IBC requires each bank to lock up a large stake in the public chain's token, which regulated banks are not permitted to hold
IBC hands the relayer a readable copy of all of the banks' private data, which would breach their confidentiality rules
Fabric has no native IBC support, so the banks would have to build and maintain custom adapter software: a major project, not an off-the-shelf connection
An IBC transfer takes about a week to become final, which is far too slow for banks that settle with one another every day
questions.correct_option_text: Fabric has no native IBC support, so the banks would have to build and maintain custom adapter software: a major project, not an off-the-shelf connection
questions.explanation: IBC needs each chain to verify the other with a light client, which Cosmos-SDK chains have built in and a Fabric or Besu consortium chain does not. Experimental adapters exist (for example in Hyperledger Labs), but they are not production-standard, so using IBC here means building and assuring the missing pieces yourself, or rebuilding on an IBC-capable stack: far heavier than the integration the banks are looking for.

questions.question: Two chains inside the same Layer 0 (two Polkadot parachains, say) exchange messages natively. What happens when one of them needs to reach a chain outside that Layer 0?
options: It cannot be done: Layer 0 chains are sealed off from all others
It still needs a bridge: native messaging only works inside the club
The Layer 0's validators extend their security to the outside chain
The outside chain must first become a rollup on top of Ethereum
questions.correct_option_text: It still needs a bridge: native messaging only works inside the club
questions.explanation: Inside a Layer 0, messaging is native and verified by the shared validators, but it only works inside the club; reaching a chain outside still needs a bridge.

questions.question: dYdX left its Ethereum rollup in 2023 to run its own Cosmos chain. According to the Cosmos slide, what does an app gain from having its own sovereign chain?
options: It can read Bitcoin's ledger directly, so its users no longer need bridges or wrapped tokens
It sets its own fees, governance and upgrades, and does not share block space with other apps
It inherits the security of Ethereum's validators without having to pay anything for it
It no longer needs any validators of its own, because the Cosmos Hub supplies them free
questions.correct_option_text: It sets its own fees, governance and upgrades, and does not share block space with other apps
questions.explanation: App-specific sovereignty: each Cosmos chain sets its own fees, governance and upgrades and does not compete for block space with other apps; the price is having its own validator set.

questions.question: Ethereum is described as a kitchen and the XRP Ledger as a vending machine. How does XRPL provide features such as its exchange, AMM pools and escrow?
options: They are built into the protocol itself, with no contract to deploy or audit
They are supplied by banks, which plug their own systems into the ledger
They run on Ethereum, and XRPL reads the results back through a bridge
Each one is a smart contract that a different company wrote and deployed
questions.correct_option_text: They are built into the protocol itself, with no contract to deploy or audit
questions.explanation: XRPL is a purpose-built rail: payments, the exchange, AMM pools and escrow are part of the protocol itself, a fixed menu with no contract to deploy or audit.

questions.question: Which project best fits the XRP Ledger's main ledger as this section describes it?
options: A lending protocol that depends on complex, custom smart-contract logic
A fully on-chain game in which every move a player makes is a contract call
A payment corridor turning euros into pesos in seconds for a fraction of a cent
A private network on which hospitals share confidential patient records
questions.correct_option_text: A payment corridor turning euros into pesos in seconds for a fraction of a cent
questions.explanation: XRPL is a payments rail, not an app platform: fast and cheap because it does less, with no general smart contracts on the main ledger, and it is a public ledger.

questions.question: An enthusiast says: "The XRP Ledger has no miners and no staking, so there is nobody you have to trust." What is the section's reply?
options: Not quite: you trust Bitcoin's miners, because the XRP Ledger is secured as a sidechain of Bitcoin
Not quite: you trust one company's server, which approves each payment and then publishes the result
Correct: because the validators agree by voting, the need for trust is removed from the system entirely
Not quite: most nodes use the default published validator list, and you trust those validators not to collude
questions.correct_option_text: Not quite: most nodes use the default published validator list, and you trust those validators not to collude
questions.explanation: Anyone can run a validator, but most nodes use the default published list; you trust the validators on that list not to collude, a different bet from proof of work or proof of stake.

questions.question: A Lisbon importer and a Shenzhen supplier use an escrow agent to hold the €50,000 payment until both sides deliver. What is the characteristic weak spot of this arrangement?
options: Either side can break the deal first, and the other must sue afterwards.
The record sits in one firm's database, and its owner can edit it.
One middleman holds everyone's money and can make mistakes, stall or go bust.
The rule runs exactly as written and cannot know whether the goods arrived.
questions.correct_option_text: One middleman holds everyone's money and can make mistakes, stall or go bust.
questions.explanation: With an escrow agent the buyer and supplier are held to the deal, but the agent has the money, so the trust (plus a fee and days of waiting) sits with that one middleman.

questions.question: The same two firms rely only on a lawyer-drafted paper contract. According to the course's comparison of ways to make a deal stick, what is the main limitation?
options: Enforcement comes afterwards through the courts: slow, expensive, and harder still across borders.
The lawyer holds the €50,000 for the whole period and could go bust before paying any of it out.
The other party cannot read the contract until the deal has been completed.
A network fee has to be paid every time one of the clauses is checked.
questions.correct_option_text: Enforcement comes afterwards through the courts: slow, expensive, and harder still across borders.
questions.explanation: A paper contract means trusting the legal system to put things right afterwards: either side can break the deal first, and suing takes months or years and is hard across borders.

questions.question: The deal is instead run as a smart contract that holds the €50,000 and releases it "when delivery is confirmed". Which weakness remains?
options: The supplier can quietly rewrite the release rule once the money is locked in.
Settlement still takes days, because an agent has to check the paperwork and approve each release by hand.
The network running the contract can hold on to the money or go bust, just as an escrow agent could.
It runs exactly what is written, bugs included, and needs a reliable feed to know the goods arrived.
questions.correct_option_text: It runs exactly what is written, bugs included, and needs a reliable feed to know the goods arrived.
questions.explanation: Provided no admin or upgrade key was left in, no one can bend the rule once it is live, but code has no judgement and cannot see the real world, so a bug or a bad delivery feed is the weak spot.

questions.question: A vendor says: "The code is the contract, so you will not need lawyers." What does the course say is actually true?
options: The vendor is right: courts everywhere treat deployed code as a signed agreement.
The vendor is right, provided the code was independently audited before launch.
Code moves assets; whether a court recognises it is a separate question, so it is paired with a legal agreement.
The vendor is wrong, because a smart contract cannot move any assets until a lawyer has reviewed and approved each transfer.
questions.correct_option_text: Code moves assets; whether a court recognises it is a separate question, so it is paired with a legal agreement.
questions.explanation: A smart contract is not a legal contract by itself, which is why real projects pair the code with a written agreement.

questions.question: A founder pitches: "Our product runs on a smart contract, so nobody can ever switch it off." Which point from the course best challenges this claim?
options: Validators can vote to delete any contract that they disapprove of.
A contract stops running automatically as soon as its developer's wallet no longer holds enough to pay the fees.
Every contract expires after a fixed number of blocks unless its developer pays to have it renewed.
Its website, data feeds and admin keys are ordinary points of control.
questions.correct_option_text: Its website, data feeds and admin keys are ordinary points of control.
questions.explanation: Tornado Cash's website went dark in 2022 while the contract kept running: the product around a contract depends on ordinary, controllable pieces, so "unstoppable" is hype.

questions.question: "Once it is live, nobody can quietly bend the rule." The course counts this as genuine value, on one condition. Which condition?
options: The contract runs on the operator's own servers.
No admin or upgrade key was left in the contract.
A court has registered the code as an agreement.
The operator keeps paying the network fees on time.
questions.correct_option_text: No admin or upgrade key was left in the contract.
questions.explanation: The rule is locked for everyone, operator included, only as long as no admin or upgrade key was left in that could change it.

questions.question: A startup plans to keep all of its customer documents inside a smart contract on Ethereum, arguing that "with no middleman it is basically free". What is wrong with the plan?
options: Every step costs a network fee, and storing data on-chain is very expensive.
A smart contract is not able to hold or keep track of any data at all.
Only licensed banks are allowed to store documents on a blockchain.
Whatever a contract stores is wiped again after each transaction.
questions.correct_option_text: Every step costs a network fee, and storing data on-chain is very expensive.
questions.explanation: "Not free" is one of the four hype corrections: you pay the network for every step, and on-chain storage is among the most expensive things a contract can do.

questions.question: The course names three genuine benefits of a smart contract: removing a middleman, locking a rule for everyone, and settling fast across borders. Which of these projects actually draws on one or more of them?
options: A bakery's stock list, kept by the owner and one employee.
A company that wants to store its staff rota more cheaply than in a database.
Importers and exporters in different countries who want payment released automatically on delivery.
A law firm that wants its contracts to use human-style judgement whenever a clause turns out to be ambiguous.
questions.correct_option_text: Importers and exporters in different countries who want payment released automatically on delivery.
questions.explanation: Project 3 removes a middleman and settles across borders. The bakery and the rota have one trusted owner and no rule to lock, so a database wins, and on-chain storage costs more, not less. A smart contract has no judgement: it only runs fixed rules. If a use case needs none of the three benefits, a database will usually win.

questions.question: Two drivers disagree about who caused a crash and how much the damage is worth. Why is settling this a poor job for a smart contract?
options: The sums involved in a car accident are too large for a smart contract to be allowed to hold safely.
Only one party is really involved, so there is nobody whose behaviour the code would need to keep honest.
Network fees would always come to more than the cost of the repair, whatever the size of the claim.
It needs someone to weigh evidence and judge; code can only run a rule fixed in advance.
questions.correct_option_text: It needs someone to weigh evidence and judge; code can only run a rule fixed in advance.
questions.explanation: A smart contract cannot judge: it only executes a rule agreed beforehand, so disputes that need judgement belong with people.

questions.question: Hundreds of strangers pledge money to a project; if the target is not reached by the deadline, everyone is refunded. Why is this a good fit for a smart contract?
options: The contract can decide on the backers' behalf whether the project really deserves to receive the money.
The rule is pure arithmetic, so code can hold strangers' money and no platform has to be trusted.
Pledging through a contract costs the backers nothing, unlike using a platform.
The pledges become legally binding on every backer without the need for any other agreement or terms.
questions.correct_option_text: The rule is pure arithmetic, so code can hold strangers' money and no platform has to be trusted.
questions.explanation: Parties who do not know each other share a rule that code can check (target met by the deadline, or not), which is exactly where a contract adds trust.

questions.question: An insurer promises an automatic payout if your flight lands more than two hours late. Which statement best captures why this fits a smart contract and what it still depends on?
options: A simple rule triggered by a public fact; it still needs a reliable feed of arrival times.
A complex judgement that code handles better than claims staff; once deployed it depends on nothing else.
A rule that only the insurer needs to see; it still needs a court to approve each individual payout.
A rule that changes with every flight; it still needs the insurer to confirm each claim by hand.
questions.correct_option_text: A simple rule triggered by a public fact; it still needs a reliable feed of arrival times.
questions.explanation: The customer no longer has to trust the insurer to honour the promise, but the contract cannot see arrival times itself and needs a trustworthy data feed.

questions.question: Nick Szabo described smart contracts in 1994, yet general-purpose smart contracts only became practical about two decades later. Why?
options: Regulators in most countries banned the concept until 2015, when the rules were relaxed.
Szabo kept the idea secret until Ethereum launched.
Businesses at the time saw no use for agreements that could enforce themselves.
No shared platform could run general-purpose contract code until Ethereum went live.
questions.correct_option_text: No shared platform could run general-purpose contract code until Ethereum went live.
questions.explanation: Szabo's idea needed somewhere to run. Bitcoin (2009) allowed only limited spending scripts; a shared platform for arbitrary programs arrived with Ethereum in 2015. The lesson for business: a good idea is not a business until the infrastructure exists.

questions.question: A popular dApp's website disappears overnight because its hosting provider suspends the account. What does this illustrate about dApps?
options: The smart contract was stored on the same hosting account as the website, so it has been deleted as well.
The network's validators voted to shut the application down.
The contract layer is decentralised, but this front end ran on an ordinary server that someone controls.
The funds held in the contract are frozen until the website has been restored.
questions.correct_option_text: The contract layer is decentralised, but this front end ran on an ordinary server that someone controls.
questions.explanation: A dApp is a full stack: the contract keeps running on-chain, but the website, data feeds and storage are usually ordinary services that someone controls.

questions.question: Why does a typical NFT project keep its images off-chain (for example on IPFS) and store only a content hash or link in the smart contract?
options: The law forbids blockchains from holding image files of any kind.
On-chain storage is very expensive, so only a reference to the file (its fingerprint) is kept there.
IPFS makes the image visible only to the current owner of the token, which keeps the artwork exclusive.
A hash lets the contract edit the image later without anyone having to send a transaction.
questions.correct_option_text: On-chain storage is very expensive, so only a reference to the file (its fingerprint) is kept there.
questions.explanation: Good design keeps heavy data off-chain (the file lives on IPFS or similar, and must be kept available there) and puts only the proof, the hash, on-chain.

questions.question: A dashboard reads a customer's token balance from a smart contract, and the customer then sends 10 tokens to a friend. Which of these actions costs gas?
options: Both: every interaction with a contract costs gas.
Neither: gas is charged only when a contract is deployed.
Only the balance check, because reading data is the expensive part.
Only the transfer: changing state costs gas, while reading is free.
questions.correct_option_text: Only the transfer: changing state costs gas, while reading is free.
questions.explanation: Read-only functions are free; functions that change the contract's stored state cost gas.

questions.question: The escrow contract in the walkthrough is written to log each deposit. How does Rui's order system learn that Ana has paid, so that it can ship the goods?
options: The contract sends Rui an e-mail as soon as the deposit arrives.
The contract emits a Deposited event, a public receipt that his system listens for.
A validator contacts the seller once the block has been confirmed.
Rui has to wait until the payment shows up on his bank statement.
questions.correct_option_text: The contract emits a Deposited event, a public receipt that his system listens for.
questions.explanation: Events are logs written on-chain that off-chain systems can pick up; the contract itself does not contact anyone.

questions.question: In the escrow deal, Rui deploys the contract, and Ana later calls deposit() and confirmDelivery(). Who pays the gas?
options: Rui pays for everything, because he is the one receiving the money.
The contract pays it out of the 2 ETH that it is holding.
Whoever sends each transaction: Rui for the deployment, Ana for her two calls.
The network's validators absorb it as a cost of doing business.
questions.correct_option_text: Whoever sends each transaction: Rui for the deployment, Ana for her two calls.
questions.explanation: Whoever sends the transaction pays for the run.

questions.question: In the escrow walkthrough, the rules written into the contract release the money only when its conditions are met (Ana confirming delivery). Ana's 2 ETH is now locked in the contract and the status reads "Funded". Which statement is correct?
options: The money is provably set aside: neither Ana nor Rui can pull it back alone.
Rui can withdraw it straight away, since it was deposited for him.
Ana can cancel whenever she likes and take the 2 ETH back.
Rui, as the deployer, can edit the rules to release the money early.
questions.correct_option_text: The money is provably set aside: neither Ana nor Rui can pull it back alone.
questions.explanation: After deployment nobody can edit the rules, Rui included; the funds move only when the contract's own conditions are met.

questions.question: A team has a working Solidity contract on Ethereum and now wants it on Arbitrum and Base as well. What does the course say this takes?
options: A full rewrite in Rust, because each of these chains has its own programming language.
Permission from Ethereum's validators, who must vote before code can be copied to another chain.
A licence from each chain's operator before the code may be listed.
Very little: the same Solidity code can be deployed to each chain, usually unchanged, then tested.
questions.correct_option_text: Very little: the same Solidity code can be deployed to each chain, usually unchanged, then tested.
questions.explanation: One Solidity contract generally works across EVM-compatible chains, which is the point of EVM compatibility, but each chain needs its own deployment, addresses and testing; only non-EVM chains such as Solana need different code.

questions.question: A company budgets its transaction fees using a quiet day's prices. What does the gas recap warn about?
options: Fees are fixed by law, so no buffer is needed in the budget.
Fees depend only on the value being transferred, not on network activity.
The price of gas is set by demand, so fees can jump 10–100× in a rush.
Fees fall when the network is busy, because the cost is shared between more users.
questions.correct_option_text: The price of gas is set by demand, so fees can jump 10–100× in a rush.
questions.explanation: Fee = work done (gas units) × price per unit, and the price rises when the network is busy.

questions.question: Which of these operations typically costs the most gas?
options: Deploying a new contract
Reading a public value
Emitting an event
Sending ETH in a simple transfer
questions.correct_option_text: Deploying a new contract
questions.explanation: Deploying stores the contract's code on every node permanently, so it normally costs far more than the others; writing data is the next most expensive, and reading a value from outside the chain is free. (Exact gas always depends on how much code or data is involved.)

questions.question: In the lending-pool example, depositors put in 100,000, borrowers took out 40,000 and paid 5% interest on it, and the pool kept no fee. Yet depositors earned only 2%. Why?
options: A bank in the middle kept the remaining 3% as its margin for arranging the loans.
Gas fees on the repayments consumed the difference.
The borrower's collateral lost value while the loan was open, which reduced the payout.
Only 40% of the pool was lent out, so the interest was spread over all deposits.
questions.correct_option_text: Only 40% of the pool was lent out, so the interest was spread over all deposits.
questions.explanation: 40,000 of the 100,000 pool was lent at 5%, earning 2,000 for the whole pool, which is 2% for every depositor.

questions.question: How can a lending pool lend to complete strangers with no credit check?
options: It lends only to wallets that a bank has approved in advance.
The borrower locks collateral worth more than the loan, which can be sold if its value falls too far.
Depositors vote on each loan application and check the borrower's history before any money is paid out.
The pool's developers have promised to repay, out of their own pockets, any loan that is not returned.
questions.correct_option_text: The borrower locks collateral worth more than the loan, which can be sold if its value falls too far.
questions.explanation: Collateral replaces trust: the contract never asks who you are, only what you locked.

questions.question: Why is it safe for a pool to hand out a $10 million flash loan with no collateral at all?
options: The borrower's identity is verified when the loan is requested, so the pool can sue if the money is not returned.
The pool insures each loan with a deposit that the borrower pays in advance.
Loan and repayment sit in one atomic transaction: if the money is not back by the end, everything is undone.
Validators freeze the borrower's wallet until the loan has been repaid in full.
questions.correct_option_text: Loan and repayment sit in one atomic transaction: if the money is not back by the end, everything is undone.
questions.explanation: A transaction is all or nothing, so the pool is either repaid in full or the loan never happened; the borrower loses only the gas fee.

questions.question: In the flash-loan example, DEX A never agreed to work with the lending pool, yet the trader used both in one transaction. Which capability does this show?
options: Permissionless composability: any contract can call another's public functions without approval.
Censorship resistance: no government or company can block a valid transaction.
Global shared state: one synchronised record that anyone can read from anywhere in the world.
Programmable money: value that carries its own built-in rules.
questions.correct_option_text: Permissionless composability: any contract can call another's public functions without approval.
questions.explanation: Protocols snap together like "money legos": one contract calls another, and nobody's permission is needed.

questions.question: When a smart contract uses an oracle, does its code reach out to the internet for the data?
options: Yes: the oracle opens a secure, encrypted channel to the internet that the contract can call at any time.
Yes, but only to websites that the validators have approved in advance.
No: the oracle lets each node look the value up for itself whenever that node runs the contract's code.
No: the oracle writes the data on-chain in a transaction, and every node reads that stored value.
questions.correct_option_text: No: the oracle writes the data on-chain in a transaction, and every node reads that stored value.
questions.explanation: The contract still never reaches out; the oracle pushes the data in, so the sandbox stays intact and all nodes agree.

questions.question: A price feed takes the median of five independent, equally weighted oracle nodes. How many nodes must collude before they can push the feed to a false price of their choosing?
options: One: any single false report sets the feed.
Three: once a majority lies, the median itself is a lie.
All five: the median ignores anything less.
It cannot happen: validators check that the price is true.
questions.correct_option_text: Three: once a majority lies, the median itself is a lie.
questions.explanation: A median ignores a minority of outliers: one or two liars can at most nudge the result within the range the honest nodes report, but three of five control it. Many reporters replace "trust this one company" with "trust that most of them are honest".

questions.question: During network congestion a price feed stops updating, and a lending smart contract keeps liquidating loans at a six-hour-old price. Which oracle failure is this, and what defence does the course give?
options: Manipulation; combine deep markets and reject outliers.
Single point of failure; add more validators to the blockchain.
Stale data; check the data's timestamp and pause when it is too old.
A coding bug; redeploy the lending contract with a fix.
questions.correct_option_text: Stale data; check the data's timestamp and pause when it is too old.
questions.explanation: The contract keeps acting on a number that is no longer true, so it should check the age of the data before using it.

questions.question: A prediction market on "the highest temperature in Paris" settled on one named airport sensor, which then showed a brief spike that nearby stations did not. What lesson does the course draw?
options: The market's smart contract contained a coding bug that misread the temperature the sensor had reported.
The blockchain's validators altered the sensor's reading before it was stored, to favour the long-shot bets.
A flash loan was used to push the temperature feed upwards.
The market paid exactly as written, on one device; a glitch or anyone tampering with it moves the payout.
questions.correct_option_text: The market paid exactly as written, on one device; a glitch or anyone tampering with it moves the payout.
questions.explanation: An oracle is a trust and definition problem, not only a technical one: ask which exact source decides, and who can touch it.

questions.question: In the price-attack walkthrough, suppose the lender values collateral with a feed that averages many markets over time instead of one small pool's live price. What happens to the attack?
options: The attacker cannot borrow enough to repay the flash loan, so the whole transaction is cancelled at the cost of gas only.
It still succeeds, but the attacker's profit is cut roughly in half because the averaged price only partly follows the pumped pool.
It succeeds once, after which the feed recognises the attacker's address and blocks any further borrowing against that collateral.
The lender loses the collateral that was posted but keeps the flash-loan fee, so the two effects roughly cancel out.
questions.correct_option_text: The attacker cannot borrow enough to repay the flash loan, so the whole transaction is cancelled at the cost of gas only.
questions.explanation: One small pool barely moves an aggregated feed, so the collateral is booked near its real value, the loan cannot cover the flash loan, and atomicity undoes everything.

questions.question: What is "the irony" of the oracle problem, as the course puts it?
options: Oracles make contracts so expensive to run that hiring a human middleman becomes the cheaper option after all.
Contracts remove the trusted middleman from the deal, then let one back in through the data feed.
Oracles are so reliable that the blockchain itself becomes unnecessary.
The more oracles a contract uses, the less data it is able to receive.
questions.correct_option_text: Contracts remove the trusted middleman from the deal, then let one back in through the data feed.
questions.explanation: A blockchain can verify signatures and arithmetic, not whether a number is true, so a contract is only as trustworthy as its data source.

questions.question: A stablecoin transfer on a Layer 2 settles in seconds, for cents, at any hour, where a bank wire takes days. What is "the catch" the course attaches to this?
options: The transfer can be seen only by banks, not by the person receiving it.
It cannot be reversed, and getting money in and out still usually goes through a bank or regulated exchange.
Each transfer must first be approved by a correspondent bank.
The recipient still has to wait until the next business day, when the banks reopen, before being able to spend it.
questions.correct_option_text: It cannot be reversed, and getting money in and out still usually goes through a bank or regulated exchange.
questions.explanation: Final means final (no chargeback), and the on/off-ramps at the edges are still banks or regulated exchanges.

questions.question: A trader places a very large buy order for ETH against a shallow AMM pool. What happens?
options: The pool matches the order with a waiting seller from its order book, at exactly the price that was quoted.
The pool rejects any order that is big enough to move the price.
The price is unaffected, because the formula holds it constant.
Buying shrinks the pool's ETH reserve, so the price climbs and the trader pays more (slippage).
questions.correct_option_text: Buying shrinks the pool's ETH reserve, so the price climbs and the trader pays more (slippage).
questions.explanation: An AMM has no order book: a formula keeps the product of the two reserves constant, so big trades move the price (strictly 'price impact'; traders loosely call it slippage) and liquidity depth is what limits it.

questions.question: A company holds dollars and Treasury bills in a bank and issues one stablecoin token per dollar. What is the main risk for holders of this design?
options: You must trust the issuer and its reserves: if they are impaired, the peg can break.
A crash in the price of ETH leaves the tokens under-collateralised.
A falling sister token removes the cushion and starts a death spiral.
The peg breaks whenever network fees rise sharply.
questions.correct_option_text: You must trust the issuer and its reserves: if they are impaired, the peg can break.
questions.explanation: Fiat-backed coins are only as trustworthy as their reserves; the other risks belong to the crypto-collateralised and algorithmic designs.

questions.question: A game studio shuts down its servers. What happens to the items players hold as NFTs?
options: They are deleted together with the studio's servers.
Players keep the tokens, which may now be worth nothing.
The blockchain keeps the game running without the studio.
The token contract automatically refunds what players paid.
questions.correct_option_text: Players keep the tokens, which may now be worth nothing.
questions.explanation: The chain records who owns the item; the servers, artwork and gameplay are still the company's.

questions.question: A visitor connects a wallet that holds only an NFT from a different collection to a members-only token gate. What happens, and why?
options: Access granted: holding any NFT shows that the visitor is a genuine crypto user.
Access granted, once the visitor has paid the gas for the check.
Denied: the gate recognises the visitor's name and address on a blocklist kept by the club.
Denied: the membership contract shows this address holds none of its tokens.
questions.correct_option_text: Denied: the membership contract shows this address holds none of its tokens.
questions.explanation: The gate never asks who you are, only what you hold: the wallet signs a one-time message, then a free read of the membership contract decides.

questions.question: Which kind of NFT use is a logical, lasting one because it relies on real utility rather than speculation?
options: Uses where the token is a key, not a speculation: ticketing, credentials, token-gating.
Uses that count on royalty income from future resales, which marketplaces can skip and the chain does not enforce.
Hype-driven collectibles bought mainly to be resold at a higher price.
Profile-picture collections, whose value rests on floor prices that keep rising year after year.
questions.correct_option_text: Uses where the token is a key, not a speculation: ticketing, credentials, token-gating.
questions.explanation: When the token works as a key (a ticket, a credential, access to a gated community), it is useful whatever its price. Utility that does not depend on the price going up is the utility that lasts. Royalties are not reliably enforced on resale, and floor-price or hype-driven collectibles are speculation.

questions.question: An analyst points to huge on-chain NFT trading volume as proof of real demand. What caution does the course give?
options: On-chain volume is always understated, because most trades are kept private.
Volume figures are set by the marketplaces and never touch the chain.
On-chain data is transparent but not necessarily true: volume can be inflated by wash trading.
Volume figures can be relied on, but only once a financial regulator has certified them as accurate.
questions.correct_option_text: On-chain data is transparent but not necessarily true: volume can be inflated by wash trading.
questions.explanation: Wash trading means selling a token to yourself from a second wallet; transparent is not the same as true, so read on-chain volume like any unaudited number.

questions.question: The course calls the word "autonomous" in DAO "generous". What is actually automatic?
options: Writing the proposals: the contract drafts them by itself from members' past votes.
Deciding which proposals are good for the organisation.
Getting members to turn out, read the proposals and cast their votes on time.
Executing the result: once an on-chain vote passes, the treasury contract carries it out.
questions.correct_option_text: Executing the result: once an on-chain vote passes, the treasury contract carries it out.
questions.explanation: People still write proposals, argue and vote; code enforces the rules, but people still choose them. (DAOs that vote off-chain rely on signers to carry the result out.)

questions.question: A DAO adds a 48-hour timelock between a passed vote and its execution. What does this buy, and what does it cost?
options: Members get time to react or exit before a passed proposal executes, but emergency response is slower.
Votes become secret, but fewer members bother to take part.
Whales lose most of their voting power, but every proposal costs considerably more gas to put to a vote.
Any member can reverse a decision during the delay, but the treasury earns less while its funds are locked.
questions.correct_option_text: Members get time to react or exit before a passed proposal executes, but emergency response is slower.
questions.explanation: A timelock delays execution of an approved proposal, which is why many DAOs add a guardian for emergencies.

questions.question: Under quadratic voting, casting n votes costs n² tokens. How many votes can a holder of 10,000 tokens cast?
questions.explanation: 100 votes cost 100² = 10,000 tokens, which is how the rule dampens the power of large holders.

questions.question: A DAO switches from one-token-one-vote to quadratic voting to curb a whale. How can the whale get its power back?
options: By casting its votes earlier than everyone else.
By splitting its holdings across many wallets, so that it looks like many separate people.
By lending its tokens to the treasury for as long as the vote stays open, then taking them back.
By paying a much higher gas fee on its voting transaction, so that its votes are counted first.
questions.correct_option_text: By splitting its holdings across many wallets, so that it looks like many separate people.
questions.explanation: Quadratic voting only dampens plutocracy if every wallet is one real person; without identity checks it is open to this Sybil attack.

questions.question: ConstitutionDAO pooled about $47M from 17,000+ people in under a week, then lost the auction. What lesson does the course draw?
options: A bug in its contract let an attacker drain the pooled funds.
Regulators blocked the bid at the last minute, because under US law a DAO is not allowed to own historical documents.
Coordination worked; governance and operations were the hard part: custody was unsettled and unwinding was costly.
Token-weighted voting let a single whale veto the bid.
questions.correct_option_text: Coordination worked; governance and operations were the hard part: custody was unsettled and unwinding was costly.
questions.explanation: Who would legally own and hold the document was never settled. After the loss, refunds were offered, but gas fees ate a large share of small contributions (some donors paid about as much in fees as they had given). Pooling money is the easy part; deciding, holding and unwinding it safely is where DAOs struggle.

questions.question: Token holders in an unincorporated DAO vote on its decisions. What legal risk did the US Ooki DAO case (CFTC, 2022–23) reveal?
options: Voters can be treated as members of an unincorporated association, personally exposed to its liabilities.
Votes that are cast on-chain are automatically void in a court of law.
Token holders must register as company directors before they may vote.
The DAO's developers alone carry all of the liability, however the token holders choose to cast their votes.
questions.correct_option_text: Voters can be treated as members of an unincorporated association, personally exposed to its liabilities.
questions.explanation: Legal status is unsettled and varies by country, which is why many DAOs now pair the contracts with a legal wrapper.

questions.question: Why have tokenised government bonds (such as US Treasuries) scaled so much faster than tokenised real estate?
options: Bonds are physical certificates, which makes them easier to store and move around than buildings or land titles.
Property owners refuse to sell their buildings in fractions.
Regulators have banned property tokens in every country.
The simpler and more standardised the legal claim, the easier the token; for property, legal title is the hard part.
questions.correct_option_text: The simpler and more standardised the legal claim, the easier the token; for property, legal title is the hard part.
questions.explanation: Short-dated sovereign debt is standardised, liquid and legally simple to wrap, so tokenised treasuries grew fastest; each property is a one-off with its own title, registry and local law. A token moves in seconds, but legal title moves at the speed of the law.

questions.question: A firm tokenises an office building and expects its shares to trade as freely as a listed stock. What does the course warn?
options: Tokens cannot be divided into smaller units, so only one buyer at a time can hold the building.
The token will always trade above the value of the building.
A token does not create buyers: secondary markets stay thin and the price can drift.
Each token holder must sign the land registry in person before a trade can be completed.
questions.correct_option_text: A token does not create buyers: secondary markets stay thin and the price can drift.
questions.explanation: Tokenising makes an asset divisible and quick to settle; it does not guarantee demand.

questions.question: A shopper scans a chicken's QR code and sees an on-chain trail saying "organic feed, no antibiotics", signed at each hand-off. What does the blockchain actually prove?
options: Who entered which record and when; it cannot prove the chicken was actually organic.
That the chicken was organic, since on-chain records cannot be false.
That a regulator inspected the farm before each entry was written.
That no partner in the chain could have made a mistake.
questions.correct_option_text: Who entered which record and when; it cannot prove the chicken was actually organic.
questions.explanation: "Garbage in, garbage forever": the chain proves who recorded what and when, not that the goods match the record.

questions.question: Why do rival luxury houses such as Louis Vuitton, Prada and Cartier share one blockchain platform (Aura)?
options: A regulator ordered the three groups to merge their product databases into a single registry.
None of them could fight counterfeiting alone, so they share the infrastructure.
The platform lets each brand see its rivals' sales figures and customer lists in real time.
It makes copying a handbag physically impossible.
questions.correct_option_text: None of them could fight counterfeiting alone, so they share the infrastructure.
questions.explanation: It is collaborative rather than competitive infrastructure; counterfeiters cannot forge the on-chain history, though they can still copy the bag.

questions.question: A fake "university" anchors a diploma's hash on the blockchain through its own smart contract, and the diploma file matches that record exactly. Why is the match not enough to treat the diploma as authentic?
options: Hashes change every day, so yesterday's match proves nothing.
A matching hash only shows that the file is the right size.
The blockchain deletes genuine records once they have been verified, so a surviving match is suspicious.
Anyone can anchor a hash; the verifier must also check that the university's own contract wrote it.
questions.correct_option_text: Anyone can anchor a hash; the verifier must also check that the university's own contract wrote it.
questions.explanation: Two checks are needed: the hash matches (the document is unchanged) and the university's own contract wrote it (who issued it).

questions.question: A graduate edits one character of a diploma that was anchored on-chain, then presents it to an employer who verifies it. What does the check show?
options: A match, because small edits do not affect the fingerprint.
