A match, flagged with the number of characters that changed.
No match: any change gives a completely different hash, so no record is found.
No result: the document must first be uploaded to the chain in full.
questions.correct_option_text: No match: any change gives a completely different hash, so no record is found.
questions.explanation: Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely; the document itself never goes on-chain.

questions.question: A university wrongly issues a diploma to someone who never graduated and anchors it on-chain through its official smart contract. What will verification show?
options: Authentic, in the sense of genuinely issued and unaltered, even if the issuer erred.
Forged: the chain detects that the underlying claim is false.
Altered: the hash will no longer match the document.
Revoked: records that later turn out to be false are removed from the chain automatically.
questions.correct_option_text: Authentic, in the sense of genuinely issued and unaltered, even if the issuer erred.
questions.explanation: A true record of a false claim: verification is instant, but the issuer's honesty when creating the record is still the weak point.

questions.question: Two hospitals want patient consent for record sharing handled by a smart contract. Following the course's design example, what goes where?
options: Records and consent both go on-chain, so every hospital can see everything.
Consent is signed on-chain and an access token is issued; the medical data stays off-chain.
The medical data goes on-chain, and the consent stays on paper.
Nothing goes on-chain: the contract simply e-mails the records from one hospital to the other when asked.
questions.correct_option_text: Consent is signed on-chain and an access token is issued; the medical data stays off-chain.
questions.explanation: The key constraint in that design is privacy law: the medical data itself must stay off-chain.

questions.question: Several organisations that distrust one another must all write to one shared record, and no third party is acceptable to all of them. They only need to record simple transfers, with no complex business logic. Where does the decision tree land?
options: A smart contract platform.
A third-party managed database.
A simple, Bitcoin-like blockchain.
A traditional database with access controls.
questions.correct_option_text: A simple, Bitcoin-like blockchain.
questions.explanation: With no trusted third party a blockchain is justified, but a smart contract platform is needed only when complex business logic is required as well.

questions.question: Four subsidiaries of the same group all need to write to a shared record, and they fully trust one another. Following the decision tree, what should they use?
options: A traditional database with access controls.
A smart contract platform.
A simple, Bitcoin-like blockchain.
A database run by an outside third party.
questions.correct_option_text: A traditional database with access controls.
questions.explanation: The tree exits as soon as the parties fully trust each other: a shared database with access controls is enough.

questions.question: For a use case where putting everything on-chain is risky, the decision framework returns a "hybrid" verdict. What does that recommend?
options: Running two public blockchains side by side for redundancy.
Hashes on-chain with encrypted data off-chain, or a permissioned chain with off-chain overrides.
Building on a database now and moving everything onto a public chain once the rules have settled down.
Letting each party keep its own separate ledger and reconcile monthly.
questions.correct_option_text: Hashes on-chain with encrypted data off-chain, or a permissioned chain with off-chain overrides.
questions.explanation: Hybrid means only the proof or the shared rule goes on-chain, while sensitive data and discretion stay off-chain.

questions.question: A smart contract would take about 80% of its inputs from oracles and external APIs. What does this suggest?
options: It is ideal: the smart contract has little left to compute, so it costs less gas to run.
It makes no difference: the on-chain logic is equally trustworthy whatever its inputs are.
It is fine, provided the external APIs are free to use and respond quickly.
It is a red flag: the trust sits in those outside sources, so rethink whether a smart contract is needed.
questions.correct_option_text: It is a red flag: the trust sits in those outside sources, so rethink whether a smart contract is needed.
questions.explanation: If most inputs come from outside, the chain adds little: you are really trusting the data feeds, not the code. This is one of the course's "when to rethink" red flags: when most of the data or logic lives off-chain, ask whether a smart contract (or a blockchain) is needed at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is a signal in favour of using a smart contract, rather than a red flag?
options: The business rules need to change every week.
One party is already trusted by everyone involved.
Users need to move their assets between platforms or wallets without lock-in.
The data involved is personal and has to stay private under data-protection law.
questions.correct_option_text: Users need to move their assets between platforms or wallets without lock-in.
questions.explanation: Portable asset ownership is on the "makes sense" list; changing rules, a single trusted party and private data are on the "rethink" list.

questions.question: A blockchain project starts from the technology with no clear business purpose, no agreed success metrics and no executive buy-in. Which adoption pillar is failing?
options: Strategic alignment
Technical infrastructure
Legal & regulatory
Financial planning
questions.correct_option_text: Strategic alignment
questions.explanation: Strategic alignment asks whether there is a clear business purpose or just blockchain for its own sake. It covers the use case, success metrics, executive buy-in and staff training, which is exactly where this project falls short.

questions.question: A pilot works well in a demo but never connects to the company's ERP and CRM, and nobody in-house is able to run it. Which adoption pillar is the problem?
options: Strategic alignment
Technical infrastructure
Legal & regulatory
Financial planning
questions.correct_option_text: Technical infrastructure
questions.explanation: Technical infrastructure covers the platform, legacy integration and the IT capacity to operate it: the chain removes a middleman, not your IT department.

questions.question: A startup plans to sell a token worldwide first and "sort out the regulators later". What does the legal & regulatory pillar advise?
options: Go ahead: tokens that are sold on a public blockchain fall outside the reach of any single country's securities law.
Go ahead, as long as the code has passed a security audit.
Avoid tokens altogether: they are illegal in every major market.
Check the token against securities rules first; the same sale can be legal in one country and not in another.
questions.correct_option_text: Check the token against securities rules first; the same sale can be legal in one country and not in another.
questions.explanation: The failing pattern is "sold first, classified by a regulator later"; one token sale can get three different answers in Singapore, the US and the EU.

questions.question: An exploit starts at 3 a.m. and the team spends the first hour arguing about who is allowed to pause the smart contract. Which element of risk management was missing?
options: A bug bounty that pays outside researchers.
Formal verification, in which the contract's key properties are proven mathematically.
A written incident response plan: who pauses the contract and who tells the users.
Live monitoring, with real-time alerts that flag unusual flows of funds as they happen.
questions.correct_option_text: A written incident response plan: who pauses the contract and who tells the users.
questions.explanation: Without a written plan, the team is "deciding who is in charge while the funds drain".

questions.question: A consortium platform launches on time, but few partners join. What does the financial-planning pillar say happens next?
options: Running costs such as gas, monitoring and compliance continue, with no savings to pay for them.
Costs fall to zero, because a network that is not used charges nothing.
The upfront investment is refunded by the network's validators.
The savings arrive anyway, since automation does not depend on usage.
questions.correct_option_text: Running costs such as gas, monitoring and compliance continue, with no savings to pay for them.
questions.explanation: Costs come first and savings arrive later, and only if the network is used.

questions.question: AXA's Fizzy sold flight-delay insurance on Ethereum: a flight-data oracle triggered automatic payouts, and the payouts worked. Why did it close in 2019?
options: The oracle kept reporting the wrong arrival times.
Regulators banned automatic insurance payouts.
A bug in the contract drained the premium pool.
Too few customers bought the cover: it proved the pattern, not the market.
questions.correct_option_text: Too few customers bought the cover: it proved the pattern, not the market.
questions.explanation: Working technology is not a business case; the attempts that lasted removed a real cost and gave others a reason to join.

questions.question: Why can smart-contract code alone rarely give a business a lasting competitive advantage?
options: Smart-contract code on a public blockchain stops working after a few years and has to be rewritten.
Regulators require all smart contracts within a sector to be identical, so nobody can stand out.
Any competitor can read and copy the code; advantage comes from the network, not the technology.
Customers cannot tell one blockchain from another.
questions.correct_option_text: Any competitor can read and copy the code; advantage comes from the network, not the technology.
questions.explanation: None of the six strategy cases won on technology alone; the ones that worked removed a real cost and gave others a reason to join.

questions.question: A project's plan depends on moving assets between several blockchains through bridges. Which challenge from the course does this run into?
options: Interoperability: cross-chain bridges are fragile and a major source of exploits.
Scarce talent: only Solidity engineers are allowed to operate bridges.
User experience: bridges take away the need for wallets.
Scalability: bridges cut each chain's throughput to zero.
questions.correct_option_text: Interoperability: cross-chain bridges are fragile and a major source of exploits.
questions.explanation: Interoperability is one of the four listed challenges, alongside scalability limits, user experience and scarce talent.

questions.question: In the chain "data source → oracle → smart contract", where does the course place the weakest link?
options: The smart contract, because its code is public.
The data source: one sensor, API or market, which nothing on-chain can check.
The validators, because thousands of them have to be coordinated for each reading.
The oracle network, because the median of several reports is the easiest value to forge.
questions.correct_option_text: The data source: one sensor, API or market, which nothing on-chain can check.
questions.explanation: The chain secures the contract, but nothing on-chain secures the number it acts on, so the system is only as strong as its weakest link.

questions.question: A smart contract pays out $20 million on the basis of one figure, and bending that figure would cost an attacker about $50,000. Using the course's three questions for any smart contract that reads outside data, what should you conclude?
options: Nothing: the blockchain's validators will reject a false figure.
The risk is low, because $50,000 is a serious sum for an attacker.
The contract is safe as long as its code has been audited.
Expect an attack: bending the number costs less than the money it controls.
questions.correct_option_text: Expect an attack: bending the number costs less than the money it controls.
questions.explanation: The third question is "what would it cost to bend it?"; if that is less than the money the number controls, expect an attack.

questions.question: To protect an insurance smart contract, a team holds each payout for 24 hours so that anyone can challenge the reading. What does this defence still leave exposed?
options: Payouts are slower, somebody has to be watching, and a dispute still needs a judge.
Nothing: a dispute window removes oracle risk completely.
The contract is no longer able to pay out at all.
Honest readings are now rejected more often than false ones.
questions.correct_option_text: Payouts are slower, somebody has to be watching, and a dispute still needs a judge.
questions.explanation: Every oracle defence moves the trust somewhere else or puts a price on it; none deletes it.

questions.question: A team adds sanity checks and a switch that pauses payouts when the feed looks wrong. What new issue does the course point out?
options: A paused contract loses the funds that it holds.
Sanity checks make the underlying data source easier for an attacker to tamper with.
A pause freezes honest claims too, and the switch-holder must now be trusted.
Validators must approve every pause by majority vote.
questions.correct_option_text: A pause freezes honest claims too, and the switch-holder must now be trusted.
questions.explanation: The pause protects against bad data but reintroduces someone you must trust (the admin-key problem).

questions.question: Why does a base-layer blockchain handle far fewer transactions per second than a card network, and what does the course say helps?
options: Validators only work office hours; adding night shifts helps.
Every validating node re-executes every transaction; Layer 2 rollups help and still settle on Layer 1.
Fees are too low to pay for fast enough hardware; raising gas prices for every user is what helps.
Smart contracts are written in slow programming languages; rewriting them in faster ones is what helps.
questions.correct_option_text: Every validating node re-executes every transaction; Layer 2 rollups help and still settle on Layer 1.
questions.explanation: Replicated execution is what makes the chain trustworthy and also what keeps base-layer throughput low.

questions.question: A team wants a smart contract to run a large machine-learning model on every transaction. What stands in the way, and what is the workaround?
options: Nothing stands in the way: a contract can run any computation, as long as the sender pays the gas.
Privacy law forbids running models on a public chain; the workaround is to move to a permissioned chain.
Each block has a hard gas ceiling; compute off-chain and post the result with a proof.
Models need random numbers, which contracts cannot produce; the workaround is to remove the randomness.
questions.correct_option_text: Each block has a hard gas ceiling; compute off-chain and post the result with a proof.
questions.explanation: Gas caps what a transaction can compute, so heavy work is done off-chain and the result is posted with a ZK proof the chain can verify.

questions.question: You submit a large swap. A bot's purchase lands just before yours and its sale just after, leaving you with a worse price. What made this possible?
options: Block producers choose the order of transactions, so a pending trade can be sandwiched.
A reentrancy bug in the exchange's contract, which let the bot call back in before your trade finished.
An oracle that was reporting a stale price.
The bot had obtained your private key.
questions.correct_option_text: Block producers choose the order of transactions, so a pending trade can be sandwiched.
questions.explanation: This is MEV (maximal extractable value): block producers decide which transactions go in and in what order, so they can front-run or sandwich a trade that is waiting.

questions.question: What does the blockchain trilemma say, and how does Ethereum respond to it?
options: A chain can be cheap, fast or legal, but not all three; Ethereum chooses to be legal.
A chain cannot be both secure and public; Ethereum responds by hiding its data.
Every chain has to choose between supporting tokens, NFTs or DAOs; Ethereum is the exception and supports all three.
Security, scalability and decentralisation cannot all be maximised at Layer 1; Ethereum pushes scale to Layer 2.
questions.correct_option_text: Security, scalability and decentralisation cannot all be maximised at Layer 1; Ethereum pushes scale to Layer 2.
questions.explanation: Ethereum keeps security and decentralisation and pushes scale to Layer 2 rollups; base-layer designs trade these three goals off against each other.

questions.question: A smart contract sends money to a caller before it updates its own record of that caller's balance. Which attack does this invite?
options: A flash-loan attack that bends the price reported by the contract's oracle.
Reentrancy: the attacker calls back in before the record is updated.
A governance attack, in which borrowed votes are used to pass a malicious proposal.
An integer overflow that wraps the balance to a huge number.
questions.correct_option_text: Reentrancy: the attacker calls back in before the record is updated.
questions.explanation: Calling back in before the state is updated lets the attacker drain the contract; this bug class cost The DAO $60M, and the fix is to update state before calling out (Checks-Effects-Interactions).

questions.question: In 2017 a user accidentally took ownership of a shared library contract and destroyed it; every wallet built on it froze, with ETH worth about $150M at the time still unreachable. What lesson does the course draw?
options: Flash loans should be banned from wallet contracts.
Price oracles need more than one data source, so that a single feed cannot be bent.
Immutability means a mistake is forever; who can call what must be designed.
On-chain votes need a timelock between approval and execution, so that members can react.
questions.correct_option_text: Immutability means a mistake is forever; who can call what must be designed.
questions.explanation: The Parity multisig freeze combined an access-control gap with immutability: nobody could undo it.

questions.question: A bridge is protected by a 5-of-9 multisig, but four of the nine keys are run by the same company. Which lesson from the course applies?
options: A multisig is only as decentralised as the people who hold its keys.
A 5-of-9 multisig cannot be compromised, because five separate signatures are always required.
The risk lies only in the contract code, which a careful audit would have cleared.
Multisigs are unsafe in general, and a single well-guarded key would be better.
questions.correct_option_text: A multisig is only as decentralised as the people who hold its keys.
questions.explanation: This was the Ronin bridge: attackers obtained five keys through social engineering, four of them run by one company, and withdrew $625M.

questions.question: A team launches the same smart contract to users around the world. Which regulatory risk does the course stress?
options: None: a public blockchain sits outside every national law.
Rules differ by country: a contract that is legal in one jurisdiction may be illegal in another.
Only the country where the developers themselves live has any say over how the contract may be used.
MiCA has already harmonised the rules worldwide.
questions.correct_option_text: Rules differ by country: a contract that is legal in one jurisdiction may be illegal in another.
questions.explanation: Laws move in years and contracts move in months; MiCA is a comprehensive framework for the EU only.

questions.question: A team stores only hashes of personal records on a public chain and declares the privacy problem solved. What caveat does the course add?
options: Any validator can reverse a hash on request.
Hashes are deleted from the chain after 30 days.
Storing hashes is itself banned under GDPR.
Even hashes can leak information through metadata and linkability.
questions.correct_option_text: Even hashes can leak information through metadata and linkability.
questions.explanation: A hash of personal data can still be linked back to a person, and short or guessable inputs can be found by trial and error. Public by design clashes with privacy law, which is why ZK proofs, permissioned chains and off-chain encryption are listed as further tools.

questions.question: What is an ERC token standard such as ERC-20?
options: A licence that Ethereum sells to companies that issue tokens.
An audit certificate issued by the Ethereum Foundation, showing that a contract is free of known bugs.
A published interface (a fixed list of functions and events) that wallets and exchanges can rely on.
A fee paid to validators whenever a new token is created.
questions.correct_option_text: A published interface (a fixed list of functions and events) that wallets and exchanges can rely on.
questions.explanation: ERC stands for Ethereum Request for Comments. A token standard is a promise about your contract's "buttons", so tools built by strangers work with it.

questions.question: A game studio wants a single smart contract to hold both interchangeable gold coins and one-of-a-kind swords, and to send many items in one transfer. Which standard fits best?
options: ERC-20
ERC-721
questions.explanation: ERC-1155 is the multi-token standard: fungible and non-fungible tokens in one contract, built for batch transfers and common in gaming.

questions.question: Who can propose a new Ethereum standard, and what is the role of the EIP editors?
options: Only the Ethereum Foundation may propose; the editors then vote on whether the idea is good enough.
Anyone can write an EIP; editors check its form, not its merit, before open review.
Only wallet companies propose; editors then write the code for it.
Anyone can propose; editors then approve or reject it in private, without any public review.
questions.correct_option_text: Anyone can write an EIP; editors check its form, not its merit, before open review.
questions.explanation: A standard is not decreed: nobody owns ERC-20, and open community review, not an authority, is what carries a proposal to Final.

questions.question: Once Final, how does an ERC (such as a token standard) take effect compared with a Core EIP?
options: Both take effect automatically on every node and in every wallet at the moment they are marked Final.
An ERC needs a network upgrade; a Core EIP is optional for everyone.
Both are only recommendations, and neither changes any software.
An ERC is adopted by choice by wallets and apps; a Core EIP must be built into node software.
questions.correct_option_text: An ERC is adopted by choice by wallets and apps; a Core EIP must be built into node software.
questions.explanation: ERCs are application-level standards that wallets and apps choose to support; Core EIPs change the protocol itself and go live in a network upgrade.

questions.question: A team asks an AI assistant to review a smart contract that will hold customer funds, and the AI replies that it found no issues. What is still missing before deployment?
options: Nothing more: a clean AI review plus a successful compile is the normal bar for a contract holding funds.
Only agreement from a second AI model, since two models rarely miss the same bug.
Automated tests and an independent professional audit: an AI review can miss real bugs and invent fake ones.
Only a trial on mainnet with a small amount of customer money, which will reveal any remaining problem.
questions.correct_option_text: Automated tests and an independent professional audit: an AI review can miss real bugs and invent fake ones.
questions.explanation: The loop is prompt, read, test, audit. An AI review is a useful extra check, but it is not evidence of safety: models miss real bugs and invent fake ones, and two models can share the same blind spot. Anything that will hold real money needs tests that exercise its rules (on a testnet, not with customers' funds) and a professional, human audit.

questions.question: You asked an AI for a minimal fixed-supply token with no owner. Its explanation of the code reveals an owner-only function that can create new tokens. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a red flag: it breaks the fixed-supply and no-owner requirements, so remove it.
Deploy it anyway: an extra function adds useful flexibility in case plans change later.
Deploy it on mainnet first, to see whether the function really works with real tokens.
Ignore it: an owner-only function cannot affect the other holders.
questions.correct_option_text: Treat it as a red flag: it breaks the fixed-supply and no-owner requirements, so remove it.
questions.explanation: The AI drafts, but your wallet signs the deployment: do not deploy until the function is removed and you can explain every line.

questions.question: When you create a wallet for the testnet deployment, which statement about its address and its recovery phrase is correct?
options: Both are public and are safe to post online.
The address is safe to share; the recovery phrase must never be shared or typed into a website.
The address must be kept secret; the recovery phrase can be given to a faucet to receive test ETH.
Both must be pasted into Remix before you can deploy.
questions.correct_option_text: The address is safe to share; the recovery phrase must never be shared or typed into a website.
questions.explanation: The address is how others pay you and how a faucet finds you; whoever has the phrase controls the wallet.

questions.question: What actually happens when you press Deploy in Remix and confirm in your wallet?
options: Remix stores the contract on its own servers and gives you a private link that you can share.
The code is e-mailed to the validators, who install it by hand.
The wallet uploads the code to a static host such as GitHub Pages, where visitors can run it.
It is a transaction: you sign it and pay gas, and the network stores your code.
questions.correct_option_text: It is a transaction: you sign it and pay gas, and the network stores your code.
questions.explanation: The code then lives at a permanent public address, which is why even a testnet deployment needs (free) test ETH for gas.

questions.question: A class project deploys from Remix in the browser. What does the course recommend for a team shipping a real product?
options: Keep using Remix on mainnet: nothing else needs to change.
Keep using Remix, but have a second team member watch each deployment step on screen.
Hardhat or Foundry: a local project with automated tests and scripted, repeatable deployments.
Deploy from Remix to mainnet first, then write tests once real users show which functions matter.
questions.correct_option_text: Hardhat or Foundry: a local project with automated tests and scripted, repeatable deployments.
questions.explanation: Same contract and same steps, but with real money at stake the code is tested and audited first, because deployed code cannot simply be edited.

questions.question: A dApp page shows a visitor's token balance with no wallet pop-up and no fee. How does it get that number?
options: It asks an RPC provider, whose node answers: free, and nothing to sign.
It sends a small transaction that the site quietly pays for on the visitor's behalf.
It looks the balance up in the static host's own database.
It asks the visitor's wallet to sign a read request.
questions.correct_option_text: It asks an RPC provider, whose node answers: free, and nothing to sign.
questions.explanation: Reads go through an RPC provider; only a wallet-signed transaction changes anything on-chain, and that costs gas.

questions.question: A team chooses a hosted RPC provider such as Infura or Alchemy over running its own node. What trade-off does the course point out?
options: A provider is slower, but it is the only way to send transactions.
A provider saves the work, but puts one company between your site and the chain.
A provider holds the users' private keys for them, while your own node would not.
A provider can change your contract's code after deployment, while your own node cannot.
questions.correct_option_text: A provider saves the work, but puts one company between your site and the chain.
questions.explanation: Running your own node removes that middleman, at the cost of storage and upkeep; either way the site never holds keys.

questions.question: After deployment, who hosts the smart contract itself?
options: The team, on the same static host that serves the website's files.
The RPC provider, on its private servers.
The wallet app of whoever deployed it.
The network: each of its many independent nodes holds a copy.
questions.correct_option_text: The network: each of its many independent nodes holds a copy.
questions.explanation: The team hosts only the front-end files; an RPC provider reads the chain and the wallet writes to it, but the contract itself is already hosted by the network.

questions.question: A company wants its ERP to release a supplier's invoice for payment as soon as a delivery is confirmed on-chain. How is this wired up?
options: The contract calls the ERP's API directly, as soon as delivery has been confirmed on-chain.
The contract e-mails the finance team, who then update the ERP.
The contract emits an event, and an off-chain listener picks it up and triggers the ERP.
The ERP is installed on-chain so that the contract can write to it.
questions.correct_option_text: The contract emits an event, and an off-chain listener picks it up and triggers the ERP.
questions.explanation: A contract cannot reach out to other systems: it announces through an event (a log entry, not a message), and everything off-chain is a reaction to it.

questions.question: A customer withdraws funds from an exchange that has verified their identity to their own wallet on a public chain. What follows for their privacy?
options: Nothing: wallet addresses are anonymous by design.
Only the exchange can ever see what the wallet does.
Only transactions made after the withdrawal are exposed; everything earlier stays hidden.
The exchange, and anyone else who learns of the link, can tie the wallet's whole history to their name.
questions.correct_option_text: The exchange, and anyone else who learns of the link, can tie the wallet's whole history to their name.
questions.explanation: Pseudonymous is not anonymous: every address, balance and transfer is visible forever, so once an address is linked to a name (by the exchange, by investigators with access to its records, or through a leak) the trail can be followed backwards and forwards.

questions.question: A firm moves its payroll and supplier payments onto a public chain with no privacy technology. What consequence does the course highlight?
options: Payment amounts are public, so salaries can be worked out and competitors can watch its treasury move.
Its payments become invisible to its own auditors and to the tax authorities.
Only the firm's own bank is able to see the payments.
Employees are able to reverse their salary payments at will.
questions.correct_option_text: Payment amounts are public, so salaries can be worked out and competitors can watch its treasury move.
questions.explanation: Suppliers could also infer its volumes and margins once its addresses are known: a public ledger is a permanent record, so privacy has to be added on purpose.

questions.question: At a venue door you can prove you are over 18 by showing a passport or by showing a zero-knowledge proof. What does the bouncer learn in the second case?
options: Your exact date of birth, but not your name.
Only that the statement "over 18" is true, and nothing else about you.
Everything on the passport, in encrypted form.
Nothing at all, so the bouncer has to take your word for it.
questions.correct_option_text: Only that the statement "over 18" is true, and nothing else about you.
questions.explanation: A zero-knowledge proof proves a statement is true without revealing anything that makes it true: one fact proven, zero facts leaked.

questions.question: In the "Where's Waldo?" analogy, a page is covered by an opaque sheet with one small hole showing Waldo. What does this demonstrate?
options: That the prover must in the end reveal Waldo's position in order to be believed.
That a proof only works if the verifier already knows the answer.
That you can be convinced Waldo is on the page yet learn nothing about where.
That hiding any information always makes a claim impossible for someone else to check.
questions.correct_option_text: That you can be convinced Waldo is on the page yet learn nothing about where.
questions.explanation: That gap is "zero-knowledge": a proof convinces by making cheating impossible, not by showing the secret.

questions.question: A 16-year-old tries to produce a valid "over 18" proof. Which property of zero-knowledge proofs stops this?
options: Completeness: true claims always pass.
Zero-knowledge: nothing else leaks.
Publication: proofs are published, so validators spot the forgery.
Soundness: a false claim cannot produce a valid proof.
questions.correct_option_text: Soundness: a false claim cannot produce a valid proof.
questions.explanation: The three properties are completeness (true claims pass), soundness (false claims fail: without a genuine credential, producing a valid proof is practically impossible) and zero-knowledge (nothing else leaks). The proof is only as good as the credential behind it: it relies on the issuer having attested the right date of birth.

questions.question: In the "KYC without handing over your identity" pattern, where does your personal data sit, and what does the app receive?
options: A bank-signed credential stays in your wallet; the app checks a proof with none of the raw data.
The bank uploads your passport to the chain; the app reads it there.
The app stores an encrypted copy of your documents, and the bank holds the only key that can open it.
Your data is split between the validators; the app asks them to vote.
questions.correct_option_text: A bank-signed credential stays in your wallet; the app checks a proof with none of the raw data.
questions.explanation: The bank verifies you once and signs a credential; your wallet proves statements such as "age ≥ 18, not sanctioned" without the data leaving it.

questions.question: Why would a business prefer this zero-knowledge KYC pattern to collecting customers' documents itself?
options: It removes the need for anyone to carry out a KYC check.
It holds no passport database that could leak, and regulators can still get proof the check was done.
It keeps customers hidden from regulators for good.
It lets the business store encrypted copies of customers' passports on-chain as a permanent backup.
questions.correct_option_text: It holds no passport database that could leak, and regulators can still get proof the check was done.
questions.explanation: Verify the claim, not the person: onboarding takes seconds, is reusable across services that trust the issuer, and carries far less GDPR exposure.

questions.question: An exchange wants to show that the assets it holds cover every customer's deposit, without publishing any customer's balance. Which zero-knowledge application is this?
options: Proof of personhood
Private voting
Proof of reserves
A mixer
questions.correct_option_text: Proof of reserves
questions.explanation: Proof of reserves proves a business fact (assets held cover customer balances) without opening the books. It is not a full solvency audit: it says nothing about the firm's other debts, or about whether the assets are borrowed or pledged.

questions.question: A community wants one-person-one-vote without collecting anyone's identity. Which zero-knowledge application addresses this?
options: Proof of personhood: prove you are a unique human without revealing which one.
Proof of reserves: prove that you hold enough tokens to be allowed to cast a vote.
Shielded payments: hide how much each voter has paid.
Web proofs: prove you know the password to the voting site.
questions.correct_option_text: Proof of personhood: prove you are a unique human without revealing which one.
questions.explanation: Proof of personhood answers "is this a unique human?" without "who are you?".

questions.question: A regulated fintech wants on-chain privacy for its customers. After the Tornado Cash story, what design guidance does the course give?
options: Use a mixer: hiding everything is the safest position with regulators.
Prefer selective disclosure and proof-of-compliance over all-or-nothing anonymity.
Avoid privacy features altogether: public chains must stay fully transparent to be legal.
Make privacy mandatory for every single user, so that no individual customer stands out.
questions.correct_option_text: Prefer selective disclosure and proof-of-compliance over all-or-nothing anonymity.
questions.explanation: For example, prove "not on a sanctions list" without revealing identity. The US sanctioned Tornado Cash in 2022 and lifted the sanctions in March 2025 after losing in court, but the lesson stands: all-or-nothing anonymity invites a collision with regulators.

questions.question: The course says "two things are true at once" about Tornado Cash. Which pair?
options: It was run by a company, and that company kept customer records.
It never handled any illicit funds, and regulators acted against it without having any reason.
The tools shielded a state-sponsored hacking group's loot, and also protected ordinary people.
It was shut down for good, and its code was deleted from the chain.
questions.correct_option_text: The tools shielded a state-sponsored hacking group's loot, and also protected ordinary people.
questions.explanation: Regulators had a genuine problem, yet sanctioning the code (in 2022; lifted in March 2025 after a US court ruling) punished users who had done nothing wrong; that tension is why the course points to selective disclosure.

questions.question: What does "selective, provable disclosure" let a regulated institution do on a public chain?
options: Keep its data confidential while still proving that it follows the rules.
Hide all of its on-chain activity from regulators and auditors, permanently and by default.
Publish all of its data in full, so that no proofs are needed and nothing is left to verify.
Choose which laws apply to its transactions.
questions.correct_option_text: Keep its data confidential while still proving that it follows the rules.
questions.explanation: For example, an exchange proves solvency or a firm proves an audit passed, without opening its books.

questions.question: Carbon credits are put on one shared ledger as unique tokens, and each token is burned when its credit is used (retired). This stops double counting. Which problem can no ledger fix?
options: A credit that was never real: the carbon saving was mis-measured or faked.
The same credit token being sold or used twice.
Proving that a credit has already been used (retired).
Showing who has held a credit over time.
questions.correct_option_text: A credit that was never real: the carbon saving was mis-measured or faked.
questions.explanation: A shared ledger handles double selling, retirement and ownership history, but it faithfully records whatever it is given, true or not. If the measurement behind a credit was wrong or faked, the token is still recorded perfectly: garbage in, garbage out. Checking the real-world claim has to happen off-chain.

questions.question: Replacing a freelance platform with an escrow smart contract cuts fees and removes the platform's discretion over funds. What does the course say disappears along with it?
options: The freelancer's ability to be paid at all.
The platform's support in a messy dispute.
The client's ability to lock funds up front.
Any record of what the two sides agreed.
questions.correct_option_text: The platform's support in a messy dispute.
questions.explanation: Existing platforms are escrow already; the contract removes their discretion and their support, so dispute resolution must be designed in.

questions.question: A group proposes stablecoins on a Layer 2 for cross-border tuition and remittances. Where does the course say the case is strongest?
options: In corridors that are already served by cheap and instant bank transfers, where habits are established.
Wherever the recipient prefers cash to digital money.
Where banking access is poor; elsewhere fintech rails often do the job cheaply.
Only between two countries that share a currency.
questions.correct_option_text: Where banking access is poor; elsewhere fintech rails often do the job cheaply.
questions.explanation: The honest alternative (Wise, SEPA Instant) already works well in many corridors, so the blockchain case depends on where it does not.

questions.question: For diploma verification, the "honest alternative" to anchoring hashes on-chain is a national verification API run by the education ministry. How does the course weigh it?
options: Cheaper, but it makes the ministry the single point of trust and failure.
More expensive, and every employer would still need a wallet.
Equally decentralised, since a ministry cannot alter its records.
Unworkable, because diplomas cannot be checked through an API.
questions.correct_option_text: Cheaper, but it makes the ministry the single point of trust and failure.
questions.explanation: A good report takes the non-blockchain alternative seriously and says what is given up either way.

questions.question: For group-buying a rare asset, the course contrasts a DAO with "a fund or cooperative with a lawyer". What is the alternative's key advantage?
options: It raises money from strangers faster than a DAO.
It needs no legal entity at all.
It lets contributors exit instantly with their share.
It is slower, but it is a legal entity that can actually own the asset.
questions.correct_option_text: It is slower, but it is a legal entity that can actually own the asset.
questions.explanation: A DAO pools money fast, but custody and legal ownership are where it struggles unless it adds a legal wrapper (the ConstitutionDAO lesson).

questions.question: A payment instruction is digitally signed but sent without encryption. What protection does the signature principally provide?
options: It lets others check authorisation and detect changes to the signed instruction.
It keeps the payment amount confidential while leaving the destination visible.
It prevents authorised observers from copying the instruction into their records.
It hides the payer's address while allowing the recipient to claim payment.
questions.correct_option_text: It lets others check authorisation and detect changes to the signed instruction.
questions.explanation: A signature supports verification of a signed instruction; it does not conceal its contents. Confidentiality requires a separate mechanism. Verification establishes control of a signing key, subject to the key remaining secure.

questions.question: A supplier signs a message using the key controlling a payment address. A buyer has never verified who owns that address. What has the signature established?
options: The signer is the company named in the buyer's purchase order.
The signer controls the relevant key, without establishing the supplier's legal identity.
The signer passed identity checks when the address was first created.
That the signer is an employee currently authorised to enter the purchase contract.
questions.correct_option_text: The signer controls the relevant key, without establishing the supplier's legal identity.
questions.explanation: Cryptographic identity is not automatically a legal identity. A signature can demonstrate key control, but the buyer still needs a reliable link between that key and the intended organisation.

questions.question: A treasurer installs two wallet apps and restores the same recovery phrase in both. She calls this diversification against theft of that phrase. How should the arrangement be assessed?
options: It reduces each stolen phrase to control of only half the addresses.
It requires both apps to approve a payment, creating a two-party control.
It separates the balances because each app maintains its own private ledger.
It adds another interface, but both apps depend on the same underlying secret.
questions.correct_option_text: It adds another interface, but both apps depend on the same underlying secret.
questions.explanation: Restoring the same seed recreates the associated keys. Two apps can improve convenience or access, but do not split authority over those keys. A compromise of the common secret remains a common failure point.

questions.question: An insurer retains a claim document's hash on-chain but loses every copy of the document. Can the hash restore the missing document?
options: Yes; knowing the original file type is enough to reverse the fingerprint.
Yes; the insurer can request the full document from the block's validator.
No; recovery fails only because the document was not digitally signed first.
No; it can help check a recovered copy, but does not encode a recoverable document.
questions.correct_option_text: No; it can help check a recovered copy, but does not encode a recoverable document.
questions.explanation: A cryptographic hash is a compact, one-way fingerprint, not a backup. If a copy is later found, its hash can be compared with the recorded value. Retaining the underlying document is a separate requirement.

questions.question: Two PDFs display the same invoice, but one was re-exported and has different file bytes. Their SHA-256 hashes differ. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The files differ at the byte level, even if the visible invoice details agree.
One file must have been created after the invoice's payment deadline passed.
At least one displayed amount must have been changed between the two PDFs.
The supplier's signing key must have changed when the file was re-exported.
questions.correct_option_text: The files differ at the byte level, even if the visible invoice details agree.
questions.explanation: Hashing compares exact input data, not business meaning or visual appearance. Re-exporting can change bytes without changing the displayed commercial terms. A different hash establishes a different file, not a particular kind of business alteration.

questions.question: A designer anchors a brochure's hash on-chain and later produces the matching brochure. Which conclusion would be unjustified?
options: That the designer created the brochure or owns its copyright.
That changing the supplied file would usually change its fingerprint.
That a later supplied file can be checked against the anchored fingerprint.
That the fingerprint was included in the accepted chain's recorded history.
questions.correct_option_text: That the designer created the brochure or owns its copyright.
questions.explanation: An accepted timestamped anchor is evidence connecting a fingerprint to recorded history. By itself it does not establish authorship or legal rights. Those claims require evidence beyond the fact that someone submitted the hash.

questions.question: Two honest Bitcoin miners find different valid blocks at nearly the same time. Merchants briefly see different chain tips. What can explain this without anyone breaking the protocol's rules?
options: Two blocks meeting the validity rules must contain identical transactions and timestamps.
Both branches become permanently final as soon as a merchant's wallet accepts either one.
Propagation can create competing valid tips before accumulated work makes one branch preferred.
Only the block with more transactions can be valid, regardless of accumulated proof of work.
questions.correct_option_text: Propagation can create competing valid tips before accumulated work makes one branch preferred.
questions.explanation: Miners can independently produce competing valid blocks before learning about one another's results. A temporary disagreement about the preferred tip is therefore possible without forged transactions or dishonest behaviour. Nodes subsequently follow the valid chain with the greatest accumulated work.

questions.question: Why does expressing a Bitcoin payment in smaller units, such as counting a payment as 100,000 satoshis instead of 0.001 BTC, not by itself increase the supply of bitcoin?
options: It creates additional bitcoin that cannot be spent until converted back into BTC.
It increases supply only for the recipient, while leaving the sender's supply fixed.
It increases supply temporarily, until the next scheduled subsidy reduction removes it.
It changes the denomination used to count value, not the total value issued.
questions.correct_option_text: It changes the denomination used to count value, not the total value issued.
questions.explanation: Denomination and issuance are different concepts. Counting the same quantity in smaller units makes smaller payments expressible; it does not create more BTC. This distinction matters when evaluating claims that divisibility undermines scarcity.

questions.question: Immediately after a Bitcoin subsidy halving, newly issued BTC per block is lower. Ignoring losses of keys, what happens to the total amount issued as further valid blocks arrive?
options: It falls each block because the protocol removes half of earlier issuance.
It returns toward the previous halving's level as miners adjust their activity.
It continues increasing, but with fewer new BTC added per block.
It stays constant until transaction fees replace the reduced subsidy.
questions.correct_option_text: It continues increasing, but with fewer new BTC added per block.
questions.explanation: A halving reduces the flow of new issuance. It does not remove previously issued BTC. Total issued supply can therefore continue rising while its rate of increase falls, subject to the existing issuance rules.

questions.question: A mining company's presentation says a subsidy halving must cut its BTC revenue per successful block by exactly half. What information is missing?
options: The number of wallets holding BTC, which determines the subsidy for that block.
The BTC/fiat price, which determines how many BTC transaction fees a block contains.
Transaction fees in the block, which also contribute to the miner's BTC revenue.
The difficulty period's length, which fixes the transaction-fee income in each block.
questions.correct_option_text: Transaction fees in the block, which also contribute to the miner's BTC revenue.
questions.explanation: The subsidy is only one part of the payment for a successful block; transaction fees are another. A halving of the subsidy alone does not establish an exact halving of total BTC revenue per block. Revenue in fiat also depends on the exchange rate.

questions.question: A miner doubles its share of network hash power, but wins no blocks during a short observation period. Does this alone show the equipment failed?
options: No; a higher expected chance of winning does not guarantee a win in a short period.
Yes; each miner is allocated a fixed block quota proportional to its hash power.
No; only total network hash rate, not the miner's share, affects its chance of winning.
Yes; doubling hash power guarantees at least one block before difficulty changes.
questions.correct_option_text: No; a higher expected chance of winning does not guarantee a win in a short period.
questions.explanation: Mining is a probabilistic race. More hash power raises the expected rate of finding blocks, given the network conditions, but short-run outcomes can vary. A production claim should distinguish expected performance from guaranteed results.

questions.question: A merchant wants to verify for itself that incoming Bitcoin payments follow Bitcoin's rules, without becoming a miner. What should the merchant do?
options: Leave validation to its wallet provider or exchange and trust the result they report.
Run its own full node, which validates blocks and transactions but does not mine.
Buy mining equipment, because only miners are able to validate payments.
Hold more BTC, because a larger balance gives a node more weight in validation.
questions.correct_option_text: Run its own full node, which validates blocks and transactions but does not mine.
questions.explanation: Validating and mining are separate roles. A full node checks every block and transaction against Bitcoin's consensus rules and rejects invalid ones, with no mining required. Leaving validation to a wallet provider or exchange means trusting their checks, mining equipment is for competing to produce blocks, and holding more BTC gives no extra say in validation.

questions.question: A retailer's blockchain payment dashboard goes offline after a Bitcoin payment is confirmed. Other independent nodes still show the payment. What is the best interpretation?
options: The customer's original authorisation must be renewed because the retailer lost its local view.
The payment loses its network confirmation until the retailer's dashboard resynchronises.
The retailer lost one view of the ledger; that outage did not itself reverse the payment.
The retailer's address becomes invalid until the wallet provider restores its server.
questions.correct_option_text: The retailer lost one view of the ledger; that outage did not itself reverse the payment.
questions.explanation: A dashboard is an access layer, not the authority that keeps a confirmed transaction in the ledger. Its outage can disrupt business operations without undoing the network's recorded state. Independent access can help distinguish a display problem from a settlement problem.

questions.question: A digital asset has an enforceable fixed issuance limit, but demand for it falls sharply. What can a treasurer infer from the supply limit alone?
options: It guarantees purchasing power because no additional units can be issued.
It fixes the exchange rate while allowing transaction fees to absorb demand changes.
It constrains issuance, but does not establish a minimum market price.
It ensures a positive long-term return so long as the asset remains transferable.
questions.correct_option_text: It constrains issuance, but does not establish a minimum market price.
questions.explanation: Scarcity is only one contributor to monetary value. Acceptance, utility, trust and demand still matter. A fixed supply rule does not by itself guarantee market demand, a price floor or suitability for a particular treasury liability.

questions.question: An open-source payment protocol publishes all its code. Which conclusion is warranted without further evidence?
options: Independent inspection is unnecessary because public code cannot contain hidden weaknesses.
Any bug must already have been fixed because attackers can also inspect the code.
Others can inspect its implementation; publication alone does not show it is secure.
The code has passed a security audit because everyone has permission to review it.
questions.correct_option_text: Others can inspect its implementation; publication alone does not show it is secure.
questions.explanation: Open source enables scrutiny and reproducibility. It does not establish that qualified review actually occurred, that reviewers found every bug or that the deployed version matches reviewed code. An opportunity to inspect is different from evidence of safety.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A company wallet holds dollar stablecoins but no ETH on Ethereum mainnet. It uses an ordinary direct transaction, with no sponsor or relayer. Why can it still be unable to send the stablecoins?
options: The wallet needs ETH to fund the transaction's network fee.
A company wallet must stake its stablecoin balance before paying transaction fees.
It must hold more stablecoins to pay both the transfer and its network fee in that token.
The stablecoin issuer must authorise the wallet's ordinary ETH fee payment before any transfer.
questions.correct_option_text: The wallet needs ETH to fund the transaction's network fee.
questions.explanation: For the stipulated direct Ethereum transaction, fees are funded in ETH even though the asset being transferred is a token. Having enough of the payment asset does not necessarily mean having the fee asset. Sponsored and abstracted payment designs can change the user experience, but are excluded here.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: An Ethereum transaction's maximum total fee per gas is below the base fee of the block being considered. Which statement is correct for inclusion in that block?
options: It can execute until the fee cap is reached, then retain the completed steps.
It can be included if the validator accepts a negative priority tip.
It can execute if the recipient agrees to accept less than the stated transfer amount.
It cannot be included at that base fee under its existing fee cap.
questions.correct_option_text: It cannot be included at that base fee under its existing fee cap.
questions.explanation: The maximum fee per gas caps what the sender authorises per unit. A block whose base fee exceeds that cap cannot include the transaction on those terms. This is distinct from an execution running out of gas after inclusion.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: An Ethereum transaction keeps both fee caps unchanged. The base fee rises close to, but remains below, its maximum total fee per gas. What can happen to the effective priority tip?
options: It must remain at the priority cap because the two fee caps are independent charges.
It can shrink because the total fee cap leaves less room above the base fee.
It remains fixed because the effective tip is settled when the sender signs the transaction.
It becomes the full maximum total fee because the sender already authorised that cap.
questions.correct_option_text: It can shrink because the total fee cap leaves less room above the base fee.
questions.explanation: The effective tip cannot exceed either the priority cap or the remaining room under the total cap after the base fee. As that room narrows, the effective tip can fall. The cap is a ceiling, not an instruction to pay it all.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A finance team doubles a transaction's gas-unit limit but changes neither its fee caps nor the work requested. Why is faster inclusion not assured?
options: The limit sets the number of blocks a request may wait, rather than its execution allowance.
The gas-unit limit permits execution work; it is not the price offered per unit.
The extra gas-unit limit is paid directly to the validator as an unconditional bonus.
The gas limit is chosen by the recipient, so the sender's higher setting cannot change it.
questions.correct_option_text: The gas-unit limit permits execution work; it is not the price offered per unit.
questions.explanation: Gas units measure permitted computational work, while fee parameters determine the offered price per unit and effective priority. Increasing the execution allowance does not itself increase the bid. Actual inclusion also depends on block capacity and the transaction's other properties.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A company treats projected ETH staking rewards as guaranteed operating income in euros. Which exposure is being overlooked?
options: The euro return is fixed once the validator has paid its entry deposit.
Both staking outcomes and the euro value of ETH can change.
Staking removes ETH price exposure because rewards are earned in ETH.
Only exit-queue length matters, because earning rewards in ETH offsets the ETH price exposure.
questions.correct_option_text: Both staking outcomes and the euro value of ETH can change.
questions.explanation: Staking rewards are paid in the asset and depend on network and operator conditions. Their euro value also depends on ETH's exchange rate. Quoting an estimated ETH yield is not the same as promising a fixed, risk-free euro return.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Two investors have similar ETH price exposure. One holds brokerage fund shares; the other holds a liquid-staking token accepted by a particular DeFi app. Which difference matters for using that app?
options: Neither instrument can be used because assets linked to staking are excluded from contracts.
The token can be used through its supported on-chain interface; the brokerage shares cannot simply be substituted.
Both instruments require the investor to operate a validator before accessing any DeFi app.
The fund shares can be used because equal price exposure makes instruments interchangeable.
questions.correct_option_text: The token can be used through its supported on-chain interface; the brokerage shares cannot simply be substituted.
questions.explanation: Economic exposure and technical/legal form are different. A compatible on-chain token may be usable within an app that accepts it. Brokerage shares represent a different instrument and do not become that token merely because both track ETH-related value.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: In Ethereum's proof-of-stake process, why does being selected to propose a block not give a validator unilateral authority to make an invalid payment valid?
options: A proposer can authorise an otherwise invalid payment if it includes a sufficiently high fee.
A proposer can change validity rules for its own block, but not for another validator's block.
The proposer has authority only over payments below the value of its stake.
Other participants check the proposed block against the protocol's validity rules.
questions.correct_option_text: Other participants check the proposed block against the protocol's validity rules.
questions.explanation: Proposal is a role in the process, not a licence to override validity rules. Other validating participants check proposals, and consensus votes operate within those rules. Stake and selection do not grant arbitrary access to users' assets.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A retailer deploys the same token-contract software on Ethereum and on another EVM-compatible chain. Why are balances not automatically shared between the deployments?
options: Both deployments share balances only after their token names are made identical.
Balances become shared as soon as a wallet imports both contract addresses.
Compatible execution software does not make separate chains share one ledger.
The chain with lower gas fees automatically becomes the master balance register.
questions.correct_option_text: Compatible execution software does not make separate chains share one ledger.
questions.explanation: EVM compatibility supports code reuse and familiar interfaces. Each chain and deployment still has its own state. A connection or asset-movement mechanism is needed where the business requires value or messages to cross between them.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A rollup publishes its transaction data in Ethereum blobs. An auditor will need that data years later. Which statement is correct?
options: Validity proofs make it unnecessary to keep transaction data for later audits.
Blobs are kept for a short window only; later access needs separate archiving.
Blob data stays private to the sequencer, so only the sequencer can supply it.
Every Ethereum node stores each blob permanently, as it does block headers.
questions.correct_option_text: Blobs are kept for a short window only; later access needs separate archiving.
questions.explanation: Under EIP-4844, nodes are required to keep blobs only for a limited window (about 18 days), not as a permanent archive. Long-term access needs separate retention or archival arrangements. That requirement is different from the proof and settlement rules that establish the rollup's state.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A ZK (validity) rollup provider says Ethereum can check its batches of transactions cheaply. Which conclusion would be a mistake?
options: That some of the work is done outside Ethereum's main chain.
That creating the proofs is also cheap and easy for the provider.
That many user transactions can be bundled into a single batch.
That Ethereum can check the result without redoing all of the work.
questions.correct_option_text: That creating the proofs is also cheap and easy for the provider.
questions.explanation: Checking a proof and creating a proof are two different jobs with different costs. Checking can be cheap for Ethereum while creating the proof still takes a lot of computing work for the provider. So cheap checking tells you nothing about the provider's own costs.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A rollup app shows a payment as accepted before its batch has settled on Ethereum. A supplier is about to release an irreversible high-value shipment. Which distinction matters most?
options: An early sequencer receipt can offer weaker assurance than the later settlement stage.
An early receipt and an L1-settled state provide identical assurance for every business purpose.
A receipt issued quickly cannot later appear in a valid Ethereum-settled batch.
Withdrawal liquidity and settlement assurance become equivalent once the app displays a receipt.
questions.correct_option_text: An early sequencer receipt can offer weaker assurance than the later settlement stage.
questions.explanation: Rollup user experience can show a quick acceptance or soft confirmation before all settlement steps complete. A business should match its release decision to the assurance stage it needs. Fast display latency and stronger settlement assurance are not interchangeable descriptions.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Ethereum remains operational, but an app's only rollup sequencer stops accepting user requests. What can happen to the app's normal transaction service?
options: Normal L2 submissions must continue because Ethereum validators take over the app's ordering.
Normal processing can be disrupted even while Ethereum itself remains healthy.
All earlier rollup transactions become invalid because the sequencer has gone offline.
The app can disregard sequencer availability whenever its quoted transaction fees remain low.
questions.correct_option_text: Normal processing can be disrupted even while Ethereum itself remains healthy.
questions.explanation: A rollup has components beyond the base chain. Availability of Ethereum alone does not establish availability of the ordinary sequencer path. Alternative submission or exit mechanisms depend on the rollup's design and are not specified in this scenario.

questions.question: A former consortium employee's Fabric certificate is revoked for future use. What should an auditor avoid concluding from the revocation alone?
options: That the network can use identity rules to restrict future participation.
That the person's credential and the ledger's historical records are different things.
That earlier committed records signed with that credential have been erased.
That a certificate's status matters when deciding whether to accept new activity.
questions.correct_option_text: That earlier committed records signed with that credential have been erased.
questions.explanation: Identity controls can restrict future use without rewriting the append-only record of past activity. Revocation is not a mechanism for deleting historical transactions. The precise acceptance rules depend on network policy, but historical erasure does not follow from revocation alone.

questions.question: A consortium chooses Fabric, which has no required native cryptocurrency. Can its application nevertheless track ownership of warehouse receipts?
options: No; all transferable records require a cryptocurrency issued by the platform.
No; a network without gas can keep documents but cannot update asset ownership.
Yes; chaincode can maintain application-level asset and ownership records.
Yes; but each receipt must first be represented by ETH on Ethereum.
questions.correct_option_text: Yes; chaincode can maintain application-level asset and ownership records.
questions.explanation: No native cryptocurrency means the platform does not require a built-in coin for its operation. It does not prevent business applications from defining balances, receipts or other assets as records governed by chaincode.

questions.question: A consortium requires every member organisation to endorse a payment. It adds more mandatory endorsers but no backup endorsement paths. Which trade-off should it anticipate?
options: Broader required approval also makes progress depend on more organisations being available.
Each added member supplies an extra signature that can replace any missing mandatory endorsement.
Adding mandatory approvers removes the need to check signatures during final validation.
Endorser availability becomes irrelevant because the orderer can supply missing approvals.
questions.correct_option_text: Broader required approval also makes progress depend on more organisations being available.
questions.explanation: An all-members policy spreads required approval across organisations, but a valid update still needs every required endorsement. Without redundancy or a policy change, an unavailable mandatory participant can block progress. Broader required participation does not automatically improve service availability.

questions.question: A ledger is publicly readable, but only approved financial institutions may validate new entries. Which classification best captures those two facts?
options: Private visibility with unrestricted participation.
Permissionless validation with private visibility.
Permissionless validation with mandatory anonymity.
Public visibility with permissioned validation.
questions.correct_option_text: Public visibility with permissioned validation.
questions.explanation: Public readability does not imply that anyone may validate or write. Read, write and validation rights are separate dimensions. Describing each explicitly is more useful than treating public and permissionless as identical labels.

questions.question: A bank consortium changes its ordering service from crash-fault-tolerant to Byzantine-fault-tolerant. Which business control still needs its own specification?
options: Whether the ordering protocol can tolerate some malicious orderer behaviour.
Which organisations must endorse a particular type of payment.
How the ordering nodes agree on a common transaction sequence.
Whether an orderer can fail without every participant losing its ledger copy.
questions.correct_option_text: Which organisations must endorse a particular type of payment.
questions.explanation: Ordering fault tolerance and transaction authorisation answer different questions. A more fault-tolerant ordering service does not determine who should approve a loan or payment. The endorsement policy and application rules still need to express that business authority.

questions.question: A stablecoin issuer burns its native tokens on one supported chain and issues the corresponding amount on another. How does this differ from a separate lock-and-mint wrapper?
options: It removes all dependence on the issuer because no token remains on the source chain.
It makes the same value spendable on both chains at once under one unchanged issuer claim.
It moves the issuer's native issuance between chains rather than creating a claim on a separate bridge vault.
It turns both native versions into claims redeemable only through the independent wrapper.
questions.correct_option_text: It moves the issuer's native issuance between chains rather than creating a claim on a separate bridge vault.
questions.explanation: The course contrasts native multi-chain issuance with bridge-issued stand-ins. Burning and minting by the issuer differs from locking an asset behind a separate wrapper. Issuer and message-verification dependencies still matter; the transfer method does not remove every trust assumption.

questions.question: A treasury sees two tokens with the same dollar-stablecoin label on one chain. One is issued natively; the other was issued by an independent bridge. What must it check before treating them as equivalent?
options: Whether a broker offers both, which establishes interchangeable creditor rights for holders.
Whether both quote near one dollar today, which establishes identical future redemption risk.
Their issuing contracts, backing arrangements and redemption routes.
Whether both use ERC-20, which establishes identical backing obligations for their issuers.
questions.correct_option_text: Their issuing contracts, backing arrangements and redemption routes.
questions.explanation: A display name or symbol is not a complete asset identifier or guarantee of backing. A native token and an independent bridged representation can expose holders to different parties, contracts and redemption mechanisms even if their market labels look similar.

questions.question: A trader notices an asset is cheaper on one chain than another. Why is that observation alone insufficient to establish a profitable arbitrage?
options: A token must have the same price everywhere whenever both chains use the EVM.
The gap shows new issuance on the cheaper chain, rather than a difference in local demand.
Trading the gap is impossible unless both chains use the same native fee asset.
Transfers, execution costs and price changes can consume the apparent price difference.
questions.correct_option_text: Transfers, execution costs and price changes can consume the apparent price difference.
questions.explanation: Separate markets can produce different prices, but exploiting a gap requires a feasible route and trades at achievable prices. Fees, time, liquidity and changing prices can outweigh the quoted difference. A visible gap is not the same as a risk-free realised profit.

questions.question: An IBC connection verifies messages with light-client proofs. Its only active relayer stops forwarding new messages. What distinction matters?
options: Proof checks can protect authenticity while delivery still depends on an available relaying path.
The destination automatically treats every unrelayed message as already received.
Light-client verification itself forwards pending messages, so no delivery path is needed.
The destination must accept the latest unproved claim until its relayer resumes delivery.
questions.correct_option_text: Proof checks can protect authenticity while delivery still depends on an available relaying path.
questions.explanation: Verification prevents acceptance of unauthorised claims, but cannot by itself cause a message to be delivered. If the available forwarding path stops, progress can be delayed even though invalid messages remain rejectable. Additional relayers may provide another path where the design allows them.

questions.question: A fund calls two application chains independent security exposures, although both rely on the same shared validator infrastructure. Which risk has it overlooked?
options: Shared security guarantees that an application loss on either chain is reimbursed by the other.
Diversification is complete whenever the chains quote assets in different native currencies.
Connecting to one security layer eliminates operational risk in each application.
A failure of the common security layer can affect both investments.
questions.correct_option_text: A failure of the common security layer can affect both investments.
questions.explanation: Different applications are not necessarily independent at every layer. Sharing validators or settlement infrastructure can create correlated exposure to failures in that common layer. It does not make all application risks identical, but it weakens a claim of complete security diversification.

questions.question: A sovereign chain connects to another chain through IBC, without entering a shared-security arrangement. What has the connection not automatically supplied?
options: The other chain's validator security for its own local blocks.
A reason to assess the proof assumptions at both ends of the connection.
A way to transport supported messages between the two chains.
A mechanism through which supported cross-chain interactions can be built.
questions.correct_option_text: The other chain's validator security for its own local blocks.
questions.explanation: An interoperability connection and a shared-security arrangement are different. In the scenario, each sovereign chain remains responsible for its own local consensus security. Connecting messages does not by itself replace one chain's validators with another's.

questions.question: A consortium publishes only a fingerprint of a confidential trade document on a public chain and keeps the document private. What can an outsider infer from the fingerprint alone?
options: It proves that every public validator independently checked the trade's commercial terms.
It authorises the outsider to query the consortium's private database for the document.
It does not provide the document's full contents or automatic permission to retrieve them.
It provides the document's full contents once the outsider knows the transaction hash.
questions.correct_option_text: It does not provide the document's full contents or automatic permission to retrieve them.
questions.explanation: An anchor connects a commitment or fingerprint to public history; it is not the same as publishing the underlying document or granting access to it. Low-entropy information and linkable metadata can still create privacy risks, so content secrecy is not an automatic compliance conclusion.

questions.question: A payment workflow makes one ordinary transaction on chain A and a later transaction on chain B. Why can it not assume the first is automatically undone if the second fails?
options: Both transactions are one transaction if they carry the same payment reference.
Separate chains do not automatically share one all-or-nothing execution boundary.
The first transaction becomes reversible whenever the same wallet uses a second chain.
Any bridge automatically rolls back both chains, regardless of how destination calls are implemented.
questions.correct_option_text: Separate chains do not automatically share one all-or-nothing execution boundary.
questions.explanation: Atomic execution applies to the operations inside the relevant transaction boundary. A later action on another chain needs an explicitly designed cross-chain coordination mechanism; ordinary separate transactions do not create automatic rollback of the earlier settled action.

questions.question: On the XRP Ledger described in the course, transaction fees are destroyed rather than paid as mining rewards. What role can those fees still serve?
options: They impose a cost on submitting transactions and help deter spam.
They become refundable deposits whose release depends on the recipient's chosen issuer.
