They give each fee payer a larger share of the ledger's validation votes.
They compensate validators directly for every ledger that those validators approve.
questions.correct_option_text: They impose a cost on submitting transactions and help deter spam.
questions.explanation: A fee need not be distributed as a validator reward to affect behaviour. A cost of submission can discourage abuse even when the protocol destroys the fee. Fee purpose and fee recipient should be assessed separately.

questions.question: Two ledger servers use trusted-validator lists with almost no overlap. Why is it unsafe to infer agreement merely because each sees a large majority within its own list?
options: Local majorities over different sets need not represent the same agreed ledger.
A local majority is automatically a majority within every other server's trusted set.
The count of published validator identities determines agreement regardless of which are trusted.
A public ledger requires every server to accept any list with more names.
questions.correct_option_text: Local majorities over different sets need not represent the same agreed ledger.
questions.explanation: A threshold is meaningful relative to the set over which it is measured. If trusted sets differ greatly, local observations alone do not establish shared agreement. List selection, overlap and the protocol's fault assumptions matter, not just the quoted percentage.

questions.question: A retailer advertises near-zero marginal Lightning payment fees as meaning its payment operation requires no committed funds. What has it missed?
options: Every off-chain payment requires a new minimum-sized on-chain mining deposit.
Capital is required only at channel closure, leaving operating liquidity unaffected before then.
Channel liquidity ties up capital that may be needed to support the payment flows.
Off-chain balances are merely accounting entries, so maintaining them cannot commit capital.
questions.correct_option_text: Channel liquidity ties up capital that may be needed to support the payment flows.
questions.explanation: Low per-payment fees do not eliminate the cost of providing liquidity. Channel capacity has to be funded and positioned to support flows, which can impose capital and operating costs. Marginal transaction cost and total economic cost are different measures.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Two ERC-20 tokens expose the same standard transfer interface. An analyst concludes they must have equivalent backing and holder rights. What is wrong with that conclusion?
options: The conclusion holds only if both tokens were created in the same month.
The conclusion holds only if both tokens appear on the same block explorer.
The interface is only a set of function signatures; it says nothing about backing, reserves or rights.
A token's backing is set by the name of its transfer function, not by its interface.
questions.correct_option_text: The interface is only a set of function signatures; it says nothing about backing, reserves or rights.
questions.explanation: A standard such as ERC-20 is only a shared set of function signatures, so wallets and apps can handle any token the same way. It guarantees nothing about what backs a token, its reserves, redemption rights or the issuer's powers. Those have to be checked separately for each token.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A wallet sends the same signed Ethereum transaction twice because it wasn't sure the first one went through. After the transaction has executed once, why isn't the account charged a second time?
options: The account nonce prevents the same signed transaction from executing twice on that chain.
The signature authorises only the first node receiving it to apply the payment.
Only the wallet provider marks the request as used and then blocks every later copy on the network.
Ethereum rejects every later payment with the same sender, recipient and token amount.
questions.correct_option_text: The account nonce prevents the same signed transaction from executing twice on that chain.
questions.explanation: Every transaction from an account carries a nonce, a counter that must match the account's next expected number. Once the transaction executes, that number is used up, so an identical copy is rejected instead of running again. Paying twice would need a new transaction with a new nonce.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: Two customers request the last available tokenised seat. The smart contract sells only to the first valid purchase it executes. Why can both requests be individually well-formed, yet only one purchase succeed?
options: Deterministic rules apply to the ordered transactions and the state each one encounters.
Deterministic execution requires the contract to divide the seat between both buyers.
The contract must give priority to whichever customer's wallet was created earlier.
Both purchases succeed on different nodes until the seller chooses its preferred buyer.
questions.correct_option_text: Deterministic rules apply to the ordered transactions and the state each one encounters.
questions.explanation: Determinism does not mean that competing transactions see an unchanged starting state. The first successful purchase changes availability; the next encounters the updated state. Agreement on ordering and execution allows nodes to reach the same final outcome.

questions.section_title: Ethereum: From Money to Programmable Blockchain
questions.question: A company performs the same Ethereum action using the same gas units and the same Gwei price per unit as last week. Its euro fee is nevertheless higher. Which change can explain this?
options: The recipient used a different wallet app to display the incoming payment.
The company's token acquired a new trading symbol on an exchange.
The transaction acquired more confirmations before the company checked the fee.
ETH's euro exchange rate rose between the two transactions.
questions.correct_option_text: ETH's euro exchange rate rose between the two transactions.
questions.explanation: The fee is first determined in ETH from the computational work and its ETH-denominated price. Expressing that cost in euros adds an exchange-rate conversion. An unchanged gas workload and Gwei price do not imply an unchanged euro cost.

questions.question: An escrow releases funds only when the buyer confirms delivery. Its published rules contain no deadline, dispute path or alternative release condition. The buyer stops responding after receiving the goods. What is the design problem?
options: The validators must decide whether the buyer's silence counts as acceptance.
The seller can recover the funds merely by showing that its wallet deployed the contract.
The contract must infer delivery from the passage of time and pay the seller.
The contract may follow its rules correctly while leaving the funds locked indefinitely.
questions.correct_option_text: The contract may follow its rules correctly while leaving the funds locked indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Correct execution is not the same as a complete agreement. If the stated rules provide no way out of a foreseeable impasse, the code cannot invent one. The question concerns missing business conditions, not necessarily a programming bug.

questions.question: An escrow smart contract marks an order as "paid" only when the buyer uses its pay function. A buyer skips that function and sends ETH straight to the contract's address. Assume the ETH arrives. What should the seller NOT assume?
options: That the contract's order record and its ETH balance are two separate things.
That paying correctly takes more than simply sending ETH to the address.
That the order is now marked as paid, because the ETH has arrived.
That the ETH which arrived increased the contract's balance.
questions.correct_option_text: That the order is now marked as paid, because the ETH has arrived.
questions.explanation: A contract's ETH balance and its order records are two different things. Sending ETH straight to the address does not run the pay function, so nothing marks the order as paid. The seller should check the order status in the contract, not just see that ETH arrived.

questions.question: A smart contract must stop a coupon being used twice. The developer's plan: emit a "coupon used" event each time, and have the smart contract read its old events later to reject a reuse. What is wrong with this plan?
options: Nothing: a smart contract can look up its own past events at any time, so reuse is blocked.
Smart contracts cannot read past events; the "used" marker must be stored in the contract's on-chain state.
Events are deleted after a few blocks, so the event must be emitted again in every new block.
Events are private to the developer, so the coupon holder's wallet must emit the event instead.
questions.correct_option_text: Smart contracts cannot read past events; the "used" marker must be stored in the contract's on-chain state.
questions.explanation: Events are logs for the outside world: apps and servers listen to them, but a smart contract cannot read past events while it runs. To reject a reused coupon, the smart contract must save a "used" marker in its own on-chain storage (state) and check it on every call. The event is still useful for off-chain reporting.

questions.question: A ticketing company's event listener was offline for an hour, but NFT purchases continued to settle. How can it recover the missed purchase notifications?
options: Have the token issuer delete the affected blocks and run the sales again.
Ask purchasers to repeat the settled purchases so new events are generated.
Read only current token balances, which necessarily reconstruct every missed purchase event.
Query the relevant past on-chain logs and process the missing events.
questions.correct_option_text: Query the relevant past on-chain logs and process the missing events.
questions.explanation: The course distinguishes live listening from searching past events through a node. The listener's outage does not erase settled transactions or their logs. Recovery can replay missed records, with appropriate controls against duplicating the company's off-chain actions.

questions.question: An app's smart contract address and customer balances stay the same, but an authorised upgrade changes the code it delegates to. Why can the app's effective behaviour change?
options: The network permits anyone holding a token to replace the code behind its address.
Customer balances are copied into every newly deployed contract on the same chain.
An unchanged address means the observed behaviour must come only from a wallet display bug.
A proxy can keep the state-facing address while delegating execution to new implementation logic.
questions.correct_option_text: A proxy can keep the state-facing address while delegating execution to new implementation logic.
questions.explanation: A proxy separates the address and state users interact with from the implementation logic it delegates to. An authorised upgrade can therefore change effective rules without changing that user-facing address. The upgrade authority is a material part of the trust model.

questions.question: An analyst inspects a token's proxy address and finds only forwarding logic. What should the analyst inspect next to understand the token's actual operations and control?
options: The oldest token transfer, because the first holder determines all later functions.
The wallet's display symbol, because it specifies which implementation must be used.
The implementation it currently delegates to and the authority permitted to upgrade it.
The proxy's ETH balance, because forwarding code changes according to that balance.
questions.correct_option_text: The implementation it currently delegates to and the authority permitted to upgrade it.
questions.explanation: Forwarding logic alone is not the complete application. For a proxy-based token, the current implementation and the upgrade controls determine important behaviour. Looking at only the wrapper can miss powers such as minting, pausing or address restrictions in the operative system.

questions.question: A company holds an issuer-controlled stablecoin in its own wallet. The token's smart contract permits the issuer to freeze specified addresses. Does holding the wallet's keys remove that token-level control?
options: Yes; any token held outside a bank becomes governed only by the wallet software.
No; every token transfer always requires both an issuer signature and a holder signature.
No; key custody and the token contract's transfer restrictions are separate controls.
Yes; issuer restrictions apply only while tokens remain in an exchange account.
questions.correct_option_text: No; key custody and the token contract's transfer restrictions are separate controls.
questions.explanation: Self-custody gives the company control over its signing credentials. It does not remove restrictions built into an issuer-controlled asset. The company can possess the key while the token's rules prevent a transfer from the specified address.

questions.question: A company authorises a purchasing smart contract to spend up to a stated allowance of one ERC-20 token. Which description best fits that authorisation?
options: It transfers ownership of every asset in the wallet to the purchasing contract.
It gives the spender authority across every ERC-20 token, not just the token granting approval.
It grants a token-specific spending permission without handing over the wallet's private key.
It lets the spender sign unrelated transactions in the owner's name without a separate permission.
questions.correct_option_text: It grants a token-specific spending permission without handing over the wallet's private key.
questions.explanation: An ERC-20 approval can authorise a spender within the token contract's allowance rules. It is not the same as disclosing the owner's private key or granting control over all unrelated assets. The spender's powers and the allowance still deserve careful assessment.

questions.question: A club's access check uses current ownership of its transferable membership NFT. A member sells that NFT and holds no other membership token. What should the unchanged access rule do at the next check?
options: Deny the seller and recognise the new holder, subject to any other stated conditions.
Continue admitting the seller because access was permanently attached to the first wallet.
Deny both wallets until the NFT is reissued by the club's original deployer.
Admit both wallets because the token retains a complete transfer history.
questions.correct_option_text: Deny the seller and recognise the new holder, subject to any other stated conditions.
questions.explanation: Under the stated rule, the membership right follows current token ownership, not the fact that someone once owned the token. Transferability changes who can satisfy the gate. Other club eligibility rules could matter, but the scenario excludes additional membership holdings.

questions.question: A university issues non-transferable achievement tokens on a transparent public chain. Does preventing token transfers make the associated public records private?
options: Yes; non-transferable records are automatically encrypted for the graduate.
No; transfer restrictions do not by themselves hide visible token records.
No; privacy requires making every achievement token transferable first.
Yes; only transferable assets appear in public block explorers.
questions.correct_option_text: No; transfer restrictions do not by themselves hide visible token records.
questions.explanation: Non-transferability restricts movement between holders. Confidentiality concerns who can learn the recorded information. These properties are independent: a non-transferable credential can still expose public associations or metadata unless privacy is designed separately.

questions.question: A watch buyer receives the product's authenticity NFT, but the physical watch remains with the seller. Which conclusion would be unjustified?
options: That the buyer may hold the token while another person holds the watch.
That the token's ownership record can show a transfer to the buyer's address.
That business processes must link the physical item and its digital record.
That physical custody of the watch has actually passed to the buyer.
questions.correct_option_text: That physical custody of the watch has actually passed to the buyer.
questions.explanation: A digital twin can record rights or provenance under a defined arrangement. Its transfer is not physical delivery. The business must maintain the connection between the unique item, custody, records and any legally enforceable rights.

questions.question: An event issues unique NFT tickets, but its door system never records whether a ticket has already been used. Why can uniqueness alone be insufficient to prevent repeated admission?
options: Uniqueness prevents two owners, so repeated scans by the same owner require no additional check.
One genuine ticket can be presented repeatedly unless the admission process tracks use.
A unique token permanently binds admission to its first buyer, regardless of any later transfer.
The transfer history alone enforces one entry even if admission never changes any use status.
questions.correct_option_text: One genuine ticket can be presented repeatedly unless the admission process tracks use.
questions.explanation: A unique token identifies a ticket; it does not by itself implement every business rule about redemption. A one-entry policy also needs a reliable check and update of use status, plus appropriate presentation/holder checks. Uniqueness and consumption are separate requirements.

questions.question: A professional certificate should prove that one specific person earned it. Why is a freely transferable token a poor choice for that kind of credential?
options: A transferable token cannot show which organisation issued it.
Transferring the token automatically changes the issuer's record of who passed.
The person who earned it always stays the holder, even after the token is sold.
It can be sold or sent to someone who never earned the certificate.
questions.correct_option_text: It can be sold or sent to someone who never earned the certificate.
questions.explanation: A credential should stay with the person who earned it. If the token can be freely sold or sent, the new holder has the token but never earned the qualification, so it no longer proves "this person earned it". That is why non-transferable ("soulbound") tokens suit diplomas, while resellable tokens suit things like tickets.

questions.question: A gold token offers fast, reliable on-chain transfers while bars remain in a custodian's vault. What dependence remains despite that transfer efficiency?
options: A common wallet interface makes gold-token issuers legally responsible for one another's reserves.
Fast settlement makes physical reserves optional because market demand supplies the backing.
On-chain token ownership alone establishes immediate physical possession of allocated bars.
The token still depends on its physical backing and enforceable custody and redemption arrangements.
questions.correct_option_text: The token still depends on its physical backing and enforceable custody and redemption arrangements.
questions.explanation: Tokenisation can change how claims transfer without eliminating the physical custody and redemption arrangements behind them. Quantity, entitlement and enforceability remain relevant. An efficient digital transfer is not proof that the underlying bars exist or can be delivered to the holder.

questions.question: A building is represented by many small fund-interest tokens. Which feature does splitting those interests into small units not establish by itself?
options: The ability to express ownership claims in units smaller than the entire fund interest.
A right to redeem each token immediately for cash or a physical slice of the building.
The need to specify what economic rights each unit actually represents.
The possibility of recording different holders' units in a token register.
questions.correct_option_text: A right to redeem each token immediately for cash or a physical slice of the building.
questions.explanation: Fractionalisation concerns the size of the recorded claim. Redemption, cash availability, sale procedures and rights in the property depend on the legal and operational arrangement. Small units do not make an indivisible building automatically redeemable on demand.

questions.question: A private loan is represented by transferable tokens. The borrower later cannot repay. Which statement best describes the effect of tokenisation on that credit problem?
options: A loan stops carrying credit risk once its ownership is represented by a token.
The original token deployer must automatically repay every holder from its own wallet.
On-chain transferability means the borrower no longer owes repayment to the eventual holder.
A transferable digital claim can still suffer losses when the borrower defaults.
questions.correct_option_text: A transferable digital claim can still suffer losses when the borrower defaults.
questions.explanation: Tokenisation represents a claim; it does not guarantee the resources needed to honour it. Faster transfers or programmable servicing do not remove the borrower's ability to default. Holders still need to understand underwriting, recovery and their actual rights.

questions.question: A stablecoin issuer says reserves remain sufficient in total value, but access to part of them is temporarily blocked. Redemptions slow and the token trades below its target. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Difficulty accessing reserves can pressure the peg without itself proving a permanent reserve shortfall.
A token cannot trade below its target while its ledger continues validating transfers.
Sufficient total reserve value guarantees that redemptions must remain immediately available.
A below-target market price proves that every reserve asset has already disappeared.
questions.correct_option_text: Difficulty accessing reserves can pressure the peg without itself proving a permanent reserve shortfall.
questions.explanation: Reserve value, reserve availability and market price are distinct. A liquidity or access problem can disrupt redemption and confidence even before any permanent loss is established. Conversely, an issuer's statement about value is not independent proof of complete backing.

questions.question: Most assets deposited in a lending pool are currently lent to borrowers. Several depositors request withdrawals at once. Why might immediate withdrawal be limited despite adequate collateral values?
options: Every withdrawal must wait until all borrowers have repaid all outstanding loans.
A collateralised loan requires the lender to keep the borrowed asset entirely unspent.
Depositors lose their ownership claims whenever any borrower draws from the pool.
Collateral backing does not mean the borrowed asset is immediately available in the pool.
questions.correct_option_text: Collateral backing does not mean the borrowed asset is immediately available in the pool.
questions.explanation: A pool can hold claims backed by collateral while having limited immediately available liquidity in the asset depositors want back. Liquidity and collateral adequacy are different. Actual withdrawal rules depend on the protocol, but sufficient collateral does not imply unlimited instant cash availability.

questions.question: A borrower adds more of the same collateral to an overcollateralised loan without increasing the debt. Prices and protocol parameters are unchanged. What is the direct effect?
options: It removes the borrower's obligation to repay the existing debt.
It guarantees the position cannot be liquidated after any future price decline.
It increases the collateral buffer against an adverse price move.
It reduces the token amount of debt even though the borrower has not made any repayment.
questions.correct_option_text: It increases the collateral buffer against an adverse price move.
questions.explanation: With unchanged prices and debt, more collateral increases the margin supporting that debt. This can reduce proximity to a liquidation threshold, but cannot guarantee safety under every later price move or protocol failure. More buffer is not elimination of risk.

questions.question: A lending app accepts a token whose value depends on another protocol. That other protocol fails, even though the lending app's own code works exactly as designed. Why can the lending app still be hurt?
options: A lending app whose code works correctly is protected from any outside token losing value.
Different contract addresses mean business risks cannot pass between the two products.
The failure matters only if both products share the same website.
An app that builds on other protocols also takes on their risks and losses.
questions.correct_option_text: An app that builds on other protocols also takes on their risks and losses.
questions.explanation: Building on other protocols ("composability") lets apps combine useful pieces, but it also passes risk along. The lending app's code can work perfectly while a token it relies on loses its value. Checking one contract on its own is therefore not a full risk check.

questions.question: A wholesaler wants to use a flash loan to pay a supplier today and repay it from customer sales next week. Why does the standard flash-loan model not provide that financing?
options: The borrowed amount is automatically converted into a long-term collateralised loan at settlement.
Repayment must complete within the same transaction, not from later business cash receipts.
Repayment can be postponed whenever the supplier's payment is irreversible.
A signed purchase order automatically lets an ordinary flash loan remain outstanding.
questions.correct_option_text: Repayment must complete within the same transaction, not from later business cash receipts.
questions.explanation: A flash loan can supply temporary liquidity within one atomic transaction. It cannot leave principal outstanding until next week's physical-business cash receipts. The financing horizon, not simply the absence of collateral, makes the proposed use incompatible with the stipulated model.

questions.question: An oracle has five independently operated reporting nodes, but all five obtain a price from the same external API. What risk is not removed by the number of operators?
options: Independent operators make the quality of their shared external input irrelevant to the result.
The five nodes cannot reach any common value because their organisations differ.
A wrong or compromised common data source can affect all five reports.
Any individual operator can necessarily replace all other operators' signing keys.
questions.correct_option_text: A wrong or compromised common data source can affect all five reports.
questions.explanation: Operator independence and source independence are different. Five organisations repeating one compromised input do not provide five independent observations of reality. The business must examine dependencies behind the reports as well as the aggregation rule and operator count.

questions.question: A risk team adds heavy time-smoothing to reduce the effect of a brief manipulated price spike. What trade-off should it examine during a genuine sudden price collapse?
options: The filtered price may react slowly to a real change in collateral value.
Once enough reporters sign an average, timeliness no longer matters for collateral liquidation.
Averaging eliminates the need to specify how old a usable price is allowed to be.
A longer average guarantees that every future liquidation occurs at a profitable price.
questions.correct_option_text: The filtered price may react slowly to a real change in collateral value.
questions.explanation: A filter can make a transient disturbance less influential while also delaying response to genuine changes. Those are two effects of using historical information. Oracle design requires balancing manipulation resistance with timeliness rather than treating smoothing as a complete cure.

questions.question: Crop insurance pays according to rainfall at a named regional gauge. The gauge reports accurately, but a covered farm gets very different rainfall. What risk remains despite accurate reporting?
options: The chosen measurement can differ from the loss the farmer actually experiences.
The difference proves the blockchain's transaction ordering must have been manipulated.
Accurate reporting requires the contract to ignore the named gauge and use the farmer's claim.
A valid oracle report makes every farm in the region experience the same rainfall.
questions.correct_option_text: The chosen measurement can differ from the loss the farmer actually experiences.
questions.explanation: A correctly reported external measure can still be an imperfect proxy for the intended business risk. The contract's data definition and coverage need to be understood separately from the oracle's reporting integrity. Accurate inputs do not guarantee a good match to an individual customer's loss.

questions.question: A DAO's published rule requires both a participation quorum and a majority of votes cast. Most votes cast favour a proposal, but participation is below quorum. What follows under that rule?
options: The treasury should execute first and verify whether the participation condition was met afterward.
The majority cancels the quorum because those who abstained accepted the outcome.
The proposal has not met the stated conditions for approval.
It passes if supporters own more tokens than any single opponent, regardless of participation.
questions.correct_option_text: The proposal has not met the stated conditions for approval.
questions.explanation: A quorum sets a minimum participation condition; a majority condition sets a support threshold within the relevant vote count. Satisfying one does not imply satisfying the other. The question states both as necessary, so the proposal is not approved.

questions.question: A DAO holds an advisory token vote off-chain. Its treasury only moves when three named multisig signers approve the payment on-chain. A proposal wins the advisory vote. What does winning that vote alone NOT do?
options: Show that most of the voting token holders support the proposal.
Make it final on-chain: no money moves until the three signers sign.
Give the three signers a clear signal of what token holders want.
Produce a recorded result that members can point to in later discussions.
questions.correct_option_text: Make it final on-chain: no money moves until the three signers sign.
questions.explanation: In this DAO the token vote only signals what members want. It does not move money and it is not final settlement: nothing happens on-chain until the three multisig signers sign the payment. To see who really controls the treasury, look at who can execute the transaction, not at who won the vote.

questions.question: A treasury multisig lists a sub-DAO wallet as one signer. Why is the top-level signer list insufficient to identify every person who can influence a treasury payment?
options: A smart-contract wallet cannot ever act as a signer for another wallet.
The sub-DAO wallet has its own approval rules and controllers that must also be examined.
Every member of the sub-DAO automatically receives a full individual top-level signing power.
The top-level treasury becomes permissionless whenever one signer is another contract.
questions.correct_option_text: The sub-DAO wallet has its own approval rules and controllers that must also be examined.
questions.explanation: A named signer can itself represent another decision structure. Understanding effective control requires following that structure to its own rules and authorised participants. Counting the top-level entries alone can hide relevant layers of influence or dependency.

questions.question: A DAO wants a guardian to stop new lending during an emergency, but not to withdraw treasury assets. Which design best expresses that separation?
options: Route every treasury payment through the guardian so it can interrupt new lending when needed.
Give the guardian every treasury key and rely on a public promise not to spend.
Give the guardian the right to change its own permissions before each pause.
Give the guardian a specific pause permission without a treasury-transfer permission.
questions.correct_option_text: Give the guardian a specific pause permission without a treasury-transfer permission.
questions.explanation: A role can be limited to specified functions. Granting a pause power need not imply granting custody or arbitrary withdrawal authority. The relevant question is what the implemented access controls permit, not merely the guardian's title or assurances.

questions.question: A DAO offers exit with a proportional share of the tokens in its treasury. Most treasury value is in illiquid investment tokens. What should a departing member not assume?
options: That the received assets may retain their own liquidity and redemption constraints.
That the exit can be defined as a transfer of a proportional token basket.
That the treasury's composition matters when evaluating the practical exit right.
That the exit necessarily delivers immediate cash equal to the quoted portfolio value.
questions.correct_option_text: That the exit necessarily delivers immediate cash equal to the quoted portfolio value.
questions.explanation: Receiving a share of assets differs from receiving instantly spendable cash. An exit mechanism can deliver the promised basket while leaving the member exposed to its illiquidity or restricted redemption. Exit rights should be evaluated alongside the assets they actually return.

questions.question: A token permits voting on protocol parameters. Why does that feature alone not establish a legal right to dividends from the organisation?
options: Every on-chain voting right is legally equivalent to an ordinary company share.
Voting functionality does not by itself define or grant that financial entitlement.
Dividend rights depend only on whether the voting token is transferable.
Dividend rights arise when the turnout on a token-weighted proposal exceeds its quorum.
questions.correct_option_text: Voting functionality does not by itself define or grant that financial entitlement.
questions.explanation: A token's implemented voting power and any financial or legal rights are distinct features. The latter depend on the instrument's actual terms and applicable structure. A governance label alone does not establish a share of profit or a company-law entitlement.

questions.question: A DAO counts balances at a published past snapshot for a particular vote. An investor acquires tokens after that snapshot. Why might those tokens not add voting weight for this vote?
options: Newly acquired tokens count automatically if their seller has not yet cast a vote.
The rule measures eligibility at the earlier snapshot, not at the time of the new purchase.
A snapshot prevents the token from being transferred until the proposal executes.
Current balances always replace the snapshot because token ownership is transferable.
questions.correct_option_text: The rule measures eligibility at the earlier snapshot, not at the time of the new purchase.
questions.explanation: A snapshot defines which historical state determines voting weight. Current ownership can differ from the recorded eligibility used for that proposal. This limits some short-term borrowing strategies, but the question concerns the timing rule itself rather than assuming every governance attack is prevented.

questions.question: A formal analysis establishes that an insurance smart contract never pays more than its available token balance. Which conclusion would be unjustified?
options: That the contract's coverage and payout rules meet customers' actual insurance needs.
That a precisely specified property can be assessed independently of marketing claims.
That the meaning of the chosen property matters when interpreting the result.
That checking a property is different from proving every desirable product characteristic.
questions.correct_option_text: That the contract's coverage and payout rules meet customers' actual insurance needs.
questions.explanation: Verification concerns specified properties under stated assumptions. A bound on payments does not prove adequate coverage, truthful inputs or fair terms. A contract can satisfy that property while still being a poor insurance design.

questions.question: A team starts with a reviewed token library, then adds custom transfer restrictions and a new administrative function. What assurance conclusion is justified?
options: The review remains complete if the added functionality is accurately described in the marketing.
The reviewed foundation helps, but the additions and their interactions need their own assessment.
The complete application inherits a review of every new function automatically.
Only new functions need review; their interactions with inherited functions cannot affect security.
questions.correct_option_text: The reviewed foundation helps, but the additions and their interactions need their own assessment.
questions.explanation: A reviewed component is useful evidence about that component and version. It does not automatically cover later custom logic, configuration or interactions. The resulting system should be assessed against its actual requirements and changed control surface.

questions.question: A student completes a successful token payment on a testnet using faucet funds. What business claim would that result alone fail to support?
options: That an equivalent real-value payment has settled on Ethereum mainnet.
That a test environment can exercise an interaction without funding it with mainnet ETH.
That the transaction can be inspected using the relevant testnet's block explorer.
That the student practised signing and submitting a transaction in the test environment.
questions.correct_option_text: That an equivalent real-value payment has settled on Ethereum mainnet.
questions.explanation: A testnet can demonstrate the mechanics of a transaction on that test network. Its faucet assets and state are separate from mainnet value. A successful exercise is evidence of that test interaction, not a real business payment on another network.

questions.question: A club's website asks you to sign a one-time login message with your wallet. Nothing is sent on-chain and no spending is approved. What does signing achieve?
options: It pays a network fee to record your club membership on-chain.
It gives the club permission to spend the tokens held at your address.
It moves your membership token into the club's custody for the session.
It proves you control that address, so the club can log you in.
questions.correct_option_text: It proves you control that address, so the club can log you in.
questions.explanation: Signing a login message is authentication: it proves you hold the key that controls the address, without moving funds, paying a fee or approving any spending. Always check what kind of request your wallet is showing before you sign.

questions.question: Two dashboards report different balances for the same address. One read the state before a payment block and the other read it after that block. Why does this not establish a failure of deterministic execution?
options: They queried different states, so agreement on the same inputs was not being tested.
Determinism requires matching answers only when the same RPC company serves both reads.
One provider must have used a different private key to execute the public balance query.
The newer answer is invalid unless both providers synchronise their website refresh intervals.
questions.correct_option_text: They queried different states, so agreement on the same inputs was not being tested.
questions.explanation: Deterministic execution means the same relevant starting state and inputs yield the same result. Reads at different block heights need not return identical balances. When comparing views, the business should first align the network, address and state being queried.

questions.question: A trusted issuer mistakenly signs an adult date of birth for a minor. The holder generates a valid proof that the signed age exceeds the admission threshold. Which statement about the remaining failure is correct?
options: Using a public attestation instead would itself correct the issuer's mistaken date of birth.
It lies in the issuer's incorrect input, which the proof does not independently correct.
An authentic issuer signature makes input authenticity equivalent to factual correctness.
A proof should remove the need to assess an issuer once its signature is authentic.
questions.correct_option_text: It lies in the issuer's incorrect input, which the proof does not independently correct.
questions.explanation: A proof can correctly establish a statement about an authenticated input even when that input is false about the real world. Issuer correctness remains an external trust assumption. Secure proof checking and accurate identity attestation solve different problems.

questions.question: A shielded-payment service hides internal transfer details, but only one customer deposits and one matching withdrawal appears shortly afterward. What privacy issue remains?
options: Timing and surrounding activity can make the customer a plausible match despite hidden internal details.
Independent proof verification establishes that no two visible actions involve the same customer.
The hidden transfer details become public only because the customer used a fresh address.
A valid zero-knowledge proof prevents observers from seeing any public deposit or withdrawal.
questions.correct_option_text: Timing and surrounding activity can make the customer a plausible match despite hidden internal details.
questions.explanation: Cryptographic hiding of specified data does not eliminate every clue around the transaction. With little other activity, timing and amount patterns can narrow possible links. The example illustrates an inference risk, not a guarantee that every shielded payment can be traced.

questions.question: A customer has a valid private credential from Bank A. A service accepts credentials only from its approved issuers, and Bank A is not on that list. What follows?
options: The service must accept it, because a valid proof cannot be refused.
The proof is mathematically invalid, because Bank A is not approved.
The proof is valid, but the service may still refuse Bank A as issuer.
The service must see the customer's raw identity data before deciding.
questions.correct_option_text: The proof is valid, but the service may still refuse Bank A as issuer.
questions.explanation: Reusable credentials depend on both technical verification and the relying service's trust and policy choices. A mathematically valid attestation from an unapproved issuer is not automatically an acceptable credential for every app. Reuse is possible across services that recognise the relevant issuer and conditions.

questions.question: A lender does not see a customer's exact salary, but repeatedly requests proofs against many different salary thresholds. What should a privacy assessment consider?
options: A zero-knowledge proof prevents the lender from learning whether the tested condition holds.
Separate proofs cannot reveal more in combination if each proof is individually zero-knowledge.
Threshold checks can narrow the salary only if the lender also receives the original payslip.
The combined yes-or-no results can narrow the salary range more than one proof alone.
questions.correct_option_text: The combined yes-or-no results can narrow the salary range more than one proof alone.
questions.explanation: Zero knowledge limits disclosure beyond the statement being proved and public inputs; it does not stop a verifier learning the answer to that statement. Repeated different questions can cumulatively reveal more. Privacy design therefore includes the choice and number of permitted predicates.

questions.question: A company provides a valid proof that a disclosed lending model was run correctly on committed inputs. Which conclusion would be unjustified?
options: That the result can satisfy the computation statement described by the proof system.
That the chosen model and inputs produce fair or commercially sound lending decisions.
That execution correctness is different from a judgement about the model's business suitability.
That the proof can be checked without the verifier repeating the whole model computation.
questions.correct_option_text: That the chosen model and inputs produce fair or commercially sound lending decisions.
questions.explanation: A computation proof can establish that a specified computation followed the agreed rules on the specified inputs. It does not establish that those rules are fair, the input data describes reality, or the model is commercially appropriate. Those are different claims needing their own evidence.

questions.question: A member holds one valid eligibility credential but can generate many different valid proofs from it. An anonymous vote accepts every proof without checking repeat use. What is missing?
options: A way to enforce one permitted vote per eligible member without simply counting proofs.
A rule treating different proof strings as evidence of different eligible members.
A new credential for every action, without any check connecting credentials to distinct voters.
A longer proof containing more cryptographic data about the same eligibility statement.
questions.correct_option_text: A way to enforce one permitted vote per eligible member without simply counting proofs.
questions.explanation: A valid proof establishes its eligibility statement. Many valid proofs do not necessarily represent many distinct members. A one-person-one-vote design also needs a way to recognise prohibited reuse while preserving the intended privacy; proof generation alone does not enforce uniqueness.
